04_concepts/actor-critic.title: Actor-critic
04_concepts/actor-critic.content:
Actor-critic
A parameterised policy improved by gradient ascent on J, with the multiplier on each score supplied by a bootstrapped value estimate of the policy being improved: the two branches of the course composed, one holding what the other lacks.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: both × no dynamics model, the bottom-right cell
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T}^\pi for the Critic, on sampled transitions, and none for the actor, which is improved by differentiating J directly
Failure modes addressed: 1 and 2, by one construction. The critic replaces a sampled tail with a prediction, which takes the variance out of the estimator, and the actor is moved by a gradient step, so no \max propagates through an approximator.
Course first appearance: Week 10, as the conclusion of the value and policy arc

Core idea
The value branch updates from one transition and needs a maximisation over actions it cannot afford in continuous control. The policy branch needs no maximisation and cannot form an update until an episode has finished. Each branch holds exactly what the other is short of, so composing them is forced by the two failure modes rather than chosen as a third family of algorithm. What results is Generalised policy iteration at the granularity of a single transition, with both steps approximated.
Formal definition
The actor ascends the advantage form of the Policy gradient theorem,
\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim d^\pi_\gamma,\,u\sim\pi_\theta}\big[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u\mid x)\,A^\pi(x,u)\big],
legitimate because subtracting V^\pi(x) from Q^\pi(x,u) is a Baseline (variance reduction) and changes no expectation. The critic supplies an estimate \hat A_t of that multiplier, and every stochastic method in this family is a different choice of \hat A_t from the GAE family
\hat A_t = \sum_{l\ge0}(\gamma\lambda)^l\delta_{t+l}, \qquad \delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma V_w(x_{t+1}) - V_w(x_t),
with \lambda = 0 the one-step residual and \lambda = 1 Week 9’s centred return. The two updates share the scalar \delta_t, computed once per transition. Read as a prediction error it corrects the critic; read as an advantage estimate it raises or lowers the probability of the action just taken.
Placed on the four-row table the course has kept since Week 3, actor-critic is the row where evaluation is one TD backup per transition and improvement is one gradient step on \theta, below policy iteration (exact solve, greedy step), Riccati (Lyapunov equation, gain update) and SARSA (one TD backup, \varepsilon-greedy on the table).
Anchor numbers
On the 961-cell swing-up with the policy frozen and a critic pre-fitted on 2\times10^4 transitions, turning \lambda from 1 to 0 divides the variance of one episode’s gradient estimate by 1.0\times10^{3} and raises the squared bias from 9\times10^{-5} to 0.79, a net factor of 949 in mean squared error on this problem. Over a full run with the critic learned online from zero, three arms sharing step size, seeds, budget and rollout code, both critic arms reach the Week 9 baseline’s final policy value on fewer transitions, 1.9\times fewer at \lambda=0.95 and 1.4\times at \lambda=0, and the inter-seed interquartile range at the end of training falls from 0.39 to 0.07 and 0.00. The \lambda = 0 arm also dips to -213 at 9\times10^{5} transitions and trails the baseline until 4.3\times10^{6} of the 6.2\times10^{6} available, because early in a run its critic is far worse than any of the three the frozen measurement scored. Choose \lambda for the critic that exists at that moment.
Connection to classical control
The scheme is the self-tuning regulator with the plant model replaced by a value function. An estimator is fitted to data the closed loop is producing, a design step recomputes the controller from the current estimate, and that controller changes what the estimator sees next. The classical difficulty transfers with the diagram, and the answer the theory gives is the same separation of rates that adaptive control uses. Convergence results are Two-timescale stochastic approximation results, in which the critic is given the faster step size so that from the actor’s slower vantage it looks converged.
Key limitation
The exact improvement guarantee of the Policy improvement theorem is gone, because the critic is approximate and the step is small rather than greedy. What remains is convergence to a stationary point of a non-concave J under stochastic-approximation conditions, which is weaker than the fixed-point theorems of Weeks 3 and 5 and weaker again than Week 9’s, since the critic’s error enters the direction the actor follows. The construction also puts Bootstrapping back beside Function approximation in RL, so two legs of the Deadly triad are present in every member of the family and the third is held off only while the data for an update come from the policy being updated.
Related concepts

04_concepts/advantage-function.title: Advantage function
04_concepts/advantage-function.content:
Advantage function
A^\pi(x,u)=Q^\pi(x,u)-V^\pi(x), how much better the action taken is than the policy’s own average behaviour at that state.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting. It is the multiplier every method in the policy and actor-critic rows is trying to estimate, and it belongs to no cell of its own.
Bellman object approximated: none by the object itself. Estimating it is where the choice of Bellman object enters, since a Monte-Carlo estimate involves no operator and a bootstrapped one solves a fixed point of \mathcal{T}^\pi.
Failure mode addressed: 2, indirectly. Centring by V^\pi removes a state’s offset from the multiplier, and how the remaining tail is estimated decides what is left of the variance.
Course first appearance: Week 9 as a consequence of the baseline, formalized in Week 10

Core idea
A return says how the episode went, and a decision needs to be graded against the alternative the policy would otherwise have taken at that state. Subtracting the state’s own value performs that comparison, so a positive advantage means the action beat the policy’s average behaviour there and a negative one means it did not. Every method from Week 9 onward estimates this same quantity, and they differ in how much of the observed tail they replace by a prediction.
Formal definition
For a policy \pi,
A^\pi(x,u) = Q^\pi(x,u) - V^\pi(x),
and since V^\pi(x) = \mathbb{E}_{u\sim\pi}[Q^\pi(x,u)] the advantage has zero mean under the policy at every state,
\mathbb{E}_{u\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)}\big[A^\pi(x,u)\big] = 0.
That identity is what makes A^\pi a centred object rather than a shifted value function, and it is the reason the policy gradient may be written
\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}\big[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u\mid x)\,A^\pi(x,u)\big],
which is the Policy gradient theorem with Q^\pi replaced by A^\pi, legal because a Baseline (variance reduction) changes no expectation.
Two estimators of the same quantity. Week 9 uses the observed tail, \hat A_t = G_t - V^\pi(x_t), whose conditional mean given (x_t,u_t) is A^\pi(x_t,u_t) and which requires the episode to finish. Week 10 uses one transition, \hat A_t = \delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma V_w(x_{t+1}) - V_w(x_t), whose conditional mean is A^\pi(x_t,u_t) exactly when V_w = V^\pi and otherwise carries the bias e(x_t) - \gamma\,\mathbb{E}[e(x_{t+1})\mid x_t,u_t] built from the Critic’s error e = V^\pi - V_w. The n-step form
\hat A^{(n)}_t = \sum_{l=0}^{n-1}\gamma^{\,l}\delta_{t+l} = \Big(\sum_{l=0}^{n-1}\gamma^{\,l}r_{t+l+1} + \gamma^{\,n}V_w(x_{t+n})\Big) - V_w(x_t)
interpolates between them, with a bias that decays as \gamma^{\,n} for bounded e, and GAE averages every n geometrically.
Anchor numbers
The choice of estimator is worth three orders of magnitude in variance and about one in bias. Measured at a frozen policy on the 961-cell swing-up, the Monte-Carlo estimate centred by the exact value reaches a relative gradient variance of 68, against 2.0\times10^{3} uncentred. Moving to the one-step estimate divides the variance again by 1.0\times10^{3} and raises the squared bias from 9\times10^{-5} to 0.79 with a critic fitted on 2\times10^{4} transitions, or to 7\times10^{-3} with the exact V^\pi.
Connection to classical control
The advantage is the discrete-time Hamiltonian of the problem measured relative to the current policy. In the HJB equation the object minimised over the input at each state is \ell(x,u) + \nabla V(x)^\top f(x,u), and subtracting its value at the current control leaves a quantity that is zero at the incumbent and negative in the direction of improvement. For LQR with V^\pi(x) = x^\top P x the advantage is quadratic in u with Hessian 2(R + \gamma B^\top P B), so the policy improvement step of the Riccati iteration is the exact minimisation of the advantage and a policy-gradient step is an inexact one.
Key limitation
A^\pi is defined relative to the current policy, so it is a moving object during training and an estimate of it is stale as soon as the actor has stepped. It also carries no information about states the policy does not reach, and it is never observed. Every use of it in this course is an estimate, and the two available estimators trade the variance of a sampled tail against the error of a value function, with no setting that avoids both.

04_concepts/baird's-counterexample.title: Baird's counterexample
04_concepts/baird's-counterexample.content:
Baird’s counterexample
A seven-state problem on which semi-gradient TD with linear features, off-policy data and bootstrapping diverges, built so that every alternative explanation is removed by construction.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no dynamics model, as the falsifier for the guarantees of that cell
Failure mode addressed: none; it is the evidence that failure mode 1 exists
Course first appearance: Week 7

Core idea
The construction removes each excuse in turn. Every reward is zero, so V^\pi = 0 everywhere and the feature matrix represents that answer exactly at w = 0, which rules out approximation error. The behaviour policy makes the state distribution uniform, which rules out starved states. The divergence appears in the noise-free expected update, which rules out sampling noise. What remains is the mismatch between the distribution weighting the fit and the policy defining the backup.
Formal definition
Seven states, two actions, eight weights, \gamma = 0.99, with V_w(i) = 2w_i + w_8 for the six upper states and V_w(7) = w_7 + 2w_8. The behaviour policy takes the dashed action with probability 6/7 and the target policy always takes the solid one, giving importance ratios \rho \in \{0, 7\}. The expected semi-gradient update is the linear iteration
w \leftarrow w + \alpha\,(b - Aw), \qquad A = \Phi^\top D\,(I - \gamma P)\,\Phi,
in which D weights states by their frequency in the data while P describes the transitions of the policy being evaluated. Under off-policy weighting two eigenvalues of A have negative real parts, -0.239 and -0.022; under on-policy weighting they stay at or above zero. The measured run grows from 12 to 8.8\times10^{64} over 6\times10^4 transitions, and the expected update grows by 1.0024 per step.
Connection to classical control
The expected update is the forward-Euler discretisation, at step \alpha, of \dot w = b - Aw. Its equilibrium w^\star = A^{-1}b is asymptotically stable exactly when every eigenvalue of A has positive real part, and the discrete iteration inherits that condition for small enough \alpha. An eigenvalue at -0.239 is therefore an unstable mode with growth factor 1 - \alpha\lambda = 1.0024 per expected update, which is the number the run measures. Reducing \alpha scales the exponent and leaves its sign alone, so it postpones the departure without preventing it, which is the whole point of the eigenvalue panel.
Key limitation
The example establishes the absence of a general guarantee. It says nothing about the empirical behaviour of any particular algorithm on any particular problem, and its approximator is linear with eight weights, so the mechanism is the triad rather than nonlinearity. Convergent off-policy methods with linear features exist, among them gradient-TD (Sutton et al., 2009) and emphatic TD (Sutton et al., 2016), and neither is developed in this course.
Related concepts

04_concepts/bandit-problem.title: Bandit problem
04_concepts/bandit-problem.content:
Bandit problem
The MDP with its state space, transition kernel and discount deleted: K actions with fixed unknown reward distributions, which is the smallest object in which “my choice determines my data” can still be asked.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no dynamics model, and it approximates no Bellman object, because with no successor state there is nothing to bootstrap from
Failure mode addressed: it isolates the exploration failure mode by removing every other difficulty
Course first appearance: Week 4

Core idea
Week 4 identifies two difficulties at once: the Bellman operator can no longer be evaluated, and our actions determine what we observe. The first has a clean answer, sample and average, developed in Week 5. The second is entangled with delayed rewards, credit assignment and state coverage inside a full MDP, so the standard move is to delete everything except the difficulty of interest. What survives the deletion is a set of actions, a reward signal, and the loop in which knowledge changes after every pull while the environment does not.
Formal definition
At each round t = 1,\dots,T the learner selects an arm a_t \in \{1,\dots,K\} and observes r_t \sim \nu_{a_t}, where each \nu_i is a fixed distribution with unknown mean \mu_i, and rewards are independent across rounds conditional on the arms chosen. Write \mu^\star = \max_i \mu_i and \Delta_i = \mu^\star - \mu_i \ge 0 for the gap of arm i. Only the reward of the selected arm is observed, which is called bandit feedback.
Three features carry the weight: the distributions are fixed, so pulling does not move a state; the feedback is bandit feedback, which is where the statistical content lives; and the horizon T counts decisions, so trials are the only resource spent.
Connection to classical control
A bandit is the \gamma = 0 case of the problem the rest of the course studies. Its estimate \hat\mu_i is \hat Q(x,a) at the only state there is, and its update \hat\mu \leftarrow \hat\mu + \alpha(r - \hat\mu) becomes the TD update \hat V(x) \leftarrow \hat V(x) + \alpha(r + \gamma \hat V(x') - \hat V(x)) the moment a successor state is restored. In control terms it is a pure experiment-design problem with the dynamics switched off, which is why the classical analogue is A/B testing and sequential design rather than regulation.
Genuine bandit problems do occur in robotics: selecting among K pre-tuned controllers or gain sets for a task that resists accurate modelling, choosing among grasp or insertion primitives where each attempt succeeds or fails, and deployment-time A/B testing across a fleet where every robot-hour is expensive.
Key limitation
Everything deleted returns with the state: delayed consequences and credit assignment (Week 5), coverage, since the states worth visiting sit behind sequences of correct actions (Weeks 6 to 7), and irreversibility, since an arm can always be abandoned after one pull while a robot on its back may have no admissible action that stands it up (Week 13). Bandit theory is a deep field and this course takes three algorithms and one lower bound from it: the vocabulary of exploration is what should survive to Week 15.

04_concepts/baseline-(variance-reduction.title: Baseline (variance reduction)
04_concepts/baseline-(variance-reduction.content:
Baseline (variance reduction)
Any function b(x) of the state alone, subtracted from the return in a policy-gradient update, which leaves the expected gradient exactly where it was and centres the multiplier so that actions better than the state’s typical outcome are pushed up.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: a policy × no dynamics model. A baseline holds a value estimate and keeps the method in the policy row, because the row rule asks whether that estimate solves a fixed-point equation and this one is fitted by regression on observed returns.
Bellman object approximated: none. b_w predicts no prediction of its own, which is the distinction Week 10 gives up when the baseline becomes a critic.
Failure mode addressed: 2, high variance in policy optimisation. It reduces the variance and does not remove it.
Course first appearance: Week 6 as the gap the hand trace exposes, formalized in Week 9

Core idea
On a plant with a negative stage cost every return is negative, so every sampled action is pushed down, including the best one available. Learning then proceeds only because better actions are pushed down less, which means the comparison between two actions happens across episodes instead of inside one. Subtracting the state’s typical return restores the comparison to where it belongs, and it costs nothing, because the score of a policy has zero mean at every state and therefore annihilates anything that is known once the state is known.
Formal definition
A baseline is any b:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}. The estimator
\hat g(b) = \sum_t \gamma^{t}\,\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u_t\mid x_t)\,\big(G_t - b(x_t)\big)
satisfies \mathbb{E}[\hat g(b)]=\nabla_\theta J for every such b, because the term it adds at a state is -b(x)\,\mathbb{E}_{u\sim\pi_\theta}[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u\mid x)] = -b(x)\nabla_\theta 1 = 0. The condition has one form that survives contact with practice. The quantity subtracted may depend on the state and may depend on \theta, and it may not depend on the sampled action. Writing s_t=\gamma^t\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u_t\mid x_t), the mean of s_t(G_t-b) is free of b, so minimising the variance is minimising the second moment and gives
b^\star = \frac{\mathbb{E}\big[\|s_t\|^2 G_t\big]}{\mathbb{E}\big[\|s_t\|^2\big]},
a return average weighted by how hard each step pushes on the parameters. Second moments of the score are not estimated in practice, so the standard choice drops the weighting and takes the plain conditional mean b(x)=V^\pi(x)=\mathbb{E}[G_t\mid x_t=x]. Two properties follow. A conditional mean is the solution of a least-squares problem, so b_w is fitted by regressing on returns the episodes already produced, with no new data. And the centred multiplier G_t-V^\pi(x_t) estimates the Advantage function A^\pi(x_t,u_t)=Q^\pi(x_t,u_t)-V^\pi(x_t).
Anchor numbers
Measured at a frozen policy on the 961-cell swing-up with five torques, reported as \mathrm{Var}(\hat g)/\|\mathbb{E}\hat g\|^2 for one episode. The estimator ladder runs 4.3\times10^{3} with the whole trajectory return on every step, 2.0\times10^{3} for the reward-to-go form, and 68 once returns are centred by the exact time-indexed value. Sweeping a constant b through the reward-to-go estimator gives 7.4\times10^{2} at b=\mathbb{E}[G]=-326 and 3.0\times10^{2} at the optimal constant b^\star=-216, worth 6.8\times against b=0, while a state-dependent b(x)=V^\pi(x) reaches 1.8\times10^{2}, worth 11.3\times. The best constant is not the mean return, since b^\star weights returns by \|s_t\|^2 and the steps where the score is large are the steps where the policy is most committed. Over a full run of 60\,000 episodes at \alpha=3\times10^{-5} with ten seeds, the baseline reaches plain REINFORCE’s final policy value using 5.4\times fewer transitions, 1.2 million against 6.5 million, and the inter-seed spread at the end of the budget falls from 3.5 to 0.4 in policy value. Variance removed from an estimator shows up as agreement between runs that differ only in their seed.
Connection to classical control
Centring a measurement by its expected value before feeding it to an estimator is the standard move of removing a known bias term so that the residual carries the information. The closer analogue is the control variate of Monte-Carlo simulation, where a quantity with known mean and positive correlation with the estimand is subtracted to shrink the spread without touching the target. The choice b=V^\pi is the control variate that a controls audience would guess, since it is the deterministic part of the return predicted by the state, and what survives the subtraction is the part attributable to the action taken and the tail that followed it.
Key limitation
Centring removes the offset between a state’s typical return and zero. It leaves untouched the spread of G_t around V^\pi(x_t), which comes from the transitions and the later actions of the same episode, and 68 is the floor that measurement reaches even with an exact time-indexed value function. A relative variance of 68 still means dozens of episodes per update. Reducing the residual requires replacing the observed tail by a prediction and accepting bias, which is what Week 10 does by changing the target in the regression step from the observed return to r_{t+1} + \gamma\,b_w(x_{t+1}). That single substitution turns b_w into a Critic and moves the method into the bottom row of the Unifying diagram. One further caveat belongs to the algorithm rather than to the identity. Fitting b_w on the very episode in which it is used couples it to G_t, so the estimator is exactly unbiased only for a baseline built from earlier episodes. The correlation is small and shrinks with the regression step size, and it should not be heard inside the word unbiased.

04_concepts/bayes-adaptive-mdp.title: Bayes-adaptive MDP
04_concepts/bayes-adaptive-mdp.content:
Bayes-adaptive MDP
The exploration problem stated exactly: augment the physical state with the posterior over the unknown model, and the resulting process is Markov, has a Bellman equation, and has an optimal policy that trades exploration against exploitation correctly.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × model unknown, written as a model-known problem over an enlarged state
Failure mode addressed: it dissolves failure mode 4 in principle and is unusable in practice, which is why the practical rules exist
Course first appearance: Week 4

Core idea
The Week 3 answer to what counts as a state is whatever makes the process Markov, and Week 4 takes that at its word. The pair (x_t, b_t) of physical state and posterior is Markov by construction, because the posterior update is a deterministic function of the previous posterior and the newest observation. Dynamic programming then applies with no approximation anywhere, and the optimal policy probes exactly as much as probing is worth. The three practical rules of Week 4 are three cheap collapses of the same belief, to a point estimate, to a bound, and to a single sample.
Formal definition
Take
s_t = (x_t,\ b_t), \qquad b_t = \text{posterior over the unknown model given the history } \mathcal{D}_t,
and solve the ordinary Bellman equation on this augmented state. The value function is defined over pairs of a state and a distribution, so the belief lives in a space of probability measures and dynamic programming over it searches a tree that branches on every possible observation at every step, with the branching factor compounding with depth. Closed-form solutions exist in a handful of cases: Gittins indices solve the independent-arm bandit exactly, and LQG with known noise covariances is solvable when the state is the only unknown. Neither survives contact with a robot, since the Gittins construction depends on independent arms and no dynamics, and the LQG result assumes the plant matrices are known.
Connection to classical control
This is Dual control written as a dynamic program, and it is the object Feldbaum was describing in 1960. The construction is also the one used for partially observed systems, with the belief taken over the state instead of over the model, which is the reading Week 12 develops for POMDP problems. Adaptive control’s usual escape is to refuse the augmentation and apply Certainty equivalence to the posterior mean, keeping the estimator healthy by persistent excitation instead of by optimising over the belief.
Key limitation
The state space is the wall. Converting a finite-dimensional problem into one whose state is a probability measure is exact and computationally out of reach on anything the size of a robot, so this concept works in the course as the statement of what the cheap rules approximate rather than as a method anyone runs. It also gives no error bound on those approximations, so knowing the exact formulation says nothing about how much the collapse costs on a given instance.
Related concepts
Dual control | Exploration-exploitation tradeoff | Thompson sampling | UCB | Epsilon-greedy | POMDP | MDP | Certainty equivalence | Curse of dimensionality

04_concepts/bellman-equation.title: Bellman equation
04_concepts/bellman-equation.content:
Bellman equation
The principle of optimality expressed as a fixed-point equation: the value of a state equals the immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state under optimal behavior.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram: foundational — underlies all cells
Failure mode addressed: none (this is the problem statement, not a solution method)
Course first appearance: Week 1

Core idea
The Bellman equation decomposes the infinite-horizon optimization problem into a one-step recursion. Instead of optimizing over all future trajectories, you need only find a function V^* that is consistent with its own one-step lookahead. This is the control-theoretic principle of optimality expressed as an operator fixed point.
Formal definition
Bellman optimality equation (discrete-time stochastic):
V^*(s) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a) \left[ r(s, a, s') + \gamma V^*(s') \right]
Equivalently, in operator form: V^* = \mathcal{T} V^*, where \mathcal{T} is the Bellman optimality operator.
This is a claim, not a definition. V^* is defined as the supremum of the expected return over all policies, a statement about what performance is achievable that says nothing about consistency between neighbouring states. That the supremum satisfies the equation above, and that acting greedily with respect to V^* recovers an optimal policy, are theorems (proved in Week 3). The distinction starts to matter from Week 7, where approximate value functions satisfy the equation only approximately: the value induced by a policy and a function that approximately satisfies the Bellman equation are then different objects.
Bellman evaluation equation (for a fixed policy \pi):
V^\pi(s) = \sum_{a} \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a) \left[ r(s, a, s') + \gamma V^\pi(s') \right]
Connection to classical control
LQR solves the Bellman equation analytically for linear-quadratic problems: the value function is quadratic (V^*(x) = x^\top P x) and the Riccati equation is the Bellman equation in closed form. The HJB equation is the continuous-time analogue.
The Bellman operator \mathcal{T} is a \gamma-contraction in the sup-norm (Banach fixed-point theorem), guaranteeing that value iteration V_{k+1} = \mathcal{T} V_k converges geometrically to V^*.
Key limitation
Exact solution requires knowing the transition model P(s' \mid s, a) and reward r. When the model is unknown, we need sample-based approximations (TD learning, Q-learning). When the state space is large or continuous, we need Function approximation in RL.
Related concepts

04_concepts/bellman-operator.title: Bellman operator
04_concepts/bellman-operator.content:
Bellman operator
The right-hand side of the Bellman equation read as a map on functions: (\mathcal{T}V)(x) = \max_u \mathbb{E}_w[r + \gamma V(f)], whose unique fixed point is V^*.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — the object every row of the diagram is measured against (“which Bellman object does this method approximate?”)
Failure mode addressed: none; its inexact application is failure mode 1 (instability, Week 7)
Course first appearance: Week 1 (asserted); contraction proved Week 3

Core idea
The decisive move is to stop reading the Bellman equation as an equation about numbers and read it as a map on functions. Optimality then becomes a fixed-point condition, V^* = \mathcal{T}V^*, rather than a search over trajectories or policies, and fixed points of contractions we know how to find, by iterating from anywhere (Value iteration).
Formal definition
For any bounded V : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R},
(\mathcal{T}V)(x) := \max_{u \in \mathcal{U}(x)} \mathbb{E}_w\Big[r(x,u,w) + \gamma\,V\big(f(x,u,w)\big)\Big],
which maps bounded functions on \mathcal{X} into themselves. \mathcal{T} is a \gamma-contraction in the sup-norm,
\|\mathcal{T}V - \mathcal{T}V'\|_\infty \le \gamma \|V - V'\|_\infty,
so Banach’s fixed-point theorem gives existence, uniqueness and geometric convergence in one stroke. The only non-obvious ingredient is |\max_u \phi(u) - \max_u \psi(u)| \le \max_u|\phi(u)-\psi(u)|; the Discount factor supplies the rest.
One backup at a single state is a fan over admissible inputs closed by the \max, and beneath each input a fan over the disturbance closed by the expectation. That is what \mathcal{T} is; one sweep is that picture applied at every x \in \mathcal{X}, hence the per-sweep cost |\mathcal{X}||\mathcal{U}||\mathcal{X}|.
The Week 3 proof is worth reading for its ingredients, because they are independent and the rest of the course loses them one at a time. The kernel forms a weighted average, which cannot enlarge the largest error. The Discount factor shrinks it, and \gamma < 1 is the only thing standing between the final line and a bare \le \|V-V'\|_\infty, which would prove nothing. The maximisation is non-expansive. Nothing else enters, in particular no controllability, no stabilisability and no distribution over states. Relaxing \gamma \to 1 costs the modulus, replacing \max by a soft maximum keeps the theorem with the same modulus, and off-policy sampling reweights the average. Composing \mathcal{T} with a projection (Week 7) touches none of the three and breaks the norm instead.
The policy-evaluation variant \mathcal{T}^\pi (no \max) is introduced in Week 3, is the first operator to be applied from samples rather than computed (TD learning, Week 5), and is the operator a critic approximates from Week 10 onward. Because it carries no maximisation it is affine in V, \mathcal{T}^\pi V = r^\pi + \gamma P^\pi V, which is what makes the Week 5 convergence argument a linear-algebra argument: the residual satisfies \mathcal{T}^\pi V - V = (I - \gamma P^\pi)(V^\pi - V), and the mean flow \dot V = \mathcal{T}^\pi V - V is exponentially stable because \gamma P^\pi has spectral radius at most \gamma. Both operators have twins on action-value functions, with the \max sitting after the expectation, over the successor’s actions:
(\mathcal{T}Q)(x,u) = r(x,u) + \gamma\sum_{x'}P(x'\mid x,u)\max_{u'}Q(x',u').
That placement is what makes the sampled version implementable without a model, since one observed transition (x,u,r,x') gives an unbiased sample of the sum and the \max is then taken over stored numbers. It is also where double DQN’s correction goes in Week 7, because a \max over noisy estimates is biased upwards even when each estimate is unbiased. Q-learning is a sampled application of \mathcal{T} in this form and SARSA of \mathcal{T}^\pi.
Connection to classical control
The same move as the discrete algebraic Riccati equation: the DARE is not derived by searching over gain matrices but written as an equation the stationary P must satisfy and then solved, often by iterating the Riccati recursion to its fixed point. \mathcal{T} makes the same move for a general nonlinear system, with the fixed point living in a function space rather than in the space of symmetric matrices.
Key limitation
\mathcal{T} remains a \gamma-contraction under function approximation. Nothing about the operator changes. What breaks is that it is no longer applied exactly: each backup is followed by a projection onto the parametric family, and the composition of contraction with fit need not be a contraction. The guarantee is lost because we stopped applying the operator, not because the operator degraded. This is the precise statement behind Deadly triad and Baird’s counterexample (Week 7).
Related concepts

04_concepts/bellman-residual.title: Bellman residual
04_concepts/bellman-residual.content:
Bellman residual
The movement between successive iterates, \|V_k - V_{k-1}\|_\infty: the one quantity a running algorithm can measure, separated from the error you care about by two conversion factors that both blow up as \gamma \to 1.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — the stopping rule of every method in the value-based row
Failure mode addressed: none; it is the diagnostic that function approximation later renders unreliable
Course first appearance: Week 3

Core idea
Value iteration is stopped when the values stop moving, and that test measures the wrong thing. Three quantities are in play: the residual, which is cheap; the value error \|V_k - V^\star\|_\infty, which is what the residual is usually taken to mean; and the loss of the greedy policy extracted from V_k, which is what actually gets deployed. Each arrow between them costs a factor set by the Discount factor.
Formal definition
\|V_k - V^\star\|_\infty \le \gamma^k \|V_0 - V^\star\|_\infty \quad\text{(a priori)},
\|V_k - V^\star\|_\infty \le \frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\|V_k - V_{k-1}\|_\infty \quad\text{(a posteriori)},
\|V - V^\star\|_\infty \le \varepsilon \;\Longrightarrow\; \|V^{\pi_V} - V^\star\|_\infty \le \frac{2\gamma\varepsilon}{1-\gamma} \quad\text{(policy loss, } \pi_V \text{ greedy for } V).
Converting a residual into a policy guarantee costs the product of the last two factors: 162 at \gamma = 0.9, about 2\times10^4 at \gamma = 0.99, about 2\times10^6 at \gamma = 0.999. A residual test at \varepsilon = 10^{-3} with \gamma = 0.99 therefore certifies a policy loss of roughly 20, often larger than the value range of the whole problem.
Both bounds are worst-case, and the Week 3 three-state MDP shows how far apart they can land on one problem at one sweep. At k=3 the residual is 8.1 and the true error is 72.9; the a posteriori bound gives \tfrac{0.9}{0.1}\times 8.1 = 72.9, exactly tight, because the sup-norm error sits at the absorbing state whose value is a pure geometric series. The policy bound at the same sweep gives 18 \times 72.9 = 1312 on a problem whose values span 100, while the actual policy loss is 0, since the greedy policy is already optimal. Same problem, same sweep, one bound tight and the other off by more than a factor of a thousand.
Connection to classical control
It is the familiar gap between a residual and an error in any iterative numerical method: checking a Riccati recursion by successive differences reports how much the iterate moved, and turning that into a distance from the DARE solution needs a conditioning-style factor. Here the factor is \gamma/(1-\gamma) and it comes from the contraction modulus, which makes it computable in advance rather than estimated.
Key limitation
The bounds hold and are usually pessimistic, which makes them awkward to use and unsafe to ignore, since a run never reveals which case it is in. The practical habit the numbers suggest is to monitor the greedy policy alongside the residual and treat a policy that has stopped changing as evidence, remembering that detecting optimality without knowing \pi^\star is impossible. Under function approximation the situation degrades further: minimising a Bellman residual in a weighted \ell_2 norm no longer bounds the sup-norm error, and this is one of the threads that leads into the Deadly triad in Week 7.
Related concepts

Secondary: Williams & Baird (1993), on the residual-to-error relationship

04_concepts/bias-variance-tradeoff-in-rl.title: Bias-variance tradeoff in RL
04_concepts/bias-variance-tradeoff-in-rl.content:
Bias-variance tradeoff in RL
The depth of a target is the knob: a shallow target hands over early to a table that is currently wrong and is biased, a deep one carries more sampled reward and is noisier, and a finite sample budget prefers a point strictly between the two ends.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting — the axis along which every value estimate in the right-hand column is positioned
Failure mode addressed: it is the frame in which failure mode 2 (high variance, Weeks 9 and 10) is later priced
Course first appearance: Week 5

Core idea
Both ends of the depth axis are defensible and both are measurably worse than the middle. Bias enters only through the stored estimate that closes the target, so pushing the handover further away shrinks it geometrically. Variance enters through every sampled reward and transition the target consumes, so pushing the handover further away grows it. Nothing about this is specific to prediction: the same axis reappears in Week 10 as the choice of how much bootstrapping to put into an advantage estimate.
Formal definition
The n-step return interpolates between the two extremes,
G^{(n)}_t = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\gamma^i r_{t+i+1} + \gamma^n V(x_{t+n}),
with n=1 giving TD(0) and n=\infty giving Monte Carlo. Writing \mathcal{T}^\pi_n for the n-step evaluation operator, \mathcal{T}^\pi_n V = \sum_{i<n}\gamma^i (P^\pi)^i r^\pi + \gamma^n (P^\pi)^n V, unrolling V^\pi = \mathcal{T}^\pi_n V^\pi cancels the leading sum and leaves
\big\|\mathcal{T}^\pi_n V - V^\pi\big\|_\infty = \gamma^n\big\|(P^\pi)^n(V - V^\pi)\big\|_\infty \le \gamma^n\|V - V^\pi\|_\infty,
which is the Week 3 contraction property in a new costume: a deeper target is a target that trusts the table less. Variance moves the other way, because n sampled rewards and n sampled transitions now enter where one did before. The error after a finite budget is the sum of both contributions and its minimum is interior.
Week 9 reaches the same axis from the policy branch and holds still at one end of it. The target there is the observed return G_t, optionally centred by a baseline, so the bias is zero at both settings and the variance grows with the length of the tail the return sums over. Bootstrapping would shorten that tail and is left alone for one more week on purpose, because it is the Deadly triad ingredient that lets failure mode 1 act, and the unbiasedness of the policy-gradient estimator is what currently denies it a mechanism. Week 10 spends that property deliberately and states the price in the same breath.
Week 10 turns the same dial from the policy branch and measures both ends of it. The object averaged is an advantage estimate rather than a return (GAE), and \lambda sets how much of the episode’s tail the Critic answers for. Two results from that measurement change how the axis should be read. The bias belongs to the value function and not to the bootstrap, since with an exact V^\pi the squared bias is flat in \lambda. And the interior optimum of the prediction problem need not survive into a control problem: on the 961-cell swing-up with a frozen policy and a pre-fitted critic, the mean squared error of one gradient estimate falls monotonically to \lambda = 0, where it is 949 times smaller than at \lambda = 1, because the variance divides by 1.0\times10^{3} while the squared bias rises only from 9\times10^{-5} to 0.79. Over a full run, where the critic starts wrong and tracks a moving policy, that same \lambda = 0 estimator trails the Monte-Carlo arm until 4.3\times10^{6} of 6.2\times10^{6} transitions. The optimum moves with how wrong the estimate currently is, which makes \lambda a schedule rather than a constant.
Connection to classical control
This is the model-order and regularisation trade of system identification, moved from the space of models to the space of targets. A short prediction horizon in an identification criterion gives a low-variance fit that inherits whatever the current model already believes, and a long one is faithful to the data and noisy. The forgetting factor of recursive least squares occupies the same position for the same reason, and Week 5 makes the correspondence explicit through Eligibility traces.
Key limitation
Where the optimum falls is a property of the problem instance, the budget, the discount and how wrong the table currently is, so it is not a number to be looked up. On the Week 5 pendulum chain the best RMS error is 1.62 at \lambda = 0.5, against 2.31 at \lambda = 0 and 2.63 at \lambda = 1, and 0.5 sits below the 0.8 to 0.95 that folklore quotes. What transfers is that the optimum is interior and that it moves with the step size. Under Function approximation in RL a second bias appears that no choice of n removes, the representational bias of the function class itself, and the tidy geometric statement above stops holding.

04_concepts/bootstrapping.title: Bootstrapping
04_concepts/bootstrapping.content:
Bootstrapping
Updating an estimate towards a target that contains the estimate being learned: the property that lets a single transition carry information, and one of the three ingredients whose combination makes approximate value learning diverge.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting — it is the rule that separates the bottom two rows of the diagram
Failure mode addressed: none; it introduces the first ingredient of failure mode 1 (Week 7)
Course first appearance: Week 5

Core idea
A Monte Carlo target is assembled entirely from things the plant produced. A TD target replaces the tail of that sum with the learner’s own current estimate, which is what allows an update after one transition and what allows a continuing task to be learned at all. The same self-reference turns the estimator into a closed loop, so it needs a stability argument that an averaging estimator does not.
Formal definition
Given a fixed policy \pi, compare the two targets for V(x_t):
\underbrace{G_t = \sum_{i\ge0}\gamma^i r_{t+i+1}}_{\text{no bootstrapping}}, \qquad \underbrace{r_{t+1} + \gamma V(x_{t+1})}_{\text{bootstrapped}}.
The first is an unbiased sample of V^\pi(x_t) whatever the table holds. The second is unbiased for (\mathcal{T}^\pi V)(x_t) at the current V, and biased for V^\pi(x_t) by
h(V) = \mathcal{T}^\pi V - V = (I - \gamma P^\pi)(V^\pi - V).
The depth of the handover is a continuous knob, the n-step return and the \lambda-return, so bootstrapping is a quantity rather than a switch. See Bias-variance tradeoff in RL and Eligibility traces.
The dividing line, stated once because the course uses it three times. A quantity bootstraps when it predicts its own next prediction, so a fixed-point problem is being solved. A Monte-Carlo baseline b(x) fitted to observed returns involves no Bellman object and does not bootstrap; a critic fitted to r + \gamma \hat V(x') does. This is why REINFORCE with a baseline stays in the policy row of the Unifying diagram while PPO, whose value network is fitted on bootstrapped targets, sits in the actor-critic row despite its policy-gradient ancestry.
What bootstrapping is not responsible for (Week 10). The habit of reading “Monte Carlo is unbiased, bootstrapping is biased” as a property of the bootstrap survives contact with a great deal of material and is wrong. Writing e = V^\pi - V_w for the error of the value estimate consulted, the bias a bootstrapped target injects into an advantage estimate is e(x_t) - \gamma\,\mathbb{E}[e(x_{t+1})\mid x_t,u_t], which is zero for every \gamma and every trajectory when e \equiv 0. Week 10 measures this directly: with the exact V^\pi supplied as Critic, the squared bias of the advantage estimate is flat across the whole \lambda dial from the one-step target to the full return. What the bootstrap does is make an estimator inherit the error of the predictor it consults, and \lambda decides how much of it. The distinction is load-bearing for Week 12, where the bias of offline methods comes from data that never covered the states the value function is asked about, which is a statement about e and not about the presence of a bootstrap.
What it buys, measured. Week 6 runs both sides of that line on one plant with one table size. Q-learning moves information through the value function one transition at a time and reaches 97\% of the optimum after 7.5\times10^5 transitions; Policy gradient (REINFORCE) assembles its target from complete observed returns and is still 8.7\% short after 6.5\times10^6. The efficiency has a matching cost in Week 7, where bootstrapping is the first of the three ingredients that make approximate value learning diverge.
Connection to classical control
An averaging estimator is open-loop: it collects a record, forms a statistic, and never consumes its own output while the record is being collected. A bootstrapped estimator is closed-loop, since its current output enters its own next measurement, which is exactly why Week 5 has to produce a mean flow and bound its spectrum before claiming convergence. The trade has the shape of every open-loop against closed-loop comparison in control, with correctness easy to certify on one side and responsiveness on the other.
Key limitation
Bootstrapping is biased at every finite time, and the bias is towards whatever the table currently holds. Under Function approximation in RL the damage is worse than bias: the backup becomes a projection composed with the Bellman operator, and a projection composed with a contraction need not be a contraction in any norm the algorithm respects, so the mean flow can acquire an eigenvalue in the right half plane. The uncomfortable symmetry of Week 5 is that the property bought the method its efficiency and will be named in Week 7 as one of the three causes of divergence.

04_concepts/cpo.title: CPO
04_concepts/cpo.content:
CPO
Constrained policy optimisation: a Trust region update with a cost constraint J_C(\pi)\le d added, giving an approximate guarantee that the constraint holds at every iterate.

Stub. This concept is planted in Week 10 and formalized in Week 13.
Expand this note after Week 13’s session.

Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: both × no dynamics model, the bottom row, since it is a Trust region update carrying a critic
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T}^\pi for the critic, and the same evaluation operator again for the cost return J_C; none for the actor
Failure mode addressed: 6, reward misspecification, by moving a requirement out of the reward signal and into a constraint. It leaves failure modes 1 and 2 exactly where its actor-critic base leaves them
Course first appearance: Week 10, named on the trust-region frame and not developed; formalised in Week 13

Planted framing (Week 10)
The trust-region update bounds the change in one accumulated quantity, the policy itself, measured in KL divergence over the visited states. A method that can do that can bound the change in a second accumulated quantity by the same argument, and CPO is that observation applied to a cost signal J_C that accumulates exactly as J accumulates reward. What the construction is after is a guarantee at every iterate rather than in the limit, which is the property a robot needs and which no convergence theorem in the course has supplied so far. Week 13 develops the constrained MDP behind it and sets it against the Lyapunov-based alternative.

04_concepts/certainty-equivalence.title: Certainty equivalence
04_concepts/certainty-equivalence.content:
Certainty equivalence
For a known linear model with additive zero-mean noise, the optimal stochastic controller is the deterministic one: design as if the disturbance did not exist and the gain is unchanged. This stops being true the moment the model is what is uncertain.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational, in the model-known column
Failure mode addressed: none; its boundary is what makes exploration a topic (Week 4)
Course first appearance: Week 2

Core idea
Add process noise to the LQR problem and nothing about the controller changes. The disturbance contributes an additive constant to the cost-to-go, and a constant cannot influence a minimiser. Intuitively: the controller cannot influence a future disturbance, and its expected value is zero, so there is nothing to be gained by acting differently. This is a genuinely useful result (combined with a Kalman filter under partial measurement it gives the separation principle of LQG), and it is also the result most often remembered in a form far broader than it is true.
Formal definition
With x_{k+1} = Ax_k + Bu_k + w_k, \mathbb{E}[w_k] = 0, \mathbb{E}[w_kw_k^\top] = W, take the ansatz J_{k+1}^\star(x) = x^\top P_{k+1}x + c_{k+1}. The cross terms vanish with \mathbb{E}[w] and the pure-noise term is a constant, \mathbb{E}[w^\top P w] = \operatorname{tr}(P W), so
J_k^\star(x) = \min_u\{x^\top Qx + u^\top Ru + (Ax+Bu)^\top P_{k+1}(Ax+Bu)\} + \operatorname{tr}(P_{k+1}W) + c_{k+1}.
The minimisation is identical to the deterministic one. Hence K_k is unchanged, P_k obeys the same Riccati recursion, and only the offset moves: c_k = \sum_{j=k+1}^{N}\operatorname{tr}(P_jW). With a known non-zero mean \bar w the ansatz needs a linear term and the policy acquires a feedforward u^\star_k = -K_kx_k + v_k, though the feedback gain is still unchanged.
Where it stops being true
The result assumes A, B, Q, R are known exactly and that the only unknown is a zero-mean disturbance. When the model is uncertain the separation generally breaks, for a structural reason: an action then has two effects on the future instead of one. It moves the state (control) and it produces an observation that sharpens knowledge of the dynamics (learning). An optimal policy must trade these off, so “plan as if the current best estimate were correct” is convenient but no longer optimal.
That trade-off is called exploration, it is the subject of Week 4, and it is one of the two genuinely new ingredients RL adds to what a control engineer already knows. Several generations of adaptive-control papers carried certainty equivalence into this setting; the counterexamples are well documented.
Week 4 puts numbers on the boundary. The two effects of an input are Dual control, named by Feldbaum in 1960, and the exact treatment is the Bayes-adaptive MDP, which augments the state with the posterior and is computationally out of reach. On the scalar plant x_{k+1} = ax_k + bu_k + w_k with b unknown, the immediate cost is minimised at a moderate input magnitude while the information gain grows with magnitude (the informative term in the parameter update scales with u_k^2), so the dual-optimal input sits at an offset from the certainty-equivalent one. Every exploration rule in the course is a cheap prescription for that offset. Certainty equivalence remains the right default when the prior variance is small enough that the offset is negligible, which Exercise 4.8 asks students to measure.
Week 5 supplies a third instance, on a chain instead of a gain. Given a fixed batch and repeated sweeps to convergence, tabular TD(0) returns the value function of the maximum-likelihood empirical MDP, so it fits a model to the data and then evaluates as though the fitted model were correct. On the eight-episode two-state batch it answers V(A) = 0.75 where Monte Carlo policy evaluation answers V(A) = 0. The move is rewarded when the model class is right, which for a chain means the Markov property, and it propagates the misspecification through every bootstrapped value when the observed state omits something the plant depends on.
Connection to classical control
This is classical stochastic control, the LQG separation result. Its value in this course is as a boundary marker: it delimits exactly how far “ignore the uncertainty while planning” can be pushed, and therefore what is left for RL to be about. Every subsequent week that estimates something from data is operating outside its scope.
Key limitation
It is a statement about disturbances, not about model uncertainty; about linear-quadratic problems, not general ones; and about zero-mean noise, not heavy tails or state-dependent noise. It also says nothing about risk: it optimises an expectation, so the same controller is returned whatever the variance of the outcome.

04_concepts/closure-under-the-bellman-op.title: Closure under the Bellman operator
04_concepts/closure-under-the-bellman-op.content:
Closure under the Bellman operator
A family of functions is closed under \mathcal{T} if applying one Bellman backup to a member of the family returns another member. That single property is what gives LQR a closed form, and its loss is what makes approximate RL hard.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — it explains why the top-left cell is computable and what breaks everywhere else
Failure mode addressed: none; its absence is the root of failure mode 1 (instability under function approximation, Week 7)
Course first appearance: Week 2

Core idea
The lesson of the LQR derivation is about representation, not algebra. In Week 1, dynamic programming stored a number at every state, so one sweep cost |\mathcal{X}|. In LQR the cost-to-go is stored as a symmetric matrix: n(n+1)/2 numbers (3 for the pendulum, 10 for a four-state cart-pole), independently of how finely you would have gridded the state space. The curse of dimensionality has not been defeated; it has been side-stepped, by restricting the value function to a finite-dimensional family that the Bellman operator cannot leave.
Formal definition
Let \mathcal{F} be a family of functions. \mathcal{F} is closed under \mathcal{T} if J \in \mathcal{F} \Rightarrow \mathcal{T}J \in \mathcal{F}.
For linear dynamics and quadratic cost, \mathcal{F} = \{x^\top P x : P = P^\top \succeq 0\} is closed, and the backup on functions collapses to a map on matrices:
\mathcal{R}(P) = Q + A^\top P A - A^\top P B (R + B^\top P B)^{-1} B^\top P A, \qquad P_k = \mathcal{R}(P_{k+1}).
The recursion over functions has become a recursion over finitely many numbers. Its fixed point P_\infty = \mathcal{R}(P_\infty) is the DARE, which is J^\star = \mathcal{T}J^\star restricted to quadratics.
Why it fails almost everywhere else
Closure is fragile in exactly the ways real plants are. One nonlinearity (\sin\theta) or one input bound (|u| \le u_{\max}) is enough: for the Torque-limited pendulum the optimal cost-to-go is non-quadratic, non-smooth (it carries a ridge where two routes round the circle tie), and not available in closed form.
From Week 7 the course attempts the same idea with far richer families, neural networks. They are expressive enough to approximate realistic value functions, but they are not closed under \mathcal{T}: after one backup the result cannot be represented exactly by another network of the same form, so the backup itself must be approximated, typically by a regression step. Every consequence of that approximation (divergence, the Deadly triad, target networks as an engineering response) traces back to this lost property.
Connection to classical control
This is the honest reading of why Riccati “just works”: a structural coincidence between the linear-quadratic problem and a two-parameter function family, rather than a computational trick or a clever solver. Stating it this way makes the rest of the course legible: Function approximation in RL is the attempt to buy expressiveness at the cost of closure, and the failure modes are the bill.
Key limitation
Closure gives exactness, not tractability in general: a closed family can still be large. And it says nothing about approximation quality. A family that is not closed may still approximate J^\star well; what it loses is the guarantee that iterating the backup stays meaningful.
Related concepts

04_concepts/composition-with-classical-c.title: Composition with classical control
04_concepts/composition-with-classical-c.content:
Composition with classical control
Every method in this course is a component of a larger stack, never a solution in itself: deployed robotic systems compose learning with identification, estimation, trajectory optimisation and safety layers.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting — it is what the middle of the column spectrum means in practice
Failure mode addressed: none directly; composition is how failure modes 5 (model bias) and 6 (reward misspecification) are contained in practice
Course first appearance: Week 1; recurs in Weeks 2, 3, 11, 12

Core idea
Real robotics almost never sits at either extreme of the Unifying diagram’s columns. The normal situation is a model that is partly known and partly learned: rigid-body structure from CAD and standard identification, contact and friction not. Learning is applied to the part that is genuinely unknown, and the rest of the stack keeps doing what it already does well.
What composition looks like in practice

Classical design where insight exists: Energy shaping plus an LQR catch solves the pendulum swing-up outright (Week 2). The course’s standing message is that when you have a model and genuine physical insight, you use them. Learning becomes attractive when an accurate model or an exploitable structure is unavailable, and telling the two situations apart is part of the skill
System identification composed with learned residual dynamics (Week 11)
MPC running on a learned model: the classical structure, a learned f (Weeks 2, 11)
Learning the tail MPC guesses (Week 3): the session opens by reading MPC as dynamic programming with the tail truncated and the remainder guessed, and everything from Week 5 onward learns that remainder. The two constructions then compose, since a learned Terminal cost approximation slots into the same optimisation
Structure written into the policy class (Week 9): a squashed mean \mu_\theta(x)=u_{\max}\tanh(f_\theta(x)) carries the actuator bound by construction, shared parameters carry a symmetry, and \mu_\theta(x)=\mu_{\text{ctrl}}(x)+\Delta_\theta(x) carries a controller that already works. See Policy parameterisation
Policy search as controller tuning (Week 9): iterative feedback tuning and extremum-seeking control perturb a fixed-structure controller and step down a measured gradient, and policy gradient takes the dither from the policy’s own stochasticity. On LQR the resulting nonconvex problem is still solved globally by gradient descent (LQR policy gradient)
Residual RL: a hand-designed controller plus a learned correction (Week 12)
Imitation learning followed by RL fine-tuning: Behavioral cloning, DAgger, then improvement (Week 14)
Safety layers (Control barrier function (CBF), constrained formulations) wrapped around a learned policy (Week 13)

Connection to classical control
The composition arguments are control arguments: a residual model is only useful if the nominal model is right about the structure; a safety filter is only sound if it has a certificate; a learned terminal cost in MPC inherits the stability discussion of the terminal ingredients. Learning changes which block is fitted from data, not what the block has to guarantee.
Key limitation
Composition is not free. Each interface is a place where assumptions can be violated silently: a learned model queried outside its training distribution, or a safety filter whose certificate assumed dynamics that the learned component has changed. The course is honest about this rather than presenting hybrid stacks as a solved recipe.
Related concepts

04_concepts/contextual-bandit.title: Contextual bandit
04_concepts/contextual-bandit.content:
Contextual bandit
A bandit in which the learner observes a context before choosing, and the next context arrives independently of that choice, so it learns a policy without ever influencing what it sees next.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no dynamics model, on the rung between the Bandit problem and the MDP
Failure mode addressed: none; it isolates exploration with a state observed and the dynamics still absent
Course first appearance: Week 4

Core idea
The bandit was obtained by deleting the state, the transition kernel and the discount from the MDP, and the deleted parts can be restored one at a time. Restoring the observation of a state gives the contextual bandit, in which the learner must map contexts to actions, which is already a policy in the sense of Week 3. Restoring the arrow from the action to the successor state gives the full MDP, and that single arrow carries most of the difficulty of reinforcement learning.
Formal definition
At round t the learner observes x_t, selects a_t, receives r(x_t,a_t), and then observes x_{t+1} drawn independently of a_t. Regret is measured against the best mapping from contexts to actions, \pi^\star(x) = \arg\max_a \mathbb{E}[r(x,a)], so the benchmark is a policy and the comparison is per context. The independence of x_{t+1} from a_t removes credit assignment and removes any reason to plan, which is what keeps the analysis close to the ordinary bandit.
Connection to classical control
The robotics instance is per-situation controller selection: a supervisor reads the current task conditions, picks one of K pre-tuned controllers, and observes the outcome, with the next task arriving from the operation schedule rather than from the supervisor’s choice. Gain scheduling has the same structure with the mapping designed offline instead of learned, so a contextual bandit is a gain schedule whose table entries are filled in from data, one trial at a time.
Key limitation
Nothing here handles delayed consequences, coverage, or irreversibility, since all three enter with the action-to-successor edge that this formulation omits. Any problem in which today’s choice changes tomorrow’s situation is outside it, which covers most of what a robot does over a whole task.
Related concepts
Bandit problem | MDP | Exploration-exploitation tradeoff | UCB | Thompson sampling | Regret | TD learning

Secondary: Sutton & Barto (2018), §2.9

04_concepts/coverage.title: Coverage
04_concepts/coverage.content:
Coverage
The requirement that the data reach every state whose value is to be learned: in the tabular case, “every state visited infinitely often”, and the one assumption no quantity of data collected elsewhere can repair.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting — the binding constraint on everything in the no-model column
Failure mode addressed: none; it is the precondition whose violation becomes failure mode 3 (distribution shift, Week 12) and motivates failure mode 4 (insufficient exploration, Week 4)
Course first appearance: Week 5, as an assumption of the TD convergence theorem

Core idea
Week 4 measured how many samples it takes to know something. Week 5 adds the prior question of whether the samples arrive at all. A state that is never visited receives no update, so its entry keeps whatever value it was initialised with, and the estimate everywhere else converging beautifully does nothing for it. Once the state is back in the problem, which states get data is decided by the policy generating it, so the data set is an output of the controller rather than a given.
Formal definition
The tabular convergence theorem for TD learning assumes every state is visited infinitely often with probability 1, together with per-state step sizes satisfying
\sum_{t\,:\,x_t = x}\alpha_t(x) = \infty, \qquad \sum_{t\,:\,x_t = x}\alpha_t^2(x) < \infty \qquad \text{for every } x \in \mathcal{X}.
Both conditions are indexed by the visits to x, which is what makes them statements about the trajectory distribution the policy induces and not about wall-clock time. The asynchronous nature of the update is where the requirement comes from: only the coordinate just visited moves.
On a robot the condition is rarely satisfied. A well-tuned balancing controller visits a thin tube around the upright equilibrium and nothing else, so the value estimate inside the tube converges while the estimate outside it stays at its initialisation. Any claim made about the controller from that estimate is a claim about the tube.
Control strengthens the index set. Week 6 replaces states by state-action pairs, since the maximisation inside \mathcal{T} ranges over a whole row and an entry that is never sampled never moves. A greedy controller supplies neither condition: the pair it ranks second is never executed, so its value is never corrected and the ordering that produced the omission is self-confirming. GLIE and Epsilon-greedy are the tabular repairs. The requirement survives the move to Off-policy learning untouched, because it attaches to the data: separating the behaviour policy from the target policy frees the algorithm to learn about a policy it never runs, and it produces no evidence about a pair nobody visited.
The policy branch makes the coupling total. Week 9 weights the states of the Policy gradient theorem by the Discounted state-visitation measure of the policy being differentiated, so the data distribution is itself the object the theorem is written against. The controller produces it, and it moves at every update. A state the current policy rarely reaches receives almost no gradient, and no separate exploration mechanism exists to send it there, because the policy explores only through its own randomness. Importance sampling reweights an older experiment onto the current one and pays in variance.
Connection to classical control
This is persistent excitation, restated for a state space instead of a regressor. Recursive identification converges only if the input is rich enough that the regressor spans the parameter directions being estimated, and coverage asks the same of the visited states. The difference is where the requirement bites: persistent excitation is a condition an engineer arranges by designing the input, whereas in policy evaluation the visiting distribution is produced by the very controller under evaluation, so improving coverage means changing the object being measured.
Key limitation
Coverage is stated here as an all-or-nothing assumption, and reality is quantitative: a state visited rarely is learned slowly rather than not at all, and the useful object is a concentrability-style ratio between the visiting distribution and the distribution the answer is wanted under. Week 5 does not build that machinery. The assumption is also the hinge on which three later weeks turn. Week 6 has the data distribution move as the policy improves and states the condition on pairs, Week 7 has Experience replay work only because the distribution inside the buffer shifts slowly, Week 9 has the visiting measure appear inside the gradient itself, and Week 12 confronts a logged data set whose coverage nobody chose.
Related concepts

04_concepts/critic.title: Critic
04_concepts/critic.content:
Critic
A value estimate whose training target contains a value estimate: the Week 9 baseline with the observed return replaced by one reward plus its own prediction at the successor state.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: it is the value half of the bottom row, both × no dynamics model. On its own it approximates \mathcal{T}^\pi on sampled transitions, and it is what moves a policy-gradient method out of the middle row.
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T}^\pi, the evaluation operator of the actor’s current policy. There is no \max in it, which is the whole difference from the \mathcal{T} of Q-learning and DQN.
Failure mode addressed: 2, high variance in policy optimisation. It reintroduces the Bootstrapping leg of failure mode 1.
Course first appearance: Week 10, derived rather than defined

Core idea
Week 9 maintained b_w and fitted it to the return the episode produced, which is ordinary regression on data the plant supplied. Change what the target is built from, so that the fit consults the estimate at the successor state instead of running the episode out, and the object stops solving a least-squares problem and starts solving a fixed-point equation. The name records the result, and the change is one substitution in one line of the Week 9 algorithm.
Formal definition
A critic is a parameterised V_w:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} trained by the Semi-gradient update
w \leftarrow w + \beta\,\delta_t\,\nabla_w V_w(x_t), \qquad \delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma V_w(x_{t+1}) - V_w(x_t),
so as to approximate the fixed point of the evaluation operator of the policy being run,
(\mathcal{T}^\pi V)(x) = \mathbb{E}_{u\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}\Big[r(x,u) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}_{x'}\big[V(x')\big]\Big], \qquad V^\pi = \mathcal{T}^\pi V^\pi.
Once V_w ranges over a parameterised class, \mathcal{T}^\pi V_w need not lie in that class and the attainable target is the Projected Bellman equation V_w = \Pi\,\mathcal{T}^\pi V_w.
What the residual is worth to the actor. At V_w = V^\pi the conditional mean of \delta_t is the Advantage function,
\mathbb{E}\big[\delta_t \mid x_t,u_t\big] = Q^\pi(x_t,u_t) - V^\pi(x_t) = A^\pi(x_t,u_t),
which is what lets one transition replace a whole sampled tail. Away from that point, writing e = V^\pi - V_w for the critic’s error,
\mathbb{E}\big[\delta_t \mid x_t,u_t\big] = A^\pi(x_t,u_t) + \underbrace{e(x_t) - \gamma\,\mathbb{E}\big[e(x_{t+1})\mid x_t,u_t\big]}_{\text{the bias}}.
Three readings follow from the shape of that term. It is a difference of errors, so a critic wrong by a constant c contributes (1-\gamma)c, a state-independent quantity that the zero-mean score annihilates like any Baseline (variance reduction). The part that survives into the expected gradient is -\gamma\,\mathbb{E}[e(x_{t+1})\mid x_t,u_t], which varies with the action only through where the action leads. And it vanishes with e and with nothing else, so it does not shrink as more episodes are averaged.
Anchor numbers
Three critics for one frozen policy on the 961-cell swing-up, scored by the squared bias of the advantage estimate they support. TD(0) on 2\times10^{4} transitions leaves a sup error of 281, which is 85\% of \|V^\pi\|_\infty over the visited states; 2\times10^{5} transitions bring it to 227; the exact V^\pi comes from a linear solve. At \lambda = 0 the squared bias runs 0.79, 0.18, 7\times10^{-3} across the three, a factor of 110 between worst and best. At \lambda = 0.95 the same three give 0.31, 0.047, 7\times10^{-3}, a factor of 44, because more of the multiplier is then reward the episode actually paid. The curve for the exact critic is flat in \lambda, and the residual 7\times10^{-3} is episode truncation.
Connection to classical control
For a linear plant under a linear policy the fixed point above is the discrete Lyapunov equation P = Q + K^\top R K + (A-BK)^\top P (A-BK), whose unique positive semidefinite solution for a stabilising K is available in closed form. A critic with the quadratic parameterisation V_w(x) = x^\top P_w x, trained on transitions from that same closed loop, reaches the same P without knowing A, B, Q or R. The classical route needs the model and returns the answer in one solve; the critic needs only transitions and pays for the model in samples. Week 11 supplies the third option by identifying the model first and then solving the equation.
Key limitation
A critic buys variance and charges bias equal to its own error, so what it is worth is set by how wrong it currently is rather than by any property of the construction. It also returns the bootstrapping ingredient the policy branch had been free of, which is why two legs of the Deadly triad are present in every actor-critic method built on an approximator. The absence of the \max weakens failure mode 1 and does not remove it, since Baird’s counterexample diverges under a policy-evaluation update with no maximisation anywhere.
Related concepts

The bias of a bootstrapped advantage estimate: Schulman et al. (2016), §3

04_concepts/curse-of-dimensionality.title: Curse of dimensionality
04_concepts/curse-of-dimensionality.content:
Curse of dimensionality
Dynamic programming removes the exponential dependence on the horizon but pays for it with a whole function over the state space, whose size grows exponentially in the state dimension.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — the cost that every cell other than small tabular problems is trying to escape
Failure mode addressed: none; it is the reason function approximation is introduced, which in turn introduces failure mode 1
Course first appearance: Week 1 (quantified); developed further in Week 3

Core idea
Brute-force open-loop search costs |\mathcal{U}|^N: for ten inputs and a two-second episode at 50 Hz, 10^{100} candidate sequences. Dynamic programming costs \mathcal{O}(N|\mathcal{X}|^2|\mathcal{U}|), which removes the exponential in N entirely. The exponential has not disappeared, it has moved: the algorithm must now represent and update a function at every state, and |\mathcal{X}| grows as (bins)^{\dim x}.
Formal definition
With d state dimensions discretised into b bins each, |\mathcal{X}| = b^{d}. For a 7-DoF manipulator (position and velocity, d = 14) at b = 100, |\mathcal{X}| = 100^{14} = 10^{28}. The exchange bought by the Markov property is:













RemovedIncurred$\mathcal{U}
Week 3 turns this into arithmetic, at b = 100 bins per axis. The torque-limited pendulum (d=2) needs 10^4 cells, the cart-pole (d=4) needs 10^8 cells or about 0.8 GB, and the 7-DoF arm (d=14) needs 10^{28}. Storage is the smaller problem: one value-iteration sweep for the arm at |\mathcal{U}| = 10 costs 10^{57} backups, which is 10^{48} seconds at a billion backups per second, against 4\times10^{17} seconds since the Big Bang. Read backwards, a fixed memory budget buys a resolution b = |\mathcal{X}|^{1/d}: eight gigabytes gives 178 bins per axis for the cart-pole and 4 bins per axis for the arm. Going from 8 GB to 1 PB, five orders of magnitude, moves the wall by \Delta d = \log_{10}(1.25\times10^5)/\log_{10} 100 \approx 2.5 state dimensions.
The dimension decides, and the properties that feel like difficulty do not. The Torque-limited pendulum is nonlinear, saturated and has a non-smooth V^\star, and tabular value iteration solves it in seconds; a quadrotor is nearly linear near hover and is out of reach. Three regimes follow: linear-quadratic, where the value function is n(n+1)/2 numbers at a cost independent of |\mathcal{X}| (Closure under the Bellman operator); discretisable nonlinear, roughly d \le 4; and everything else.
Connection to classical control
LQR escapes the curse not by a better algorithm but by a representation: the quadratic ansatz reduces an unknown function to \mathcal{O}(n^2) unknown numbers, and the Bellman recursion collapses into the Riccati recursion. Every escape route in this course is a variation on that trick: restrict the function class, or stop representing the function at all. Solving the HJB equation numerically is worse, not better: a PDE in n dimensions must also resolve spatial derivatives.
Key limitation
There is no way around it, only ways through, and Week 3 prices each one by what it surrenders. Updating only visited states and sampling the successor gives up the exact expectation (Week 5), and MPC was already doing this, since it only ever evaluates a value along the trajectory it is on. Replacing the table with a parametric approximator gives up the contraction, because the backup leaves the family and the projection back into it need not contract in any norm (Function approximation in RL, Deadly triad, Week 7). Parametrising the policy and differentiating the return gives up the Bellman equation itself, so no fixed point and no error bound of the form in Bellman residual (Policy gradient (REINFORCE), Week 9). None of the three removes the exponential; they stop paying it in full. Week 7 adds the fine print on the first route. A generic fixed basis, tile coding or radial basis functions, needs b^n cells to cover n dimensions at resolution b, so the exponential has moved from the length of the table to the number of features. It is escaped only when the basis encodes a real assumption about the shape of the value function, which is what a learned representation is trying to supply.
Related concepts
Dynamic programming | Value iteration | Policy iteration | MDP | Function approximation in RL | LQR | HJB equation | Markov property | Closure under the Bellman operator | Torque-limited pendulum

04_concepts/ddpg.title: DDPG
04_concepts/ddpg.content:
DDPG
An off-policy actor-critic whose actor is a deterministic map u=\mu_\theta(x), differentiated through the critic rather than through a score function, which restores the replay buffer and all three legs of the Deadly triad at once.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: both × no dynamics model, the bottom row, on the off-policy and deterministic corner of the Design-space diagram
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T}^\pi nominally, with a maximisation hidden in the actor, since \mu_\theta is trained to ascend Q_w and therefore approximates \arg\max_u Q_w(x,u)
Failure mode addressed: 2, by removing the score function entirely, and sample efficiency through replay. It reintroduces failure mode 1 in full.
Course first appearance: Week 10

Core idea
A stochastic actor pays for its exploration twice, once in the variance of the score-function estimator and once in the samples that variance costs. Committing to a single action per state removes the score function from the gradient, which is then taken through the critic by the chain rule and needs no expectation over actions. The gradient is then an expectation over states alone, so it may be taken over any state distribution with adequate coverage, and a replay buffer becomes legal again.
Formal definition
The deterministic policy gradient is
\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\Big[\nabla_u Q_w(x,u)\big|_{u=\mu_\theta(x)}\;\nabla_\theta\mu_\theta(x)\Big],
where \rho is any state distribution with sufficient Coverage. The critic is trained by the usual bootstrapped regression on transitions drawn from a buffer, with exploration supplied externally by adding noise to \mu_\theta(x) during data collection.
TD3, the stabilised version. Three devices repair the three failures the construction invites, and each is a Week 7 device in new clothes. Twin critics with the smaller of the two used in the target counteract the upward bias of a maximisation over noisy estimates (Maximisation bias). A delayed actor, updated once per several critic updates, imposes the separation of Two-timescale stochastic approximation by construction. Target smoothing averages the target over a small perturbation of the action, which prevents the actor from exploiting a sharp spurious peak in Q_w.
Connection to classical control
The update is gradient descent on a cost through a learned model of that cost, which is the structure of any indirect adaptive scheme that differentiates a fitted criterion with respect to the controller parameters. The critic plays the part of the identified model and the actor the part of the controller being tuned, and the known hazard transfers unchanged. A controller tuned against a model is only as good as the model is where the controller is taking it, and nothing in the data collection guarantees the buffer covers that region.
Key limitation
Bootstrapping, off-policy data and function approximation are all present, and a maximisation sits inside the actor, so this is the fullest exposure to failure mode 1 in the course after DQN. The deterministic actor has no exploration mechanism of its own, which leaves failure mode 4 to an external noise process that has to be tuned per environment. Published results for DDPG are notoriously sensitive to the seed and the hyperparameters, and TD3 exists because of that record rather than because of a theoretical gap.
Related concepts

Original paper: Lillicrap et al. (2016), Continuous control with deep reinforcement learning
