04_concepts/dqn.title: DQN
04_concepts/dqn.content:
DQN
Q-learning with a neural action-value function, a replay buffer and a target network: an engineering response that makes instability under function approximation survivable without removing any ingredient of the deadly triad.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no dynamics model, the same cell Week 6 occupied, with the table replaced by a network
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T} on sampled transitions, composed with a fit onto what the network can represent
Failure mode addressed: 1, instability under function approximation, made survivable rather than solved
Course first appearance: Week 7

Core idea
Control needs an action-value function, because reading a greedy action out of V requires a one-step lookahead through the model while \arg\max_u Q_\theta(x,u) needs only the learned parameters. Writing the last layer explicitly, Q_\theta(x,u) = w^\top\phi_\psi(x,u), shows what the network changes relative to Week 7’s linear theory. The feature map now has parameters of its own, so the representation is learned together with the value function instead of designed in advance. The rest of the algorithm is the Week 6 loop with two objects inserted, Experience replay between acting and learning and a Target network outside the gradient.
Formal definition
One gradient step on a squared TD error with the target held fixed,
L_t(\theta) = \bigl(y_t - Q_\theta(x_t,u_t)\bigr)^2, \qquad y_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma\max_b Q_{\theta^-}(x_{t+1},b),
with transitions collected \varepsilon-greedily into a buffer \mathcal{D}, minibatches drawn uniformly from it, and \theta^- \leftarrow \theta every C gradient steps. On Atari the original settings were |\mathcal{D}| = 10^6, C = 10^4 and batch size 32. All three triad ingredients are visible in one line. The target contains the learner’s own estimate, it is greedy while the data are not, and the entries have been replaced by a parametric function.
Connection to classical control
Freezing \theta^- for C steps is a two-time-scale separation. Between synchronisations the labels are fixed, so the fast loop minimises an ordinary regression loss, and the slow loop performs one approximate Bellman backup when it refreshes them. Adaptive control uses the same device, letting a fast loop approximately settle before a slow loop changes the problem it is solving. The analogy stops short of a guarantee, since the regression is nonconvex, the inner loop is truncated, and the target is only approximately separated from the parameters being fitted. Choosing between a designed basis and a learned one is also the identification choice of Week 11, where rigid-body mechanics supplies the structured part and a learned residual takes what the physics does not explain.
Key limitation
There is no theorem at the end. Measured on the Week 6 pendulum chain against J^\star = -123.1, full DQN reaches -125.8, the run without replay reaches -145.4 after passing through -219.9, and the run without a target network ends at -128.5 having passed through -140.6, so instability shows in the worst policy of a run long before it shows in the last one. The learned values sit 7.7 above the true value of the policy they induce (Maximisation bias). The maximum in the target needs a finite action set, which is one of the two arguments for the policy branch of Week 9. Sample cost stays large, roughly 3\times10^4 transitions here against 7.5\times10^5 for the tabular method, and about 5\times10^7 frames per Atari game, some 58 days of continuous interaction for a robot sampling at 10 Hz. The cheap diagnostic is to track \max_{x,u}|Q_\theta| against R_{\max}/(1-\gamma), since a value function an order of magnitude beyond the scale its own rewards permit is diverging whatever the return curve is doing.

04_concepts/deadly-triad.title: Deadly triad
04_concepts/deadly-triad.content:
Deadly triad
Bootstrapping, off-policy data and function approximation: each safe alone, each safe in any pair, and admitting divergence when all three are combined.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no dynamics model, once the table is replaced by parameters
Failure mode addressed: this is failure mode 1, instability under function approximation
Course first appearance: Week 7

Core idea
Each ingredient entered the course for a reason argued at the time. Week 5 took Bootstrapping because it cut the variance of Monte-Carlo returns; Week 6 took off-policy targets so that data collected under any behaviour policy could teach the greedy one; Week 7 took Function approximation in RL because a robot-sized state space has no table. Every pair is safe, with linear features wherever approximation is one of the two. Tabular Q-learning bootstraps off-policy and converges, on-policy TD with linear features bootstraps under approximation and converges, and regression onto Monte-Carlo returns is off-policy approximation with no Bellman object anywhere. The three together admit problems on which the iterate leaves every bounded set.
Formal definition
The Bellman operator is untouched. \mathcal{T} and \mathcal{T}^\pi are the Week 3 operators, with the same fixed points and the same sup-norm contraction proofs. What the parametric method actually iterates is a backup followed by a fit, \Pi_\mu\mathcal{T}^\pi or \Pi_\mu\mathcal{T}, and the projection is nonexpansive only in the norm the data impose. On-policy data make \mu = d_\pi, which is the one weighting in which P^\pi is also nonexpansive, so the composition contracts (Projected Bellman equation). Off-policy data weight the projection by d_b while the backup still belongs to \pi, the alignment is gone, and the expected update
w \leftarrow w + \alpha(b - Aw), \qquad A = \Phi^\top D\,(I - \gamma P)\,\Phi
can acquire eigenvalues with negative real part. Baird’s counterexample puts them at -0.239 and -0.022.
Counting the legs, method by method (Week 10). The list is an accounting device and the count is what a method may be held to. Policy gradient (REINFORCE) with a Monte-Carlo baseline holds none of the three, which is why failure mode 1 has no mechanism to act through there. An on-policy Actor-critic holds two, bootstrapping and approximation, and holds the third off only by discarding every batch after the update that used it. DDPG, SAC and every method with a replay buffer hold all three, which is why their stabilisation machinery is the Week 7 machinery under new names. The arithmetic also fixes what “weaker” means. A critic’s operator is \mathcal{T}^\pi, linear in V once the policy is fixed, where Q-learning’s \mathcal{T} carries a \max that selects for approximation error instead of averaging it out. Removing the maximisation removes one amplifier and leaves the mechanism intact, since Baird’s counterexample is a policy-evaluation update with no maximisation anywhere.
Connection to classical control
The diagnosis matters more than the phenomenon, since it says where to look for a repair. A student who leaves believing that function approximation damages the Bellman equation will look in the wrong place. The equation and its contraction are intact, and the loop closed around them has changed. In the linear expected-update picture this is an ordinary stability question, forward Euler on \dot w = b - Aw, with the step size setting the rate and the spectrum of A setting the sign. Reducing \alpha slows the departure and cannot prevent it.
Key limitation
The triad states the absence of a general guarantee, and three over-readings have to be blocked. It is not about neural networks, since Baird’s approximator is linear with eight weights. It does not say that deep RL fails, since it makes no claim about any particular algorithm on any particular problem. And it does not say that no convergent method exists. Gradient-TD (Sutton et al., 2009), emphatic TD (Sutton et al., 2016) and residual gradient (Baird, 1995) keep guarantees under conditions this course does not develop, the last of them at the cost of two independent successor samples from the same state. What the field does in practice is DQN, which keeps all three ingredients and adds mechanisms that make the instability slower and easier to detect.

04_concepts/design-space-diagram.title: Design-space diagram
04_concepts/design-space-diagram.content:
Design-space diagram
Three axes on which every modern actor-critic method is a point: on-policy against off-policy, stochastic actor against deterministic, and which objects the method explicitly represents.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting. It refines the bottom row of the Unifying diagram, which by Week 10 holds every deep actor-critic method and has stopped discriminating between them.
Failure mode addressed: none. It is an orientation device, and each axis names a trade whose cost is a failure mode.
Course first appearance: Week 10; recurs to Week 15, the third structural artifact of the course after the unifying diagram and the failure-modes list

Core idea
The named algorithms of deep RL are combinations of a small number of decisions taken independently, so the useful skill is placing a method that is not on the diagram rather than recalling where each name sits. Three questions do it. Does an update use data collected by the policy being updated? Does the actor output a distribution or a single action? Which objects does the method explicitly represent?
The three axes, and what each one costs






























AxisWhat it buysWhat it costsOff-policy data instead of on-policysample efficiency, an order of magnitude or more on continuous controlthe third leg of the Deadly triad, and with it the stabilisation machinery of Week 7Deterministic actor instead of stochasticvariance, since the score function leaves the gradientexploration, which then needs an external noise process, failure mode 4An entropy term in the objectiveexploration written into what is optimisedone temperature to tune, and the optimum of a modified problemA Trust region on the updatereliability of each step, independently of the parameterisationthe freedom to take a large step, and a second-order solve unless it is clipped
The placements that follow: PPO and TRPO on-policy and stochastic; SAC off-policy and stochastic; DDPG and TD3 off-policy and deterministic; CPO beside TRPO with one added constraint. All of them represent a policy and a bootstrapped value function, so the third axis reads the same for the whole group and it is the axis that put them in the bottom row in the first place.
Connection to classical control
The diagram is a design-choice table of the kind a control engineer uses when selecting an estimator and a regulator, where the entries are combinations of independent decisions and the columns record what each decision costs. It carries the same warning as those tables. It records structure and says nothing about whether a given combination will work on a given plant, which is a question about the plant.
Key limitation
Placing a method on the diagram predicts nothing about its performance, its sample cost or its behaviour on hardware. The measured differences between the points on it are frequently smaller on standard benchmarks than the spread induced by the seed, the reward scale or the network initialisation, so a comparison between two of these names without inter-seed bands establishes very little.

04_concepts/discount-factor.title: Discount factor
04_concepts/discount-factor.content:
Discount factor
The weight \gamma \in (0,1) applied to future reward; it makes infinite sums finite, makes the Bellman operator a contraction, and sets the effective planning horizon of the task.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — every cell inherits it
Failure mode addressed: none; a badly chosen \gamma creates a different problem than the one you meant to solve
Course first appearance: Week 1

Core idea
\gamma plays three roles that are routinely conflated. The mathematical role carries the proofs: with reward bounded by r_{\max} the return is bounded by r_{\max}/(1-\gamma), and \gamma is the contraction modulus of the Bellman operator. The engineering role is the one used when designing a task: \gamma sets how far ahead the objective actually looks. The economic role (future reward is worth less, as under an interest rate) is true but useless in robotics, so discard it first if the three blur.
Formal definition
\text{effective horizon} \approx \frac{1}{1-\gamma}\ \text{steps},
since \sum_{k\ge 0}\gamma^k = 1/(1-\gamma) and the weights \gamma^k act as a soft window of that width. (The exact mean of k under the normalised weights (1-\gamma)\gamma^k is \gamma/(1-\gamma), one less; immaterial at the values used.)

























\gamma1/(1-\gamma)wall-clock at 50 Hz0.9010 steps0.2 s0.99100 steps2 s0.9991000 steps20 s
\gamma also fixes the number of sweeps of Value iteration: reducing the initial error by a factor \eta needs k \ge \ln(1/\eta)/\ln(1/\gamma) sweeps, i.e. 44, 90 and 459 sweeps for \eta = 10^{2} at \gamma = 0.9, 0.95, 0.99. As \gamma \to 1 convergence becomes arbitrarily slow, with a perfect model and exact arithmetic. Long-horizon tasks are intrinsically expensive, independently of any learning.
Connection to classical control
\gamma is the closest analogue of the prediction horizon in receding-horizon control: both trade the fidelity of the objective against computational cost, and both raise the same question of what happens beyond the window (terminal cost in MPC, geometric truncation here). Undiscounted average-cost formulations exist in control and lose the contraction argument that all convergence results here rest on.
Key limitation
The mathematical and engineering roles pull against each other, and Week 3 makes the tension quantitative. A larger \gamma describes the far-sighted problem you meant to pose, while a smaller one converges faster and tightens every bound in Bellman residual, where the two conversion factors \gamma/(1-\gamma) and 2\gamma/(1-\gamma) multiply to about 2\times10^4 at \gamma = 0.99. Planning with \gamma_{\text{plan}} < \gamma_{\text{eval}} solves a different problem than the one being scored, and with an imperfect model that trade can favour the shorter horizon, since planning error accumulates over the effective horizon. The Week 3 challenge problem measures exactly this.
\gamma is a design parameter of the problem, not a hyperparameter to tune blindly. On a 200-step episode at 50 Hz (4 s), \gamma = 0.9 weights an end-of-episode reward by \gamma^{200} \approx 7\times10^{-10}: the task has been silently redefined into one where reaching the target is worthless. Choose \gamma from the timescale of the task first, and only then consider its effect on convergence speed.
Related concepts
Bellman equation | Bellman operator | Value iteration | Value function | MPC | Reward engineering
References

Primary: Bertsekas (2019), Ch. 1; Meyn (2022), Ch. 1
Secondary: Sutton & Barto (2nd ed.), Ch. 3

04_concepts/discounted-state-visitation-.title: Discounted state-visitation measure
04_concepts/discounted-state-visitation-.content:
Discounted state-visitation measure
d^\pi_\gamma(x)=\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t\,\mathbb{P}(x_t=x\mid x_0\sim\rho,\pi), the expected discounted number of visits to a state under a policy, and the object that weights the states in the Policy gradient theorem.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational. It describes the closed loop rather than a method, and it appears wherever a policy-based method is written in state form.
Bellman object approximated: none. It is a measure induced by the closed-loop kernel, and it satisfies a linear recursion of its own rather than an optimality equation.
Failure mode addressed: none. It is the reason failure mode 3 has a foothold in the policy branch, since the weighting moves whenever the policy does.
Course first appearance: Week 9

Core idea
The Stationary distribution of Week 7 describes where a fixed closed loop spends its time in the long run, and it is the weighting the data impose on a value fit. The discounted visitation measure answers a different question about the same closed loop, namely how much a visit is worth to the objective, with a visit far in the future discounted exactly as its rewards are. The gradient of J accumulates at every state in proportion to this quantity, which is what makes a \gamma^t-weighted rollout the right sampling scheme.
Formal definition
For an initial-state distribution \rho and a policy \pi_\theta,
d^\pi_\gamma(x) = \sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^{t}\,\mathbb{P}\big(x_t = x \mid x_0\sim\rho,\ \pi_\theta\big).
It is a measure and not a probability distribution, since it sums to 1/(1-\gamma) over \mathcal{X}. Normalising it multiplies \nabla_\theta J by the constant 1-\gamma, which is absorbed into the step size, and that is why both conventions circulate in the literature without causing visible trouble. It is never computed. Substituting the definition into the theorem and exchanging the sums gives
\sum_x d^\pi_\gamma(x)f(x) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_\theta}\Big[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^{t}f(x_t)\Big],
so running \pi_\theta from x_0\sim\rho samples the measure for free. This is the practical content of the theorem.
Connection to classical control
It is the closed-loop experiment, written as a measure. A control engineer identifying a plant while a regulator is running knows that the input is generated by the loop, so what the data can reveal depends on the controller in it, and persistent excitation is the side condition imposed to keep the experiment informative. In policy gradient the coupling is total, because d^\pi_\gamma is the experiment design and it is chosen by the policy being optimised rather than by the engineer. It also moves at every update, which is a situation closed-loop identification handles by holding the controller fixed for the duration of an experiment.
Key limitation
The measure belongs to the current policy, and that hypothesis is what makes policy-gradient methods on-policy by construction. One parameter update invalidates every stored trajectory as a sample of the right weighting, so no replay buffer is available and the data are disposable. Importance sampling recovers the correct weighting from an older policy and pays for it with a product of per-step ratios whose variance grows with the horizon. A second, quieter consequence is that states the current policy rarely reaches receive almost no gradient, so a region that matters for the final controller and is not visited early is improved slowly or not at all.

04_concepts/distribution-shift.title: Distribution shift
04_concepts/distribution-shift.content:
Distribution shift
A method is evaluated, trained, or validated on one distribution of states and deployed on another: failure mode 3 of the course taxonomy.

Stub. This concept is planted in Week 2, revisited in Weeks 7 and 9, and formalized in Week 12. Expand this note after Week 12’s session.

Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting, and binding hardest on the right-hand column, where the controller generates the data distribution and nobody chooses it
Bellman object approximated: none. It is a statement about the measure a backup is weighted by, which is why it enters the Projected Bellman equation through D and not through \mathcal{T}
Failure mode addressed: none. It is failure mode 3, and Coverage is the assumption whose violation produces it
Course first appearance: Week 2, in a purely classical setting; revisited in Weeks 7 and 9; formalised in Week 12

Planted framing (Week 2)
Its first appearance in this course is in a purely classical setting, with no learning anywhere in sight, which is the reason it is planted here. The saturated LQR law on the Torque-limited pendulum “solves 74 % of initial conditions” over a sampled box, 19 % of the low-energy band, and 0 % of the one initial condition the task actually starts from, hanging at rest. The aggregate statistic was not wrong; it was measuring a distribution of initial conditions that has nothing to do with the task.
The lesson generalises to every benchmark number quoted for the rest of the course: ask which distribution the number was averaged over before asking how large it is.
Revisited (Week 7)
Week 7 gives the mechanism a place inside the mathematics. The weighting of the projection in the Projected Bellman equation is the distribution the data have over states, the backup belongs to the policy being evaluated, and a divergence appears exactly when the two come apart (Baird’s counterexample). Experience replay survives that mismatch because a buffer refreshed by the current policy does not shift much, which is the assumption Week 12 removes.
Revisited (Week 9)
Week 9 shows the same mismatch from the policy branch. The Policy gradient theorem weights states by the Discounted state-visitation measure of the policy being differentiated, so the distribution the data carry is the distribution the theorem is written against, and it moves at every update. That is why the method is on-policy by construction and why every batch collected under an older policy has to be reweighted by Importance sampling or thrown away. Week 12 takes the case where no new batch can be collected at all.
Related concepts

04_concepts/dual-control.title: Dual control
04_concepts/dual-control.content:
Dual control
Feldbaum’s observation that every input has two effects at once, a directive effect that moves the physical state and an investigative effect that produces data about the plant, and that an optimal input must account for both.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational, and it is the reason the right-hand column exists at all
Failure mode addressed: none; it names the mechanism that makes exploration necessary
Course first appearance: Week 4

Core idea
In Weeks 1 to 3 the channel from the input to our knowledge of the plant was absent from every block diagram, because a plant that is already known has nothing left to reveal. Delete the assumption that the model is known and one arrow appears: the trajectory we choose decides which regions of the state-action space produce data, so the input shapes the posterior over the model as well as the state. Estimation and control are then coupled through the input, and the Certainty equivalence argument that separated them no longer applies.
Formal definition
For a scalar plant x_{k+1} = a x_k + b u_k + w_k with a known, b unknown with posterior mean \hat b and variance \sigma_b^2, and w_k zero-mean, one input magnitude buys two things that move in opposite directions. The immediate control cost is minimised at a moderate magnitude set by \hat b and the current state. The information gain grows with the magnitude, because the informative term in the parameter update scales with u_k^2 while the noise does not. Two competing terms with different minimisers reduce exploration to one scalar, the offset between those minimisers, and every rule in Week 4 is a prescription for choosing that offset without solving the dual problem.
Exact dual control optimises over the joint evolution of the physical state and the information state, which is the Bayes-adaptive MDP construction and is tractable in a handful of special cases only.
Connection to classical control
This is classical control. Feldbaum named the two effects in 1960 while studying adaptive regulators, two decades before reinforcement learning existed, and the intractability of the exact solution is the reason adaptive control largely proceeds by certainty equivalence with the estimator kept healthy by separate means. Persistent excitation is exactly that: a richness condition on the input, imposed as a side constraint on a controller designed for another purpose, with no accounting of what the richness costs. The composition line for Week 4 is that RL asks the costed version of a question control theory posed first.
Key limitation
Naming the two effects does not tell us how to trade them. The exact solution is out of reach on any system with a robot’s dimension, so the concept operates in this course as a statement of what the practical rules approximate rather than as a method anyone runs.
Related concepts
Certainty equivalence | Exploration-exploitation tradeoff | Bayes-adaptive MDP | Composition with classical control | Bandit problem | Model-based RL
References

Primary: Feldbaum (1960), Dual control theory I–IV
Secondary: Åström & Wittenmark, Adaptive Control, on certainty equivalence and persistent excitation

04_concepts/dynamic-programming.title: Dynamic programming
04_concepts/dynamic-programming.content:
Dynamic programming
Backward recursion that replaces one N-stage optimisation by N one-stage optimisations, producing an optimal cost-to-go function and a feedback policy at every state.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value function × dynamics model available (the top-left cell — where all of Week 1 lives)
Failure mode addressed: none; it introduces the cost that everything later tries to escape (Curse of dimensionality)
Course first appearance: Week 1

Core idea
Given the Principle of optimality, define the optimal cost-to-go J_k(x) and build it backwards from the terminal cost. Each step is a static optimisation over one input, not a trajectory optimisation: the horizon has been eliminated from the optimisation and pushed into the number of times the loop runs. The output is a feedback law at every state, not a single trajectory.
Formal definition
J_k(x) = \min_{u \in \mathcal{U}(x)} \mathbb{E}_w\Big[g_k(x,u,w) + J_{k+1}\big(f_k(x,u,w)\big)\Big], \qquad J_N(x) = g_N(x),
for every x \in \mathcal{X} and k = N-1,\dots,0. The minimiser is the optimal policy: \pi_k^*(x) \in \arg\min_u \mathbb{E}_w[g_k + J_{k+1}(f_k)].
Four properties, each of which a later method relaxes: the recursion runs backwards against physical causality; each step is a one-stage minimisation; the output is a feedback policy defined everywhere; and it is model-based in the strongest sense, since f_k, g_k and the expectation \mathbb{E}_w must all be known and computable.
Cost: \mathcal{O}(N|\mathcal{X}|^2|\mathcal{U}|) versus |\mathcal{U}|^N for brute-force open-loop enumeration, reducing to \mathcal{O}(N|\mathcal{X}||\mathcal{U}|) in the deterministic case.
Connection to classical control
For linear dynamics and quadratic cost the recursion is the finite-horizon Riccati recursion (see LQR). The quadratic ansatz J_k(x) = P_k x^\top x collapses an unknown function into finitely many numbers; that collapse is why LQR is tractable and is exactly what fails for a general nonlinear system.
Key limitation
The exponential cost in the horizon has been removed, but the difficulty has been transferred entirely into the factor |\mathcal{X}|: the algorithm must represent and update a whole function over the state space. For a 7-DoF manipulator with 100 bins per dimension, |\mathcal{X}| = 10^{28} and the method is unusable. It also requires a known model, which is exactly the assumption reinforcement learning drops.
Related concepts
Principle of optimality | Value iteration | Bellman equation | Curse of dimensionality | LQR | Value function | MPC
References

Primary: Bertsekas (2019), Ch. 1
Original: Bellman (1957), Dynamic Programming

04_concepts/eligibility-traces.title: Eligibility traces
04_concepts/eligibility-traces.content:
Eligibility traces
One scalar per state, set on a visit and decayed by \gamma\lambda every step, which routes each temporal-difference error back to the states that preceded it and thereby implements the \lambda-return online.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value function × no dynamics model — the same cell as TD learning, with the depth of the target turned into a parameter
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T}^\pi on sampled transitions, averaged over every horizon at once
Failure mode addressed: partial relief of failure mode 2 (variance), by trading it against the bias of Bootstrapping
Course first appearance: Week 5

Core idea
Choosing a single n for an n-step target discards every other n, and every one of them is a legitimate target. The \lambda-return averages them geometrically, which turns a discrete choice into one continuous knob between TD(0) and Monte Carlo policy evaluation. That average cannot be computed at time t because it contains rewards that have not arrived, so the bookkeeping is reversed: instead of asking which future rewards enter each state’s target, ask which past states each arriving reward should reach.
Formal definition
Forward view. With \lambda \in [0,1],
G^\lambda_t = (1-\lambda)\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda^{n-1} G^{(n)}_t, \qquad G^{(n)}_t = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\gamma^i r_{t+i+1} + \gamma^n V(x_{t+n}).
The weights are a proper convex combination, since (1-\lambda)\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda^{n-1} = 1. For an episode ending at T the sum truncates and the leftover weight \lambda^{T-t-1} is placed on the full return G_t. At \lambda = 0 all weight sits on n=1, giving TD(0); at \lambda = 1 all weight sits on G_t, giving Monte Carlo.
Backward view. Give every state a trace e_t(x), decayed by \gamma\lambda each step and set to 1 on a visit (the replacing convention; the accumulating variant adds 1 instead), and apply each error to every state in proportion to its trace:
e(x) \leftarrow \gamma\lambda\, e(x)\ \ \forall x, \quad e(x_t) \leftarrow 1, \qquad V(x) \leftarrow V(x) + \alpha\,\delta_t\, e(x).
A state visited three steps ago receives (\gamma\lambda)^3 of the correction.
Equivalence. With accumulating traces and the updates held to the end of the episode, the backward view reproduces the total forward-view update with targets G^\lambda_t exactly. Applied online with constant \alpha the two differ by O(\alpha^2), and the online version is what everyone runs. Replacing traces correspond to a slightly different forward view, and at \lambda = 1 they sit closer to first-visit than to every-visit Monte Carlo.
Connection to classical control
The trace is a first-order discrete-time filter with its pole at \gamma\lambda, driven by an impulse at every visit, with time constant -1/\ln(\gamma\lambda) steps. That is the exponential forgetting factor of recursive least squares answering the same question, which is how far back in time present evidence is allowed to reach. Choosing \lambda is choosing that pole, and the consequences are the ones forgetting factors always have: too close to one and stale evidence contaminates the estimate, too small and the estimator throws away information it has already paid for.
Key limitation
The best \lambda is a property of the problem instance and the sample budget, not a constant to look up. On the Week 5 pendulum chain the optimum is \lambda = 0.5 at RMS error 1.62, against 2.31 for TD(0) and 2.63 for TD(1), and it sits well below the 0.8 to 0.95 range folklore quotes. Worse for a tuning workflow, \lambda and \alpha interact: the best step size moves from 0.6 at \lambda = 0 to 0.2 at \lambda = 1, so sweeping one at a time finds the wrong pair. The traces also cost one write per state with a nonzero trace instead of one write per step, which an implementation manages by keeping a list of active states and dropping entries below a threshold.
Related concepts
TD learning | Bias-variance tradeoff in RL | Monte Carlo policy evaluation | Bootstrapping | Stochastic approximation | Discount factor | GAE | Actor-critic | Torque-limited pendulum
References

Primary: Sutton & Barto (2018), Ch. 12 (forward and backward views, and the equivalence); Ch. 7 for n-step returns
Original paper: Sutton (1988) for TD(\lambda); Singh & Sutton (1996) for replacing traces and how they differ near \lambda = 1

04_concepts/energy-shaping.title: Energy shaping
04_concepts/energy-shaping.content:
Energy shaping
Regulate a mechanical system’s total energy to the value it has at the target, rather than regulating its state: the classical swing-up solution, and the course’s standing example of what physical insight buys when you have it.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: not on the diagram — it optimises nothing, so it approximates no Bellman object
Failure mode addressed: none
Course first appearance: Week 2

Core idea
The Torque-limited pendulum cannot be driven to the upright by any law reading only the instantaneous error, because the route requires moving away from the goal. Energy shaping sidesteps the difficulty by changing the regulated variable: drive the mechanical energy E to E^{\text{top}} and the trajectory pumps itself up over successive swings, each one respecting |u| \le u_{\max}. It does not stabilise the upright by itself, because many states share the same energy, so it is switched to an LQR catch once the state enters the neighbourhood where the linear law is valid.
Formal definition
With E(\theta,\dot\theta) = \tfrac12 m\ell^2\dot\theta^2 + mg\ell(1-\cos\theta) and E^{\text{top}} = 2mg\ell, the pumping law is
u = -k\,\dot\theta\,(E - E^{\text{top}}).
For the frictionless idealisation b = 0, \dot E = \dot\theta u, so V = \tfrac12(E - E^{\text{top}})^2 gives \dot V = -k\dot\theta^2(E-E^{\text{top}})^2 \le 0; LaSalle confines the trajectory to the largest invariant set inside \{\dot\theta = 0\} \cup \{E = E^{\text{top}}\}, which is the target energy level plus the two equilibria. With the course value b = 0.1 the identity acquires a -b\dot\theta^2 term and the conclusion survives only while k outruns the dissipation.
Connection to classical control
This is a Lyapunov design, and it is a good one: a conserved quantity is identified, a candidate is built from its error, and convergence follows. It is worth keeping as the reference point for what the course is not arguing. When you have a model and genuine physical insight, use them. Learning-based methods become attractive exactly when an accurate model or an exploitable structure is unavailable, which is often but not always, and telling the two situations apart is a large part of the skill being taught.
Key limitation
Three, and they are the reasons the rest of the semester exists.

Bespoke. It needs a conserved quantity and a designer who knows the plant well enough to write it down. There is no energy identity for a manipulator making and breaking contact, and the method does not survive its loss.
It optimises nothing. Time, torque effort and clearance from obstacles appear nowhere in the law. It reaches the goal; it makes no claim about doing so well, and offers no way to trade one objective against another.
Brittle to parameters. Change the payload by 30 % and E^{\text{top}} is wrong, so the target the law drives to is wrong.

Related concepts
Torque-limited pendulum | LQR | Underactuation | Composition with classical control | MPC
References

Primary: Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics, Ch. 3
Original: the swing-up energy-pumping law is generally attributed to Åström & Furuta (2000), Swinging up a pendulum by energy control

04_concepts/epsilon-greedy.title: Epsilon-greedy
04_concepts/epsilon-greedy.content:
Epsilon-greedy
Act on the current best estimate with probability 1-\varepsilon and pull a uniformly random arm with probability \varepsilon, which ignores the uncertainty in the estimate instead of measuring it.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no dynamics model, as the exploration rule attached to a sample-average estimate
Failure mode addressed: insufficient exploration (secondary failure mode 4), addressed badly enough to expose what a good rule needs
Course first appearance: Week 4

Core idea
The rule separates the two jobs an action can do and gives each its own branch, with a coin deciding which one runs. Nothing in the exploring branch consults the data, so the arm it selects is chosen with the estimates switched off. That independence is what makes the rule trivial to implement and what caps its performance, because the pulls it spends are spent at a rate fixed before the run began.
Formal definition
Maintain the empirical mean \hat\mu_i = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{t: a_t = i} r_t, updated incrementally as \hat\mu \leftarrow \hat\mu + \alpha(r - \hat\mu) with \alpha = 1/n_i. At round t,
a_t = \begin{cases}\arg\max_i \hat\mu_i & \text{with probability } 1-\varepsilon,\\ \text{uniform on } \{1,\dots,K\} & \text{with probability } \varepsilon.\end{cases}
The exploring branch costs \frac{\varepsilon}{K}\sum_i \Delta_i per round whatever the estimates say, so
R_T \ \ge\ \frac{\varepsilon}{K}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{K}\Delta_i\Big) T,
linear in the horizon. A constant rate therefore never lets average reward reach \mu^\star. Decaying the rate as \varepsilon_t \propto 1/t makes the exploration budget \ln T, and a schedule that also leaves each arm enough pulls to resolve its gap behaves like \varepsilon_t \sim K/(\Delta^2 t), where \Delta is the smallest gap: the tuning constant is the quantity the algorithm exists to estimate.
In control (Week 6). With a state present the rule is written over the admissible actions at x,
\pi_\varepsilon(u\mid x) = \begin{cases} 1-\varepsilon + \dfrac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal{U}|}, & u \in \arg\max_b Q(x,b),\[4pt] \dfrac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal{U}|}, & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}
so every action keeps probability at least \varepsilon/|\mathcal{U}| whatever the table says, which is what makes the visitation condition of Coverage hold on a communicating chain. Two consequences follow. Decaying the rate turns the rule into a GLIE schedule and SARSA converges to Q^*. Holding it fixed leaves the algorithm converging to the fixed point of the Exploration-aware Bellman operator instead, so the exploration rate becomes part of the problem being solved. The rule survives into Week 6 for two reasons: the tabular convergence theorems are stated for it, and on a table it is enough.
Connection to classical control
The update line is the same stochastic-approximation step Robbins and Monro analysed, and it is the TD learning update with the bootstrapped term deleted. The exploration branch corresponds to injecting a fixed dither signal into a loop for identification purposes, chosen once and applied regardless of what the identification has already established, which is persistent excitation in its crudest form. Adaptive control has the same problem with the same shape: an excitation designed without reference to the cost it incurs.
Key limitation
The random branch never switches off and never looks at the data, so on hardware it keeps issuing full-magnitude actions long after its own measurements have shown them to be damaging (Safe exploration). The Week 4 experiment adds a second warning about tuning. A swept \varepsilon has a broad minimum, and \varepsilon = 0.05 beats UCB1 on that instance, yet the location of the minimum depends on the gaps and on the horizon, both unknown when the value must be chosen.
Related concepts
UCB | Thompson sampling | Bandit problem | Regret | Exploration-exploitation tradeoff | Sample complexity | Safe exploration | TD learning | SARSA | Q-learning | GLIE | Exploration-aware Bellman operator | Coverage | DQN
References

Primary: Sutton & Barto (2018), Ch. 2
Secondary: Lattimore & Szepesvári, Bandit Algorithms (2020), Ch. 6, for the explore-then-commit family and its linear-regret failure

04_concepts/experience-replay.title: Experience replay
04_concepts/experience-replay.content:
Experience replay
Storing transitions in a buffer and reusing them for later updates, which is available to any method whose update reads a single transition and does not refer to the policy that produced it.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no dynamics model, as one of the two objects DQN adds to Week 6’s loop
Failure mode addressed: 1, the correlation part of it; it deepens the off-policy mismatch that is the mechanism of the rest
Course first appearance: planted Week 6, formalized Week 7

Core idea
Consecutive transitions from one trajectory are strongly correlated, so successive gradient steps see nearly the same data, and each transition is otherwise consumed once and discarded. A buffer sits between acting and learning and decouples their rates. The batch a gradient step consumes was written across many episodes rather than in the last few milliseconds. Replay is legal here for a reason specific to Q-learning that Week 12 withdraws. The target contains the reward, the successor state, and a maximum the learner computes for itself, with no action sampled from the behaviour policy, so a transition collected under an older policy is still a valid sample of the same Bellman-optimality target. SARSA, whose target quotes the action the behaviour policy took, cannot reuse stale transitions this way.
Formal definition
A store \mathcal{D} of the most recent N transitions (x,u,r,x'), overwritten oldest-first, with each update drawing a minibatch of m of them uniformly at random. The original DQN used N = 10^6 and m = 32; the Week 7 pendulum ablation used N = 5\times10^4 and m = 32.
Connection to classical control
The buffer is a moving window of an identification data set, so the usual experiment-design questions apply. What excitation does the window contain, how old is it, and does it cover the region the controller being designed will operate in. The recency policy is what keeps the answer tied, imperfectly, to the current behaviour, in the way a forgetting factor in recursive least squares keeps an estimate tracking a plant that drifts.
Key limitation
Replay repairs correlation and deepens the mismatch it is often credited with fixing. Stored transitions come from behaviour policies earlier in training, so the distribution weighting the projection sits further from the current greedy policy’s distribution than online data would, and that mismatch is the mechanism Baird’s counterexample isolates. Its measured worth on the Week 7 pendulum chain is nonetheless the largest of the three stabilisers, -125.8 with replay against -145.4 without, on an optimum of -123.1. Replay works because the distribution inside a refreshed buffer does not shift much. Freeze the buffer, or receive a fixed log of somebody else’s operation, and that recency argument disappears while the algorithm stays syntactically identical, which is Offline RL in Week 12.
Related concepts
DQN | Target network | Q-learning | Off-policy learning | Deadly triad | Coverage | Distribution shift | Offline RL | Bootstrapping | Stationary distribution | SARSA

04_concepts/exploration-aware-bellman-op.title: Exploration-aware Bellman operator
04_concepts/exploration-aware-bellman-op.content:
Exploration-aware Bellman operator
\mathcal{T}_\varepsilon, the Bellman optimality operator of the MDP whose commanded action is replaced by a uniformly drawn admissible one with probability \varepsilon; its fixed point Q^*_\varepsilon is what SARSA converges to when exploration is held at a constant rate.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — an operator, and the object that explains why two correct algorithms disagree
Bellman object: it is one, sitting between \mathcal{T}^\pi at \varepsilon = 1 and \mathcal{T} at \varepsilon = 0
Course first appearance: Week 6

Core idea
An on-policy method evaluates whatever policy generates its data, exploration included. Holding \varepsilon constant therefore does not break the algorithm, it changes the question the algorithm answers, and the new question has a well-posed answer: which policy is best among those that keep exploring at rate \varepsilon. Writing the operator down turns a vague statement about on-policy contamination into a fixed point that can be computed exactly and compared against Q^*.
Formal definition
Taking the expectation of the SARSA target under the \varepsilon-greedy rule gives
(\mathcal{T}_\varepsilon Q)(x,u) = r(x,u) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}_{x'}\!\left[(1-\varepsilon)\max_b Q(x',b) + \frac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal{U}|}\sum_b Q(x',b)\right].
Each inner term is non-expansive in the sup norm, the bracket is a convex combination of the two with weights 1-\varepsilon and \varepsilon, and the reward cancels, so \|\mathcal{T}_\varepsilon Q - \mathcal{T}_\varepsilon W\|_\infty \le \gamma\|Q-W\|_\infty and the fixed point Q^*_\varepsilon exists and is unique. Setting \varepsilon = 0 recovers \mathcal{T}; setting \varepsilon = 1 gives the evaluation operator of the uniform random policy. The distance from the optimum is bounded by
\|Q^*_\varepsilon - Q^*\|_\infty \le \frac{\gamma\,\varepsilon}{1-\gamma}\,\Delta, \qquad \Delta = \max_x\Big(\max_b Q^*(x,b) - \tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{U}|}\textstyle\sum_b Q^*(x,b)\Big),
so a long effective horizon amplifies a fixed exploration rate.
Connection to classical control
\mathcal{T}_\varepsilon is the optimality operator of a plant with a known stochastic actuator fault, one whose commanded torque is discarded and replaced at rate \varepsilon. Under that reading, SARSA at fixed \varepsilon solves an optimal control problem exactly, for the perturbed plant. The design question it raises is familiar: a controller synthesised for the nominal plant and one synthesised for the perturbed plant are different controllers, and the second is the one to deploy when the perturbation is genuinely part of the hardware.
Key limitation
Q^*_\varepsilon is the right answer to its own question and the wrong answer to a different one. A policy that accounts for its own random torques keeps a margin away from expensive regions, and that margin is a cost the moment exploration is switched off at deployment. The operator also assumes the perturbation is exactly uniform over admissible actions at a known rate, which is a description of \varepsilon-greedy rather than of any physical fault.
Anchor numbers
On the swing-up chain with an overspeed trip, computed exactly by value iteration with no learning involved, the two fixed points separate by 5.3\% at \varepsilon = 0.05, 11.4\% at 0.10 and 22.1\% at 0.20 when executed with exploration in place, and coincide at \varepsilon = 0. Evaluated greedily instead, the same two fixed points differ by 0.8\% and in the opposite direction, -124.0 against -125.0.
Related concepts
SARSA | Q-learning | Bellman operator | Epsilon-greedy | GLIE | Value iteration | Safe exploration | Exploration-exploitation tradeoff | Certainty equivalence | Torque-limited pendulum

04_concepts/exploration-exploitation-tra.title: Exploration-exploitation tradeoff
04_concepts/exploration-exploitation-tra.content:
Exploration-exploitation tradeoff
When the model is unknown, an action buys performance and information at the same time, and the controller has to decide how much performance to spend on information it may never need.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: the right-hand column as a whole, since it is the price of having interaction as the only access to the dynamics
Failure mode addressed: introduces the exploration failure mode (numbered as secondary failure mode 4 when the taxonomy arrives in Week 7)
Course first appearance: Week 4

Core idea
Weeks 1 to 3 could evaluate the Bellman operator at any state, so the order in which states were visited was a matter of convenience. Once the only access to P and r is execution, the states at which a backup can be performed are the states actually visited, and those are chosen by the controller. What looks good gets executed, what gets executed produces data, and what produces data is what sharpens. An action that currently looks poor because of an unlucky first estimate is never revisited, and nothing in the estimator repairs that, because the defect sits in the data rather than in the fitting.
Formal definition
There is no single equation for the tradeoff itself. Its cleanest quantitative statement is the Regret decomposition on a Bandit problem,
R_T = \sum_{i=1}^{K} \Delta_i \, \mathbb{E}[n_i(T)],
which prices exploration in the same currency as performance: every pull spent gathering information about a suboptimal arm costs its gap \Delta_i, and the algorithm chooses only the counts \mathbb{E}[n_i(T)]. The exact formulation of the tradeoff is the Bayes-adaptive MDP, whose optimal policy weighs both effects correctly and cannot be computed.
Connection to classical control
Certainty equivalence is the classical answer, and it prices only the directive effect of an input: plan with the current parameter estimate as though it were correct. Adaptive control keeps that design and adds persistent excitation, a side condition asking that the input be rich enough to keep the regressor informative, chosen without reference to what the richness costs in tracking performance. Dual control is the classical name for the full problem. Reinforcement learning asks the same question with the cost attached: how much performance should be sacrificed now for knowledge that may pay later.
Key limitation
Framing exploration as a tradeoff prices information against reward and says nothing about outcomes that cannot be traded. A pull that damages hardware, or an action that moves a robot into a region no policy escapes, is not a reward shortfall to be recovered later, which is why Safe exploration adds a constraint alongside the objective rather than a term inside it.
Related concepts
Dual control | Certainty equivalence | Bandit problem | Regret | Epsilon-greedy | UCB | Thompson sampling | Safe exploration | Bayes-adaptive MDP | Sample complexity
References

Primary: Lattimore & Szepesvári, Bandit Algorithms (2020), Ch. 1
Secondary: Recht (2019), A Tour of Reinforcement Learning: The View from Continuous Control, exploration sections

04_concepts/failure-modes-of-approximate.title: Failure modes of approximate RL
04_concepts/failure-modes-of-approximate.content:
Failure modes of approximate RL
A course-specific list of six ways approximate RL breaks down, used from Week 7 onward as the organising question at the start of every theory session.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting, since a method’s cell records what it represents and this list records what goes wrong with it
Course first appearance: Week 7, at the end of the session that formalizes mode 1
Recurs: every theory session from Week 8, opening with one question, which failure mode does today’s method address?

The six failure modes
Three dominant, which drive the value, policy and actor-critic arc



































#Failure modeAddressed byWeek formalized1Instability under function approximationDQN: Experience replay, Target network, double DQN72High variance in policy optimizationMonte-Carlo baselines (Baseline (variance reduction)), then GAE and Actor-critic9, 10and mode 1 again, weakened: the actor takes a gradient step, so no \max enters103Distribution shift in dataOffline RL, Residual RL12
Three secondary, real and not what the arc is built from





























#Failure modeAddressed byWeek introduced4Insufficient explorationUCB, Thompson sampling, curiosity45Model bias in model-based methodsmodel ensembles, MBPO116Reward misspecificationControl barrier function (CBF), CMDP, reward design13
Mechanism of mode 2, as Week 9 states it
The multiplier attached to one decision in a policy-gradient update is the return over the whole remaining episode, so it carries the randomness of transitions the decision did not cause and of later actions it did not take. Two rollouts from the same state under the same policy can differ by more than a good action differs from a bad one, and the estimator cannot tell the two apart. Measured at a frozen policy on the 961-state swing-up, one episode of the reward-to-go estimator has \mathrm{Var}(\hat g)/\|\mathbb{E}\hat g\|^2 = 2.0\times10^{3}. A state-dependent baseline removes the state’s offset and buys 11.3\times, and the residual spread of G_t around V^\pi(x_t) survives it, which is what Week 10 attacks by accepting bias.
Why Week 10 highlights two modes at once
Week 10 is the first session to mark two of the six on the figure, and the mark is a claim about mechanism rather than a summary of coverage. One construction reaches both. Replacing the sampled tail of the episode by a Critic’s prediction removes the dominant source of spread from the policy-gradient estimator, which is mode 2, and it divides the variance of one episode’s estimate by 1.0\times10^{3} on the swing-up. The actor is still moved by a gradient step, so no maximisation propagates through a function approximator, which removes one amplifier of mode 1 and replaces \mathcal{T} by the milder \mathcal{T}^\pi. Neither is a repair. Mode 2 survives at a reduced level and is traded against a bias equal to the critic’s error, and mode 1 keeps two of its three ingredients, since Bootstrapping returns with the critic and Baird’s counterexample needs no maximisation to diverge. Mode 4 is untouched by the construction, and SAC is the one method in that week’s design space that addresses it, by putting an entropy term into the objective.
The caveat that travels with the list
This is not a complete taxonomy. It privileges the failure modes that organise this course, and several real ones sit outside it: non-stationarity in deployment, partial observability (POMDP, touched and not centered), multi-agent dynamics (out of scope), and reproducibility together with hyperparameter sensitivity (Week 15). A method that addresses none of the six can still be the right method for a particular robot.
What “addresses” means
The verb is weak on purpose. Week 7 makes mode 1 survivable and removes no ingredient of the Deadly triad, recovers no theorem, and each of its mechanisms is dated to a specific instability somebody observed. Tagging a method with a failure mode means that much for the rest of the course, and no more.
Related concepts

04_concepts/function-approximation-in-rl.title: Function approximation in RL
04_concepts/function-approximation-in-rl.content:
Function approximation in RL
Replacing the tabular value function with a parametric approximator: the escape from the curse of dimensionality, and the source of failure mode 1.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting, a statement about representation, and the cell a method occupies says nothing about it
Failure mode addressed: none; it introduces failure mode 1 (instability under function approximation)
Course first appearance: Week 1 as an escape route, formalized in Week 7

Core idea
Every convergence result of Weeks 5 and 6 carries one hypothesis that was never listed, since it was built into the notation. The value function is stored exactly, one independent number per state or per state-action pair, so an update writes to one entry and leaves the rest alone. Replacing the table by d \ll |\mathcal{X}||\mathcal{U}| shared parameters makes one observation reach many states, which is what a robot-sized state space requires. Generalisation and error propagation travel through that same channel, so an estimate learned at one state moves the estimates of states no data have visited.
Formal definition
Linear approximation in value space chooses a feature map \phi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^d and represents
V_w(x) = w^\top\phi(x), \qquad \mathcal{V} = \{\Phi w : w \in \mathbb{R}^d\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{X}|},
with the table recovered as the special case \phi(x) = e_x, where \Phi = I and \mathcal{V} is the whole space. A network makes the feature map itself parametric, Q_\theta(x,u) = w^\top\phi_\psi(x,u) with \theta = (\psi,w), so the representable set becomes a curved subset of \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{X}||\mathcal{U}|} instead of a subspace. The arithmetic that forces the move is the following. A 7-DOF arm has 14 state dimensions, and 31 bins per dimension give 31^{14} \approx 7.6\times10^{20} cells, about 6\times10^{25} state-action entries with five torques per joint.
Connection to classical control
This is the modelling choice of system identification, applied to the cost-to-go. A fixed basis keeps the approximation linear in its parameters, which makes least-squares methods available (LSTD) and leaves a residual that can be inspected. Physics sometimes supplies the basis outright, as in LQR, where V(x) = x^\top P x needs n(n+1)/2 numbers at any grid resolution and the family is closed under the backup. A learned parameterisation buys shapes no fixed regressor basis captures, at the cost of a nonconvex fit and weaker guarantees, and identification has long handled that trade by structuring what the physics explains and reserving flexibility for the remainder (Week 11).
Key limitation
Three prices are paid for the flexibility. The nonexpansiveness argument behind the Projected Bellman equation uses linearity at every step, so a curved family removes it and on-policy TD with a nonlinear approximator can diverge on its own, independently of any off-policy mismatch. The fit becomes a nonconvex optimisation whose result depends on initialisation, schedule and data order, with no closed-form solve. And the approximation floor \min_\theta\|Q_\theta - Q^\star\| is unknown on a real problem, so the reference point that made the linear error bound useful as a diagnostic disappears. What replaces the theory is measurement.

04_concepts/gae.title: GAE
04_concepts/gae.content:
GAE
Generalized advantage estimation: the geometric averaging of Eligibility traces applied to advantage estimates instead of returns, so that one parameter \lambda sets how much of the episode’s tail the critic answers for.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: both × no dynamics model. It is the estimator that every stochastic method in the bottom-right cell uses, and its two endpoints are the Week 9 and Week 10 multipliers.
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T}^\pi, at a depth \lambda chooses. At \lambda = 1 the value terms telescope away and no Bellman object is left.
Failure mode addressed: 2, high variance in policy optimisation, at a bias set by the Critic’s error
Course first appearance: Week 5 as the \lambda-return, applied to advantages in Week 10

Core idea
Committing to a single depth n is a hard choice, and Week 5 already solved that problem for returns by averaging every n geometrically. The same weighting applied to advantage estimates turns the depth into a continuous parameter with the one-step residual at one end and the Monte-Carlo estimate at the other. What moves along the dial is which of two errors the estimate carries, the noise of sampled rewards or the error of a value function.
Formal definition
Summing n discounted TD residuals telescopes the value terms and leaves the n-step advantage,
\hat A^{(n)}_t = \sum_{l=0}^{n-1}\gamma^{\,l}\delta_{t+l} = \Big(\sum_{l=0}^{n-1}\gamma^{\,l}r_{t+l+1} + \gamma^{\,n}V_w(x_{t+n})\Big) - V_w(x_t).
Averaging these geometrically gives
\hat A^{\mathrm{GAE}(\lambda)}_t = (1-\lambda)\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda^{\,n-1}\hat A^{(n)}_t = \sum_{l\ge0}(\gamma\lambda)^{\,l}\,\delta_{t+l},
where the second equality collects the coefficient of \delta_{t+l}: that residual appears in \hat A^{(n)}_t for every n > l, always with the factor \gamma^{\,l}, so its total weight is \gamma^{\,l}(1-\lambda)\sum_{n>l}\lambda^{\,n-1} = (\gamma\lambda)^{\,l}. Implementations compute it backwards at one multiplication and one addition per step,
\hat A_t = \delta_t + \gamma\lambda\,\hat A_{t+1}, \qquad \hat A_N = 0.
At \lambda = 0 only l = 0 survives and \hat A_t = \delta_t. At \lambda = 1 the coefficients become \gamma^{\,l}, the value terms telescope completely, and \hat A_t = G_t - V_w(x_t), which is Week 9’s centred return with V_w serving as the baseline. Fitting the critic on \hat A_t + V_w(x_t) makes it a regression onto the \lambda-return, so the actor’s dial and the critic’s target are the same choice.
Anchor numbers
Measured at a frozen policy with a frozen critic on the 961-cell swing-up, turning \lambda from 1 to 0 divides the variance of one episode’s gradient estimate by 1.0\times10^{3} and raises the squared bias from 9\times10^{-5} to 0.79, so on this problem the mean squared error of a single estimate is 949 times smaller at the one-step end. That ordering is a property of the instance. A 300-step swing-up has an enormous return variance and a tabular critic on 961 cells is accurate enough that its bias never catches up, whereas a neural critic on a continuous state space is far more wrong, which is why published continuous-control work settles near \lambda = 0.95. Over a full run, where the critic starts at zero and tracks a moving policy, the ordering reverses for most of the budget: the \lambda = 0 arm dips to -213 at 9\times10^{5} transitions and trails the Monte-Carlo baseline until 4.3\times10^{6} of 6.2\times10^{6}, while \lambda = 0.95 reaches the same final value on 1.9\times fewer transitions.
Connection to classical control
The recursion \hat A_t = \delta_t + \gamma\lambda\hat A_{t+1} is a first-order filter run backwards along the trajectory, with pole at \gamma\lambda, which is the same object Eligibility traces introduced forwards over states. Read \lambda as a forgetting factor. A value near one keeps a long memory of sampled reward and trusts the model less, a value near zero discards the sampled tail and leans on the stored estimate, and the choice is the identification trade between fidelity to data and reliance on a prior fit.
Key limitation
The bias of the estimate is not a property of \lambda alone. It is e(x_t) minus a \lambda-weighted average of \gamma^{\,n}\mathbb{E}[e(x_{t+n})], so it is set by the critic’s error and \lambda only decides how much of that error the estimator inherits. With an exact V^\pi every \lambda is unbiased, which is the measured statement that Bootstrapping is not what introduces bias. A single fixed \lambda across a training run is therefore conservative early, when the critic is still wrong, and wasteful late.
Related concepts

04_concepts/glie.title: GLIE
04_concepts/glie.content:
GLIE
Greedy in the limit with infinite exploration: the pair of conditions on a behaviour policy, infinitely many visits to every state-action pair together with an exploration rate that vanishes, under which tabular on-policy control converges to Q^*.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting — a hypothesis on the data-generating policy, not a method
Failure mode addressed: it is the tabular repair for failure mode 4, insufficient exploration, and it addresses none of the others
Course first appearance: Week 6, as the hypothesis of the SARSA convergence theorem

Core idea
A greedy controller executes the action its table currently ranks first, so a pair ranked second is never tried, never updated, and never corrected. The estimate becomes self-confirming, accurate about the trajectories it produces and uninformed about every alternative it declined. Exploration repairs that, and exploration held at a constant rate then contaminates the object being learned, so the two requirements have to be satisfied together and in the right order.
Formal definition
A sequence of behaviour policies \{\pi_k\} is GLIE when, with probability 1,

every state-action pair (x,u) \in \mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U} is visited infinitely often, and
the policies become greedy in the limit, \pi_k(u\mid x) \to \mathbf{1}\{u \in \arg\max_b Q_k(x,b)\} for every x.

The clauses do separate jobs. Clause 1 makes learning possible, by supplying infinitely many samples of every entry the maximisation will range over. Clause 2 makes the limit the right object, by removing exploration from the policy whose value is being reported. Drop clause 1 and some entries stop being learned. Drop clause 2 and the algorithm still converges, to the fixed point of the Exploration-aware Bellman operator. The schedule \varepsilon_k = 1/k satisfies both, since the harmonic series diverges and the rate still vanishes.
Connection to classical control
This is persistent excitation with a schedule attached. Adaptive control injects a dither deliberately and chooses its amplitude against the same trade, enough to identify the parameters and little enough to leave the closed loop undisturbed, and the schedule here answers the further question of how long that payment continues. The balance between the two clauses is the balance the Robbins-Monro conditions struck in Week 5 between reaching and settling, applied to the exploration rate instead of the step size.
Key limitation
GLIE describes an infinite horizon and a robot has a deadline. Every exploratory action inside that deadline is executed on hardware and charged at the moment it is taken, so the useful question on a physical system is quantitative: how much information does this exploratory torque buy, and what does it cost when it goes wrong. On the Week 6 swing-up, an action that trips the drive costs 3000 units, about twenty-four nominal swing-ups. Nothing in the GLIE conditions prices that.
Related concepts
SARSA | Q-learning | Epsilon-greedy | Exploration-aware Bellman operator | Coverage | Exploration-exploitation tradeoff | Stochastic approximation | Safe exploration | Generalised policy iteration | Regret | Torque-limited pendulum
References

Primary: Sutton & Barto (2018), Ch. 5 and Ch. 6
Original statement: Singh, Jaakkola, Littman & Szepesvari (2000), Convergence results for single-step on-policy reinforcement-learning algorithms

04_concepts/gaussian-policy-class.title: Gaussian policy class
04_concepts/gaussian-policy-class.content:
Gaussian policy class
The policy family for a continuous command that adds isotropic Gaussian noise of scale \sigma to a differentiable mean \mu_\theta(x), whose score pulls the action-space displacement u-\mu_\theta(x) back through the Jacobian of the mean.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: a policy × no dynamics model. It is the class that makes the policy row reachable for a torque command, where the value branch would need a maximisation over a continuous set at every control step.
Bellman object approximated: none. The class is the object being optimised, and no fixed-point equation is attached to it.
Failure mode addressed: none directly. Through \sigma it sets both the exploration of failure mode 4 and the estimator variance of failure mode 2, in opposite directions.
Course first appearance: Week 9

Core idea
A joint torque or a wheel speed is a point in \mathbb{R}^m, and the deterministic controller a robotics engineer would write is a map x\mapsto\mu(x) into that space. The class keeps that map, parameterises it, and adds zero-mean noise so that the policy has a density to differentiate. The mean carries the control law and the noise carries the exploration, which is the same split an identification experiment makes between the nominal input and the probing signal injected on top of it.
Formal definition
With \mu_\theta(x)\in\mathbb{R}^m differentiable in \theta and fixed isotropic covariance,
\pi_\theta(u\mid x)=\mathcal{N}\big(\mu_\theta(x),\sigma^2 I\big)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-m/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|u-\mu_\theta(x)\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),
and writing \nabla_\theta\mu_\theta(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p} for the Jacobian of the mean,
\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u\mid x)=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\big(\nabla_\theta\mu_\theta(x)\big)^{\top}\big(u-\mu_\theta(x)\big).
The update therefore moves the mean towards the action that was sampled, by an amount set by how far that action fell and by how strongly each parameter moves the mean. For a scalar action with \mu_\theta(x)=\theta the Jacobian is 1 and the score is (u-\theta)/\sigma^2, with
\mathbb{E}\big[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u\mid x)\big]=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}\big(\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u\mid x)\big)=\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^4}=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}.
Halving \sigma doubles the typical score magnitude and quadruples its variance. Structure enters through \mu_\theta and holds at every \theta. A squashed mean \mu_\theta(x)=u_{\max}\tanh(f_\theta(x)) respects the actuator bound, parameters shared across a quadruped’s four legs impose a gait symmetry, and \mu_\theta(x)=\mu_{\text{ctrl}}(x)+\Delta_\theta(x) learns a correction on top of a controller that already works.
Connection to classical control
This is a fixed-structure controller with a dither on the input. Iterative feedback tuning perturbs the parameters of such a controller, measures the closed-loop cost and steps down an estimated gradient, and extremum seeking does the same with a sinusoidal probe. The Gaussian class supplies the probe from the policy itself, and the Likelihood-ratio identity converts that randomness into an unbiased gradient rather than a finite difference. The persistent-excitation reasoning of identification transfers intact. A probe too small to move the output teaches nothing about the parameter, and here it also drives the score, so the same \sigma that stops exciting the plant stops informing the estimator.
Key limitation
The class is unimodal. If two well-separated actions are both good at a state and everything between them is bad, the mean can settle between the modes and command an action that is good at neither, which is exactly the situation a time-optimal bang-bang solution creates. A Softmax policy class over a torque grid represents both branches without difficulty, so the continuous class is not automatically the more expressive one. The support is also unbounded. Squashing the mean bounds what the policy aims at and not what it draws, so a broad policy still commands torques past u_{\max} and relies on the actuator to clip them. And exploration and estimation share one parameter, so a run in which \sigma collapses early has stopped exploring and has a badly conditioned estimator at the same time.
Related concepts
Policy parameterisation | Softmax policy class | Score function estimator | Likelihood-ratio identity | Policy gradient theorem | Policy gradient (REINFORCE) | LQR policy gradient | Torque-limited pendulum | Residual RL | Composition with classical control | Exploration-exploitation tradeoff | Safe RL | SAC
References

Primary: Sutton & Barto (2018), §13.7
On the Gaussian class in robotics: Peters & Schaal (2008), Reinforcement learning of motor skills with policy gradients
On squashed policies and the entropy coupling: Haarnoja et al. (2018)

04_concepts/generalised-policy-iteration.title: Generalised policy iteration
04_concepts/generalised-policy-iteration.content:
Generalised policy iteration
Evaluation and improvement run against each other continuously, at whatever grain size the data permits, with neither process required to finish before the other begins.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — it is the shape shared by Policy iteration, Value iteration and every tabular TD control method
Failure mode addressed: none; it is the arrangement that makes control possible when estimation error rules out exact evaluation
Course first appearance: Week 6, as the weakening of the Week 3 alternation

Core idea
Week 3 alternated in a strict order: evaluate the current policy to convergence, improve it greedily, repeat, and stop after finitely many steps. The guarantee behind that staircase is the Policy improvement theorem, and its hypothesis is that Q^\pi enters the greedy step exactly. A learner interacting with a robot never has an exact Q^\pi, so improvement acts on an estimate that is still moving, and the staircase becomes a feedback process between two approximations.
Formal definition
Three grain sizes of the same two processes, ordered by how much evaluation happens before each improvement:






























MethodEvaluation before each improvementGuaranteePolicy iterationto convergencefinite terminationValue iterationone sweep of the state spacegeometric at rate \gammaTabular TD control (SARSA, Q-learning)one transitionasymptotic, with probability 1Actor-criticone transition, with the improvement step approximated toostationary point of J, under two-timescale conditions
At the finest grain there are no sweeps left to organise and the two processes have merged into one line of code, the temporal-difference update itself. The guarantee weakens monotonically down that list, from a finite staircase to a statement that holds in the limit under GLIE and the Robbins-Monro step-size conditions.
The fourth row is Week 10’s, and it is the first in which both processes are approximated. Rows one to three keep an exact improvement step, a maximisation over a table, and weaken only the evaluation. Actor-critic replaces the maximisation by a small gradient step in a parameterised policy class, which is what makes it usable over continuous actions and what removes the last exact operation from the scheme. The Policy improvement theorem then has no hypothesis left to stand on, and the guarantee becomes convergence to a stationary point of a non-concave J under Two-timescale stochastic approximation conditions.
Connection to classical control
This is the self-tuning regulator’s block diagram. An estimator updates a plant model from the data the closed loop is producing, a design step recomputes a controller from the current estimate, and that controller changes what the estimator sees next. Generalised policy iteration is that diagram with the plant model replaced by an action-value function and the control design replaced by a maximisation. The known difficulties transfer with it, in particular that an adaptive loop can settle on a wrong model which is nonetheless consistent with the closed-loop data it generates. That is why persistent excitation appears as a hypothesis in every convergence proof in that literature, and why GLIE appears in this one.
Key limitation
Nothing here is a finite-time statement. The improvement step is taken with respect to a guess, the guess is built from data that the guess itself selected, and the theorems that repair this ask for infinitely many visits to every state-action pair. Between the first update and the limit there is no guarantee that any intermediate policy is safe, monotone, or even sensible, which is the gap the safety thread of this course occupies.
Related concepts
Policy iteration | Value iteration | Policy improvement theorem | SARSA | Q-learning | GLIE | TD learning | Epsilon-greedy | Coverage | Dual control | Certainty equivalence | Safe exploration | RL as approximate dynamic programming | Actor-critic | Critic | Two-timescale stochastic approximation

Primary: Sutton & Barto (2018), §4.6; Bertsekas (2019), Ch. 5
Adaptive-control parallel: Astrom & Wittenmark, Adaptive Control, on self-tuning regulators and persistent excitation

04_concepts/hjb-equation.title: HJB equation
04_concepts/hjb-equation.content:
HJB equation
The principle of optimality in continuous time: a partial differential equation for the optimal cost-to-go, solved backwards from a terminal condition.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value function × dynamics model available — the continuous-time reading of the same cell
Failure mode addressed: none
Course first appearance: Week 1 (orientation only; nothing later depends on it)

Core idea
Apply the Principle of optimality over a short interval \delta t, expand the cost-to-go to first order, divide by \delta t and let \delta t \to 0. The recursion becomes a PDE. This section exists so that the continuous-time literature can be read without translation friction. The course itself stays in discrete time, because real controllers are digital and sampled.
Formal definition
For \dot x = f(x,u) with cost \int_0^T \ell(x,u)\,dt + h(x(T)) and optimal cost-to-go J(x,t):
-\frac{\partial J}{\partial t}(x,t) = \min_{u \in \mathcal{U}}\Big\{\ell(x,u) + \nabla_x J(x,t)^\top f(x,u)\Big\}, \qquad J(x,T) = h(x).
The terminal condition plays the role of J_N = g_N in the discrete recursion, and the equation is integrated backwards from t = T.
Connection to classical control
With f = Ax + Bu, \ell = x^\top Qx + u^\top Ru and the ansatz J = x^\top P(t)x, the minimisation gives u^*(x) = -R^{-1}B^\top Px and the PDE collapses into the matrix differential Riccati equation
-\dot P = A^\top P + PA - PBR^{-1}B^\top P + Q,
whose stationary form is the CARE. The PDE became an ODE because the quadratic ansatz reduced an unknown function to finitely many unknown numbers, the same collapse and the same fragility as in the discrete LQR case.
Key limitation
Three reasons the course does not live here, in increasing order of importance: the differentiability assumed in the derivation generally fails (optimal cost-to-go functions develop kinks, and rigour requires viscosity solutions); solving a PDE in n state dimensions is worse than the discrete Curse of dimensionality, since spatial derivatives must also be resolved; and real controllers are sampled anyway.
Related concepts
Principle of optimality | Bellman equation | LQR | Dynamic programming | Curse of dimensionality
References

Primary: Bertsekas (2019), Ch. 1; Liberzon, Calculus of Variations and Optimal Control Theory, Ch. 5
Viscosity solutions: Crandall & Lions (1983)
