04_concepts/importance-sampling.title: Importance sampling
04_concepts/importance-sampling.content:
Importance sampling
Reweighting samples drawn under one distribution so that they estimate an expectation under another, by multiplying each sample by the ratio of the two densities.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting. It is the device that lets a method in the model-free column use data its current policy did not generate.
Bellman object approximated: none. It is a change-of-measure identity, exact before any algorithm is built on it.
Failure mode addressed: it is the standard answer to failure mode 3, distribution shift, and it pays for that answer in failure mode 2, variance.
Course first appearance: Week 9, as the escape hatch from the on-policy hypothesis; formalized for fixed data sets in Week 12

Core idea
The Policy gradient theorem weights states by the visitation measure of the current policy, so one parameter update turns every stored trajectory into a sample from the wrong distribution. The identity below says that the old data can still answer the new question, provided each trajectory is scaled by how much more or less likely the new policy was to have produced it. The identity is exact and the resulting estimator is unbiased. Its cost is in the ratio, which is a product over the horizon.
Formal definition
For any f and any two policies with the same support,
\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_\theta}\big[f(\tau)\big] = \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\theta'}}\left[\left(\prod_{t}\frac{\pi_\theta(u_t\mid x_t)}{\pi_{\theta'}(u_t\mid x_t)}\right)f(\tau)\right].
The transition kernels cancel from the ratio for the same reason they cancel in the policy gradient theorem, since both trajectory densities carry the same P(x_{t+1}\mid x_t,u_t) at every step. The weight is therefore computable from the two policies alone, with no model. Its variance is the problem. A product of hundreds of per-step ratios is a random variable whose spread grows rapidly with the horizon and with the distance between the two policies, so the reweighted estimate is frequently noisier than collecting fresh data would have been. The support condition is not cosmetic, since a trajectory the old policy could not have produced receives an infinite weight and one the new policy cannot produce receives zero.
Connection to classical control
It is the reweighting that lets an experiment run under one controller answer a question about another, and its variance is the price of asking. A control engineer meets the same coupling in closed-loop identification, where the input is generated by the loop and what the data reveal about the plant depends on the controller in it. The practical rule that comes out of both settings is the same. Data from a nearby controller can be reused, data from a distant one cannot, and the honest way to use the identity is to keep the two policies close rather than to trust the weights.
Key limitation
Unbiasedness is recovered and usability is not. The variance of the product grows with the horizon, so the identity relieves the on-policy constraint on paper and rarely relieves it in practice at full episode length. The standard repairs all trade the exactness away. Truncating or clipping the ratios introduces bias, per-decision weighting shortens the product without removing the growth, and trust regions enforce closeness so that the weights stay near one. Week 10 introduces the third of these, and Week 12 takes up the case where no new experiment can be run at all, so the mismatch cannot be reduced by collecting more data.
Related concepts
Discounted state-visitation measure | Policy gradient theorem | Off-policy learning | Distribution shift | Coverage | Offline RL | Experience replay | PPO | Monte Carlo policy evaluation | Sample complexity
References

Primary: Sutton & Barto (2018), Ch. 5.5 to 5.9, for the per-decision and weighted variants
In the offline setting: Levine et al. (2020)
It is well established in simulation as the change-of-measure or likelihood-ratio weighting

04_concepts/lqr-policy-gradient.title: LQR policy gradient
04_concepts/lqr-policy-gradient.content:
LQR policy gradient
Policy search restricted to linear state feedback on a linear plant with quadratic cost, where the objective is nonconvex in the gain and gradient descent nevertheless converges to the Riccati gain.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: a policy × no dynamics model, run on the one plant where the top-left cell also has an exact answer, which is what makes the comparison possible
Bellman object approximated: none by the method. The reference solution it is measured against is the exact fixed point of \mathcal{T} for the linear-quadratic case.
Failure mode addressed: none. It is the setting in which the cost of failure mode 2 can be read against a known optimum.
Course first appearance: Week 9, theory and practical

Core idea
Every convergence statement in the policy branch is about stationary points of a non-concave objective, which is a weak guarantee and easy to mistake for a fatal one. LQR is the case where the whole landscape can be written down. Restricting to \pi_K(x)=-Kx on x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k with quadratic cost gives a J(K) that is smooth on the open set of stabilising gains and nonconvex in K, and it still satisfies a gradient-domination inequality of Polyak-Lojasiewicz type. Gradient descent therefore reaches K^\star with no spurious local minima to be trapped by, including when the gradient is estimated from rollouts.
Formal definition
The scalar instance carries every quantity in closed form. Take x_{k+1}=2x_k+u_k with cost \sum_k (3x_k^2+u_k^2) and \mathbb{E}[x_0^2]=1. The closed loop is x_{k+1}=(2-K)x_k, so the cost sums as a geometric series,
J(K) = -\,\frac{3+K^2}{1-(2-K)^2},
finite exactly on the stabilising set K\in(1,3). The scalar Riccati equation p = 3+4p-4p^2/(1+p) reduces to p^2-6p-3=0, giving p=3+2\sqrt3, K^\star = 2p/(1+p)=\sqrt3\approx 1.7321, J(K^\star)=-(3+2\sqrt3)\approx -6.4641, and a closed-loop pole at 2-\sqrt3\approx 0.268. The derivative vanishes at K=\sqrt3 and nowhere else in (1,3), with J=-7 at both K=1.5 and K=2 and the gradient pointing inward from each. A model-free learner receives none of A, B, Q, R. Running a Gaussian policy \pi_\theta(u\mid x)=\mathcal{N}(-Kx,\sigma^2) makes the score equal to -x(u+Kx)/\sigma^2, and REINFORCE with a baseline averages it against centred returns until it lands near \sqrt3.
Connection to classical control
The comparison is the point of the example. With A, B, Q and R known, one Riccati solve returns K^\star in milliseconds, and the model-free route has to discover the same gain from trajectories at a cost Week 6 measured. The method earns its place where the model is missing, and the LQR result is valuable as a proof that the nonconvexity introduced by parameterising the policy is not automatically fatal. The domain is the part to read twice. J(K) diverges as K approaches 1 or 3, so one step large enough to leave the stabilising set sends the objective to -\infty and no later rollout recovers it, which is the familiar statement that a learning step is a change of controller and can destabilise the loop.
Key limitation
The guarantee belongs to one problem class and does not transfer. Gradient domination is a property of the linear-quadratic landscape, and nothing about it survives contact with a torque limit, a contact mode or a neural policy class. Two costs of the model-free route are visible in the same example. The expectation of the estimator is the derivative of the noisy policy’s cost, which carries an extra term proportional to \sigma^2, and driving \sigma down to remove that term inflates the estimator variance as 1/\sigma^2. A scalar J with one stationary point is unimodal, so this instance exhibits the mechanism, and the nonconvexity itself needs the matrix case.
Related concepts
LQR | Policy gradient theorem | Policy gradient (REINFORCE) | Policy parameterisation | Baseline (variance reduction) | Certainty equivalence | Composition with classical control | Sample complexity | RL as approximate dynamic programming
References

Context: Recht (2019), A Tour of Reinforcement Learning: The View from Continuous Control
Course level: the convergence result is stated and not proved; the worked scalar instance is the examinable part

04_concepts/lqr.title: LQR
04_concepts/lqr.content:
LQR
Linear dynamics plus quadratic cost: the one case where the Bellman recursion has a closed form, because the value function stays quadratic and the Riccati recursion is the Bellman recursion.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value function × dynamics model available (top-left, with Dynamic programming and Value iteration)
Failure mode addressed: none — it is the analytical anchor against which approximate methods are checked all semester
Course first appearance: Week 1 (as prior knowledge, re-read as dynamic programming); developed in full in Week 2

Core idea
Students arrive knowing LQR as a Riccati computation. Week 1 relabels it: the recursion on P_k is simultaneously the finite-horizon Riccati recursion, the finite-horizon Bellman equation specialised to linear-quadratic data, and, when the horizon is dropped and the recursion iterated to its fixed point, Value iteration. Three names, one algorithm. That relabelling is what makes the rest of the course legible as approximate dynamic programming rather than as a new field.
Formal definition
Scalar worked case: x_{k+1} = x_k + u_k, g_k = x^2 + u^2, g_N = x^2. The ansatz J_k(x) = P_k x^2 gives
u_k^*(x) = -\frac{P_{k+1}}{1+P_{k+1}}x, \qquad P_k = 1 + \frac{P_{k+1}}{1+P_{k+1}} = 1 + P_{k+1} - \frac{P_{k+1}^2}{1+P_{k+1}},
(the two forms are algebraically identical; the slides use the second, the notes derive the first)
converging to P^2 - P - 1 = 0, i.e. P^\infty = (1+\sqrt5)/2 \approx 1.618, gain K \approx 0.618, closed loop x_{k+1} \approx 0.382\,x_k, asymptotically stable, as it must be for a finite infinite-horizon cost.
General case: the discrete Riccati sweep P \gets Q + A^\top P(A - BK) with K = (R + B^\top P B)^{-1}B^\top P A is exactly one application of the Bellman operator restricted to quadratic value functions. Its fixed point is the DARE. In continuous time the HJB equation with the ansatz J = x^\top P(t)x collapses to -\dot P = A^\top P + PA - PBR^{-1}B^\top P + Q.
The three modelling choices that do the work (Week 2)
The derivation is one Bellman backup done by hand, and it uses each assumption exactly once. Linear dynamics make the successor state affine in the decision variable. Quadratic, jointly convex cost makes the one-stage problem convex. Unconstrained input means that convex problem is solved by setting a gradient to zero rather than by examining a boundary, and that single step is what produces a linear policy. Take the bound away and \pi^\star saturates; see Torque-limited pendulum.
Writing S_k := R + B^\top P_{k+1}B \succ 0, completing the square gives 2u^\top B^\top P_{k+1}Ax + u^\top S_ku = (u + K_kx)^\top S_k(u + K_kx) - x^\top K_k^\top S_kK_kx, which exhibits the minimiser without differentiating anything. The bracket that remains is symmetric, so the ansatz reproduces itself. This is Closure under the Bellman operator, and it is the whole reason a closed form exists.
Dropping the horizon without a discount (Week 2)
For (A,B) stabilisable and (A,Q^{1/2}) detectable, the recursion converges from any P_N \succeq 0 to the unique PSD solution of the DARE, and u = -K_\infty x is optimal and stabilising. The argument is worth contrasting with Week 3’s, because it is completely different in character: from P_N = 0 the sweep is monotonically non-decreasing (each extra stage adds a non-negative cost) and bounded above (stabilisability supplies some F with A - BF Schur, whose infinite-horizon cost dominates every truncation), so it converges by monotone boundedness. A general P_N is squeezed between two such sweeps because \mathcal{R} is monotone, which is immediate from \mathcal{R}(P) = \min_F\{Q + F^\top RF + (A-BF)^\top P(A-BF)\}.
No discount appears anywhere: this is an undiscounted problem, \gamma = 1, and it converges anyway. Stabilisability does the job that \gamma < 1 will do in Week 3. A discount is one way to make the tail negligible, a stabilising policy plus a cost vanishing at the target is another, and it is worth knowing which one a given guarantee rests on. See Discount factor.
With additive zero-mean process noise the gain is unchanged and only an additive constant moves: Certainty equivalence.
Connection to classical control
This is the classical control side. The point of the note runs the other way: the object control engineers call P is a value function, the object they call the Riccati recursion is a Bellman backup, and the DARE is a fixed-point equation of the same kind as V^* = \mathcal{T}V^*.
Key limitation
Everything clean here is clean because of the quadratic ansatz: the value function stays in a two-parameter family, the minimisation has a closed form, the fixed point is a root of a quadratic. None of it survives nonlinearity: for the Torque-limited pendulum (Week 2) the optimal value function is not smooth, not quadratic and not available in closed form. Keep both examples in mind together, or LQR will mislead you.
Every one of the four assumptions fails on a real robot. Linear dynamics: most systems are linear only near an operating point, and Week 2 measures how near, with the saturated LQR law capturing 19 % of the pendulum’s low-energy band and none of the hanging equilibrium. Unconstrained inputs: every actuator saturates, and many have rate limits. Quadratic cost: real objectives include obstacles, contact conditions, joint limits and logical requirements, none of which is a quadratic form. Known model and measured state: parameters are identified with error and the full state is rarely measured.
Related concepts
Dynamic programming | Value iteration | Bellman equation | Bellman operator | HJB equation | MPC | iLQR | Curse of dimensionality | Closure under the Bellman operator | Certainty equivalence | Torque-limited pendulum | Terminal cost approximation
References

Primary: Bertsekas (2019), Ch. 1 and Ch. 4; Anderson & Moore, Optimal Control: Linear Quadratic Methods, Ch. 2–4
Software: control.dare (python-control) for reference solutions

04_concepts/lstd.title: LSTD
04_concepts/lstd.content:
LSTD
Least-squares temporal-difference learning: assemble the projected Bellman equation from the observed transitions as a d\times d linear system and solve it once, with no step size anywhere.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no dynamics model, alongside TD learning and DQN
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T}^\pi, solved exactly inside the representable subspace
Failure mode addressed: it removes the step-size sensitivity of failure mode 1 in the linear on-policy case and leaves the triad itself untouched
Course first appearance: Week 7

Core idea
The convergence theorem for on-policy TD with linear features names the equation the iterates approach, and that equation is linear in w. A method that accumulates the equation directly and solves it is then available, which is the same move as fitting a model by least squares instead of by gradient descent. Each observed transition contributes one rank-one term, the sampling supplies both the state weighting and the successor expectation, and the answer is the Projected Bellman equation fixed point rather than an approach to it.
Formal definition
Expanding the projection in \Phi w_{\mathrm{TD}} = \Pi_{d_\pi}\mathcal{T}^\pi \Phi w_{\mathrm{TD}} gives A w_{\mathrm{TD}} = b with
A = \Phi^\top D\,(I - \gamma P^\pi)\,\Phi, \qquad b = \Phi^\top D\, r^\pi,
neither factor of which is known when the plant is unknown. Each transition (x_t, r_{t+1}, x_{t+1}) supplies one term of each sum,
A \approx \sum_t \phi(x_t)\bigl(\phi(x_t) - \gamma\,\phi(x_{t+1})\bigr)^{\!\top}, \qquad b \approx \sum_t \phi(x_t)\,r_{t+1},
with a regulariser \epsilon I keeping A invertible until d independent transitions have arrived, and a terminal successor contributing \phi = 0. Placing the state-action version inside policy iteration, with a greedy improvement step between solves, gives least-squares policy iteration (Lagoudakis and Parr, 2003).
Connection to classical control
This is least-squares system identification with a value function as the object being identified. Empirical moment matrices are accumulated from data and a linear system is solved for the parameters, so the usual numerical lessons carry over unchanged. Conditioning of A governs sensitivity to finite-data error, collinear or badly scaled features make A ill-conditioned the way collinear regressors do in ordinary regression, and regularisation is the same remedy. One structural difference is worth keeping. The successor features enter through the temporal-difference term, which is what puts the factor I - \gamma P^\pi inside A and makes it asymmetric.
Key limitation
The final solve costs O(d^3), which is routine at d = 10^3 and unavailable for networks with millions of parameters, so LSTD is the method of choice when a compact and physically meaningful basis exists rather than a general replacement for incremental learning. It evaluates a fixed policy with linear features, and the guarantee it inherits is the on-policy one. Off-policy weighting removes the contraction that makes its fixed point meaningful, exactly as for incremental TD.
Related concepts
Projected Bellman equation | TD learning | Function approximation in RL | Policy iteration | Generalised policy iteration | Stationary distribution | DQN | Deadly triad | Certainty equivalence
References

Original paper: Bradtke & Barto (1996), Linear least-squares algorithms for temporal difference learning
LSPI: Lagoudakis & Parr (2003)
Primary: Bertsekas (2019), Ch. 6

04_concepts/likelihood-ratio-identity.title: Likelihood-ratio identity
04_concepts/likelihood-ratio-identity.content:
Likelihood-ratio identity
The calculus fact \nabla_\theta p_\theta = p_\theta\,\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta, which rewrites the derivative of a density, an object that cannot be sampled, as the density itself times a quantity that can be evaluated on each draw.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational. It is the differentiation step that makes the policy row of the model-free column reachable at all.
Bellman object approximated: none. It is an identity of calculus, and nothing about it is specific to a Markov decision process.
Failure mode addressed: none. It is exact, and the variance of what it produces is failure mode 2.
Course first appearance: Week 6, in the derivation of Policy gradient (REINFORCE)

Core idea
Differentiating an expectation is easy when the parameter sits in the integrand and hard when it sits in the measure. Policy search is the hard case, because R(\tau) carries no \theta and all the dependence lives in p_\theta. The identity moves the derivative onto \log p_\theta, where a product of densities becomes a sum of logarithms and every factor free of \theta differentiates to zero. That is why the unknown transition kernel leaves the expression without ever being estimated.
Formal definition
For a density positive and differentiable in \theta, the chain rule applied to \log p_\theta gives
\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)=\frac{\nabla_\theta p_\theta(\tau)}{p_\theta(\tau)}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \nabla_\theta p_\theta(\tau)=p_\theta(\tau)\,\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau).
Substituting it under the integral sign, for any f that carries no \theta,
\nabla_\theta\int p_\theta(\tau)f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau=\int p_\theta(\tau)\,\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)\,f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_\theta}\big[f(\tau)\,\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)\big].
An integral against \nabla_\theta p_\theta, which is not a probability measure, has become an expectation under p_\theta, which is the distribution a Rollout draws from. Two conditions are doing work. The interchange of \nabla_\theta and the integral needs a dominating function, which holds for the classes used in this course, and the ratio needs p_\theta>0 wherever the integrand is supported. Taking f\equiv1 gives the corollary the rest of the course leans on,
\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_\theta}\big[\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)\big]=\nabla_\theta\!\int p_\theta(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau=\nabla_\theta 1=0,
so the object being averaged has zero mean, which is what later licenses dropping the acausal terms and subtracting a Baseline (variance reduction).
Connection to classical control
The quantity \nabla_\theta\log p_\theta is the score of classical statistics, the same object whose covariance is the Fisher information and whose zero mean underlies the Cramér-Rao bound. An engineer who has designed an identification experiment has already used it, since the information matrix is what says how much a chosen input sequence reveals about a parameter. The identity is what connects that estimation-theoretic object to a control objective. Its cancellation needs only that the plant does not depend on \theta, so it holds unchanged for a system that is nonlinear, discontinuous, or making and breaking contact.
Key limitation
The identity is exact and silent about cost. It converts a derivative into an expectation without saying how many draws the resulting average needs, and in the policy-search case a single scalar return multiplies the entire gradient vector, whose variance grows with the horizon. It also requires a density that is positive and differentiable, which a deterministic policy does not have. Methods that want deterministic actions therefore need a different route to the gradient, differentiating through the action instead of through the log-density, which is the step DDPG takes in Week 10.
Related concepts
Score function estimator | Policy gradient (REINFORCE) | Policy gradient theorem | Rollout | Baseline (variance reduction) | Softmax policy class | Gaussian policy class | Importance sampling | Monte Carlo policy evaluation | Stochastic approximation | DDPG
References

Primary: Sutton & Barto (2018), §13.2
Original paper: Williams (1992), Simple statistical gradient-following algorithms for connectionist reinforcement learning
Background: the identity is standard in simulation optimisation, where it is known as the likelihood-ratio or score-function method

04_concepts/mdp.title: MDP
04_concepts/mdp.content:
MDP
A discounted Markov decision process (\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{U}, P, r, \gamma) is discrete-time stochastic optimal control, and it is the smallest formalism in which the problem of choosing a policy under uncertain dynamics can be stated exactly.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — the object over which every cell of the diagram is defined
Failure mode addressed: none; its five standing assumptions are what the rest of the course removes one at a time
Course first appearance: Week 3 (the Markov property itself is used from Week 1)

Core idea
Weeks 1 and 2 wrote the plant as a disturbed difference equation x_{k+1} = f(x_k, u_k, w_k). The MDP replaces f and the distribution of w by the single object they induce, the transition kernel P(x' \mid x, u), and every derivation in the theory depends on that conditional law alone. Deterministic dynamics are the degenerate case where P(\cdot \mid x,u) puts all its mass on f(x,u). The formalism earns its place by making Gap 2 of the Week 3 opening statable: under uncertainty an open-loop plan u_{0:N-1} and a policy \pi(\cdot) are different objects, and only the second one can react to the disturbance after it lands.
Formal definition
\mathcal{X} is a finite state space, \mathcal{U} a finite action space, P(x'\mid x,u) \ge 0 with \sum_{x'} P(x'\mid x,u) = 1, r : \mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U} \to \mathbb{R} a bounded reward, and \gamma \in (0,1) the Discount factor. The reward is the negative of the Weeks 1–2 stage cost, r = -g, and the sign convention has to be applied consistently or every inequality reverses.
Five standing assumptions, each false about robots and each made for a reason:



































AssumptionWhat it buysDropped\mathcal{X},\mathcal{U} finite, r boundedevery max attained, every expectation a finite sumWeeks 6–7P, r stationaryone stationary policy is meaningful (the discrete analogue of restricting to LTI)not dropped\gamma < 1finite return, \gamma-contractionundiscounted problems need proper policies or stabilisabilityx measured exactlypolicies are functions of the statePOMDP (Weeks 4, 12)P and r knownevery backup evaluable exactlyWeeks 4 onward
Policies come in four nested classes, from history-dependent stochastic down to stationary deterministic. For a finite discounted MDP the supremum of V^\pi over the largest class is attained inside the smallest, by one stationary deterministic \pi^\star that is optimal simultaneously at every state. That theorem is why every algorithm in the course searches only the smallest class. Reinforcement learning still uses stochastic policies from Week 4 onward, for exploration and for differentiability, both consequences of the model being unknown.
Connection to classical control
The whole tuple would be recognised by a control engineer from 1960; the vocabulary is the only thing that has moved. State to state, input to action, dynamics to kernel, stage cost to reward with a sign flip, cost-to-go J^\star to value V^\star = -J^\star, control law to policy. The one genuine addition is that the RL column also admits stochastic policies. Reading Sutton & Barto against Bertsekas is a translation exercise over that dictionary and nothing deeper.
Key limitation
Two rows of the table carry all the difficulty. Finiteness of \mathcal{X} is what the Curse of dimensionality destroys, since a kernel is stored state by state while f and the noise distribution are usually a handful of parameters. Knowledge of P and r underlies every proof in Week 3, and Week 4 opens by removing it, at which point \sum_{x'} P(x'\mid x,u)(\cdot) can no longer be evaluated at all.
Related concepts
Markov property | Value function | Bellman equation | Bellman operator | Value iteration | Policy iteration | Discount factor | POMDP | Curse of dimensionality | Open-loop vs feedback | RL as approximate dynamic programming
References

Primary: Bertsekas, Dynamic Programming and Optimal Control, Vol. II, Ch. 1
Secondary: Meyn, Control Systems and Reinforcement Learning (2022), Ch. 1–2; Sutton & Barto (2nd ed.), Ch. 3

04_concepts/mpc.title: MPC
04_concepts/mpc.content:
MPC
Dynamic programming with the horizon truncated at N and the discarded tail replaced by a terminal cost: solve a finite-horizon optimal control problem online, apply only its first input, and re-solve from the measured state one sampling period later.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: both × dynamics model available — the awkward cell. MPC represents a model and a terminal value function, but its policy is implicit: recomputed online by optimisation, never stored
Failure mode addressed: none yet (the taxonomy arrives in Week 7); MPC introduces the model-bias exposure that becomes failure mode 5 once f is learned
Course first appearance: Week 2; reframed at the start of Week 3 as DP with the tail truncated and the remainder guessed; returns in Week 11 with a learned model

Core idea
MPC is the Bellman equation with two named approximations and nothing else changed. The infinite horizon is truncated to N steps, and everything beyond step N is summarised by a single terminal cost \hat J. Inside the horizon the true nonlinear model and the true state and input constraints are used exactly, which is what distinguishes it from LQR: no linearisation, no saturation applied after the fact. Performance is therefore determined by exactly two design choices, the horizon length and the quality of \hat J (see Terminal cost approximation).
Formal definition
At each sampling instant k, measure x_k and solve
\min_{u_{0:N-1}} \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} g(\hat x_i, u_i) + \hat J(\hat x_N) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \hat x_{i+1} = f(\hat x_i, u_i),\; \hat x_0 = x_k,\; u_i \in \mathcal{U},\; \hat x_i \in \mathcal{X}.
Apply u_k = u_0^\star, discard u_1^\star,\dots,u_{N-1}^\star, and repeat from the newly measured state.
Where the feedback comes from
Each solve produces an open-loop sequence, which appears to contradict Open-loop vs feedback. It does not: the feedback is in the recomputation, not in the plan. Only the first input is ever applied; before the second would have been, the plant has moved somewhere the plan did not predict, and the controller solves a new problem from the measured state. The applied inputs are therefore a function of realised states, which is what a policy is. In Week 1’s branching language, MPC re-decides at every node of the disturbance tree instead of committing one number to all branches.
The price is that \pi^{\text{MPC}} has no formula: it is defined pointwise by an optimisation problem, which is why the diagram cell is awkward.
One Bellman equation, two ways to pay for it (Week 3)
Dynamic programming and MPC sit at the ends of a single spectrum, and what separates them is when the computation happens. DP pays once, offline, over the entire state space, and leaves a global object that reduces the online work to a table lookup and one \arg\max. MPC stores only the model, pays at every sampling instant, and pays only at the state it is actually in. That second choice is also the first escape route from the Curse of dimensionality: MPC never evaluates a value at a state the system does not visit. Most of this course lives between the two, storing a value function as parameters fitted offline and using it to shorten the online horizon, and the exchange rate between the quality of \hat J and the horizon N it buys is what Weeks 5 to 15 compute. If \hat J = J^\star exactly, then by the Principle of optimality a horizon of N=1 is already optimal, and every extra prediction step in a real implementation is compensating for \hat J being wrong.
Connection to classical control
This is classical control; the reframing runs the other way. What control engineers call the prediction horizon is a truncation of the Bellman recursion, and what they call the terminal cost is an approximation of the optimal cost-to-go. The stability theory makes the connection sharp: with a control-invariant terminal set and a terminal cost that is a local Lyapunov function upper-bounding the true cost-to-go, closed-loop stability and recursive feasibility are theorems (Rawlings, Mayne & Diehl, Ch. 2). Those terminal ingredients are the same object RL spends the rest of the course learning.
Worked evidence (Week 2, torque-limited pendulum, 20 Hz, \hat J = 0)
Same plant, same u_{\max}, same stage cost, same solver, and only N differs. With N = 10 (0.5 s) the controller saturates towards the goal and oscillates forever, final error 2.40 rad: the swing-up is not a feasible point of the problem it was given, so a short horizon with no terminal value is a greedy controller. With N = 60 (3.0 s) it moves away from the goal first, pumps energy, and captures the upright to within 10^{-3} rad. Cost: 13 vs 36 ms per step against a 50 ms budget. Horizon is bought with computation, and the control rate sets the budget.
Key limitation
An optimisation runs inside the control loop against a hard deadline, and a missed period is not a slower controller, it is an open-loop controller for that period. Nonlinear f makes the problem nonconvex, so the solver returns a local minimum, and which local minimum can change between periods, producing a discontinuous effective policy for reasons that have nothing to do with J^\star. And re-planning does not repair a systematic model error, because every re-plan uses the same wrong model (see Model bias).
Related concepts
Bellman equation | Terminal cost approximation | Open-loop vs feedback | LQR | iLQR | Trajectory optimisation | Torque-limited pendulum | Model bias | Composition with classical control | Model-based RL
References

Primary: Rawlings, Mayne & Diehl, Model Predictive Control: Theory, Computation and Design, Ch. 2
Secondary: Bertsekas (2019), Ch. 2 — MPC as approximate dynamic programming with truncated rollout

04_concepts/markov-property.title: Markov property
04_concepts/markov-property.content:
Markov property
The next state depends on the past only through the current state and input: a property of the state variable you chose, not of your robot.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — it is the hypothesis every cell of the diagram silently assumes
Failure mode addressed: none; its failure is partial observability, formalised in Week 12
Course first appearance: Week 1 (used); the MDP formalism arrives in Week 3

Core idea
Together with additivity of the cost, the Markov property is what makes the Principle of optimality true: additivity splits total cost into head plus tail, and Markov guarantees the tail depends on the past only through x_i. It is also what makes a Value function possible at all, since one number per state can summarise the future only if the state summarises the past.
Formal definition
\mathbb{P}\big(x_{k+1} \mid x_k, u_k, w_k, x_{k-1}, u_{k-1}, \dots\big) = \mathbb{P}\big(x_{k+1} \mid x_k, u_k, w_k\big),
with the disturbance w_k drawn from a distribution that may depend on (x_k, u_k) but not on the past.
Connection to classical control
It is the state-space assumption of modern control, stated in probabilistic form: the state is by definition the smallest quantity from which the future can be predicted given future inputs. Enlarging the state to restore the property is the standard fix in both fields: delay states for dead time, augmented states for coloured noise, belief states for partial observation.
Key limitation
The assumption is a claim about your representation. Joint encoder readings alone are not a Markov state for a manipulator under contact, backlash or thermal drift: the future depends on quantities your state vector does not contain. When it fails, the whole chain fails, the principle of optimality no longer applies to your model, and a value function of your state does not exist. A large part of the practical difficulty of applying RL to real robots consists of arranging for this property to hold.
Week 5 turns the assumption into a measurable choice between two estimators. TD assumes the observed state is Markov and is paid for the assumption when it holds, at a factor of 17 in target variance on the pendulum chain, because the fitted chain recovers the value function from less data. Monte Carlo policy evaluation declines to assume it: its target stays an unbiased estimate of the expected return given whatever was observed, Markov or not, and it pays that factor for the caution. Which estimator is right is therefore a question about the sensor suite rather than about the algorithm.
Related concepts
Principle of optimality | MDP | POMDP | Value function | Dynamic programming | Curse of dimensionality
References

Primary: Bertsekas (2019), Ch. 1
Secondary: Sutton & Barto (2nd ed.), Ch. 3

04_concepts/maximisation-bias.title: Maximisation bias
04_concepts/maximisation-bias.content:
Maximisation bias
The maximum of unbiased estimates is a biased estimate of the maximum, and the bias points upwards, so any method whose target applies \max to a row of noisy numbers systematically overestimates action values.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no dynamics model, wherever a target contains a maximum over estimates
Failure mode addressed: 1, the bias component, repaired by double DQN
Course first appearance: planted Week 6, formalized Week 7

Core idea
The \max in a Q-learning target is applied to estimates, so whichever action happens to carry the largest positive error wins the maximisation and its inflated value is written into the target. Each backup then writes that offset into the estimate the next backup will maximise over, so the bias propagates. Week 6’s table escaped this asymptotically, since decaying step sizes drive the estimation noise to zero and the bias goes with it. A network fitted on a distribution that keeps moving, from a buffer that keeps turning over, holds the noise away from zero for as long as training lasts.
Formal definition
With n actions of equal true value q and estimates \hat q_i = q + \sigma z_i for independent standard normals z_i,
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\max_i \hat q_i\bigr] = q + \sigma\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\max_i z_i\bigr] = q + 1.16\,\sigma \quad (n = 5),
so the offset scales with the noise in the estimates. Double DQN (van Hasselt et al., 2016) splits selection from evaluation, using the online network to pick the action and the target network to price it,
y = r + \gamma\,Q_{\theta^-}\Bigl(x',\ \arg\max_b Q_\theta(x',b)\Bigr).
The two networks carry different errors, so the action whose error is largest under \theta is not the action whose value is largest under \theta^-, and the coupling that produced the offset is broken. On the Week 7 pendulum chain the overestimation drops from 7.7 to 0.6 against the exact value of the induced policy, and the final policy improves from -125.8 to -124.4.
Connection to classical control
This is the winner’s curse of any selection made on noisy measurements, familiar from choosing the best-performing controller from a bank on the basis of one short experiment each. The measured winner is optimistic about itself, and the repair has the same shape in both settings. Select on one data set and evaluate on another.
Key limitation
Double DQN is a bias correction and touches nothing else. It removes no ingredient of the Deadly triad, restores no convergence theorem, and leaves the correlation and moving-target problems to Experience replay and the Target network. A badly fitted Q can also order actions correctly despite a large value error, which is why the Week 7 ablation reports the value of the induced policy rather than the size of the value error.
Related concepts
Q-learning | DQN | Target network | Deadly triad | Function approximation in RL | Bias-variance tradeoff in RL | Bootstrapping | Failure modes of approximate RL
References

Original paper: van Hasselt (2010), double Q-learning; van Hasselt et al. (2016), double DQN
Primary: Sutton & Barto (2018), Section 6.7

04_concepts/monte-carlo-policy-evaluatio.title: Monte Carlo policy evaluation
04_concepts/monte-carlo-policy-evaluatio.content:
Monte Carlo policy evaluation
Estimating V^\pi by averaging the returns that actually occurred, with no operator and no fixed point anywhere in the target.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value function × no dynamics model
Bellman object approximated: none. The method estimates a conditional expectation by sampling it, so no operator is being inverted
Failure mode addressed: none; it avoids the Bootstrapping ingredient of failure mode 1 and pays in variance instead
Course first appearance: Week 5

Core idea
The value of a policy is defined as an expected discounted return, and an expectation can be estimated by averaging draws of it. Running the policy to the end of an episode produces exactly one such draw, so the elementary statistics of Week 4 apply with a more complicated random variable in place of a single reward. This is the honest competitor of TD learning, and comparing the two is how the course introduces the depth axis.
Formal definition
G_t = \sum_{i\ge0}\gamma^i r_{t+i+1}, \qquad V(x_t) \;\leftarrow\; V(x_t) + \alpha\big(G_t - V(x_t)\big).
Correctness is immediate from the definition of the value function: G_t is one draw of the random variable whose mean is V^\pi(x), so
\mathbb{E}\big[G_t \mid x_t = x\big] = V^\pi(x)
holds whatever the table currently contains. Compare this with the TD identity, whose right-hand side depends on the current V.
The batch characterisation separates the two methods sharply. On a fixed batch swept to convergence, tabular TD(0) returns the value of the maximum-likelihood empirical MDP, which is Certainty equivalence applied to a chain, while Monte Carlo returns the least-squares fit to the observed returns and uses no transition structure at all. On the eight-episode two-state batch of Week 5, both agree that V(B) = 6/8 = 0.75; Monte Carlo answers V(A) = 0, the one return observed from A, and TD answers V(A) = 0 + 0.75, because the single transition out of A went to B. Neither answer is a mistake.
Connection to classical control
Monte Carlo is open-loop estimation, which is why it needs no stability argument: it forms a statistic from a record and never feeds its own output back into the record. Its closest classical relative is a batch least-squares identification run offline on logged data, as against the recursive estimator that updates while the plant runs. The comparison in Week 5 is the familiar one between an offline fit that is easy to certify and a recursive scheme that responds sooner.
Key limitation
Three costs, all measured on the Week 5 pendulum chain. Variance: at the worst state, V^\pi = -25.38 and about 36 steps from the goal, the Monte Carlo return has standard deviation 6.37 against 1.53 for the one-step TD target formed with the exact V^\pi, a variance ratio of 17.4 at the same mean. Latency: nothing is learned until an episode terminates, so the update rate is set by episode length instead of by the controller’s sampling rate. Structure: a continuing task has no episode boundary, so a balancing controller meant to run for hours produces no G_t at all.
One property points the other way and is the reason the method survives. Unbiasedness needs G_t to be a sample of the conditional return given the observed signal, and it does not need that signal to be a Markov state. When the observation omits a joint velocity, a contact state or a thermal effect, Monte Carlo stays unbiased for what was observed while TD propagates the misspecification through every value that bootstraps through the affected states.
Where it returns
Week 9 uses it as a component rather than as a method. Line 7 of REINFORCE with a baseline regresses b_w on the observed return, which is Monte-Carlo policy evaluation in the form Week 5 introduced it, and the absence of a bootstrapped target there is what keeps the algorithm in the policy row of the Unifying diagram. See Baseline (variance reduction).
Related concepts
TD learning | Bootstrapping | Bias-variance tradeoff in RL | Eligibility traces | Markov property | Certainty equivalence | POMDP | Value function | Baseline (variance reduction) | Sample complexity
References

04_concepts/off-policy-learning.title: Off-policy learning
04_concepts/off-policy-learning.content:
Off-policy learning
Learning about one policy from data generated by another: the behaviour policy decides which state-action pairs appear in the data, the target policy is the one whose value the update aims at, and the two are separate objects.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting — a property of the update, applicable anywhere in the no-model column
Failure mode addressed: none; it is one of the three ingredients of the Deadly triad and the precondition for everything in Week 12
Course first appearance: Week 6, as the structural difference between SARSA and Q-learning

Core idea
SARSA ties the two roles together, since its target contains the value of the action the behaviour policy actually took. Q-learning separates them by taking the maximum over the row, and the behaviour policy then decides only which entries receive updates. What the separation buys is freedom in where data comes from. What it does not buy is information, because a pair the behaviour policy never visits carries no evidence about its value whatever target policy is chosen.
Formal definition
The two targets differ in one term,
\underbrace{r_{t+1} + \gamma\,Q(x_{t+1},u_{t+1})}_{\text{on-policy: the action the behaviour policy takes}} \qquad\longrightarrow\qquad \underbrace{r_{t+1} + \gamma\,\max_b Q(x_{t+1},b)}_{\text{off-policy: the best action available}} .
The separation is legitimate because conditioning on the executed pair (x,u) fixes the successor distribution at P(\cdot\mid x,u) regardless of what chose u, so the behaviour policy \mu disappears from the mean of the off-policy target and remains inside the mean of the on-policy one. The hypothesis that survives is a condition on the data: every pair visited infinitely often. That is Coverage, and it attaches to the trajectory distribution instead of to the algorithm.
The policy branch reaches the same distinction from the other side, and Week 9 shows that there it is a theorem rather than a design choice. The Policy gradient theorem weights states by the Discounted state-visitation measure of the policy being differentiated, so a policy-gradient method is on-policy by construction and one update expires every stored trajectory. Importance sampling reweights data from an older policy and recovers unbiasedness, at the cost of a product of per-step ratios whose variance grows with the horizon. Reuse is available in both branches. What differs is the price, since a value method with an off-policy target pays nothing per sample and a policy method pays in weights.
Connection to classical control
This is identification from data collected under a controller other than the one being designed. A closed-loop experiment run with an existing regulator can identify a model used to synthesise a different regulator, and the condition for that to work is that the experiment excited the modes the new design depends on. The correspondence includes the failure: a balancing controller produces data about balancing and none about swing-up, so the region the data covers is a thin tube around whatever the collecting controller did well, and off-policy learning cannot invent transitions outside it.
Key limitation
Off-policy freedom removes a constraint on the policy and leaves the constraint on the data untouched. Under function approximation it also stops being free, because bootstrapping plus off-policy data plus a parametric approximator is exactly the combination that can diverge (Deadly triad, Week 7). Week 7 gets away with Experience replay because the distribution inside a buffer refreshed by the current policy does not shift very much; with a fixed log the buffer stops being refreshed and coverage becomes the binding constraint, which is Offline RL in Week 12.

04_concepts/offline-rl.title: Offline RL
04_concepts/offline-rl.content:
Offline RL
Learning a policy from a fixed data set, with no further interaction with the plant, so nothing the algorithm decides can change what it gets to see.

Stub. This concept is planted in Week 7 and formalized in Week 12.
Expand this note after Week 12’s session.

Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no dynamics model, with the interaction taken away. The algorithms are unchanged and the assumption that made them work is gone
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T} on logged transitions, evaluated at state-action pairs the log need never contain, which is where the extrapolation error comes from
Failure mode addressed: none. It is where failure mode 3 is formalised, and Coverage is the assumption it withdraws
Course first appearance: Week 7, as the one sentence that says why Experience replay is safe; formalised in Week 12

Planted framing (Week 7)
Experience replay is a moving window of experience. It breaks temporal correlations and reuses past transitions, and discarding the oldest transitions keeps the buffer tied, imperfectly, to the recent behaviour policy. Replay works because the distribution does not shift much. Freeze the buffer, or receive a fixed log of somebody else’s operation, and that recency argument disappears while the algorithm stays syntactically identical. The same week supplies the mechanism that makes this dangerous, since off-policy weighting is what breaks the alignment behind the Projected Bellman equation and the buffer only ever kept the mismatch small (Deadly triad).

04_concepts/open-loop-vs-feedback.title: Open-loop vs feedback
04_concepts/open-loop-vs-feedback.content:
Open-loop vs feedback
Optimal control optimises over policies (functions of state), not over control sequences (numbers); the two coincide only when the problem is deterministic.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — it is why the top-left cell stores a policy rather than a trajectory
Failure mode addressed: none
Course first appearance: Week 1

Core idea
The optimisation variable in a stochastic optimal control problem is a sequence of functions \pi_k : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{U}, not a sequence of numbers \{u_0,\dots,u_{N-1}\}. This is a modelling decision, not notation. A policy can react to the realised state, which encodes the disturbances that have already occurred, while an input sequence, committed at k=0, cannot. The class of open-loop sequences is a strict subset of the class of policies, so its optimum can only be worse or equal.
What matters is the randomness of the disturbance, not its size: a large but known disturbance can be planned for in advance, and feedback buys nothing against it. Feedback is worth exactly as much as the future is unpredictable at planning time.
Formal definition
On the two-stage problem x_{k+1} = x_k + u_k + w_k, x_0 = 0, cost \mathbb{E}[x_2^2 + u_0^2 + u_1^2] with w_k = \pm 1 equiprobable, the open-loop optimum must write down u_1 before w_0 exists, forcing the same number onto both branches; the feedback optimum evaluates \pi_1 at whichever x_1 occurred. The gap in expected cost is 0.50 (Exercise 2.2). Note that neither formulation can react to w_1, which arrives after the last decision is taken; the entire gap comes from reacting to w_0.
The same distinction is what licenses the exchange of \min and \mathbb{E} in the DP recursion: the input u is minimised outside \mathbb{E}_w because it precedes w_k, while J_{k+1} sits inside, so tail decisions may depend on the realised w_k through the state they land in. Restricted to open-loop sequences the exchange would be illegal and the recursion would not hold.
Connection to classical control
This gap is precisely what MPC recovers: it re-solves an open-loop problem at every timestep from the current measured state, buying back feedback by recomputation rather than by storing a policy. Week 2 makes the point concrete: the plan is recomputed, not continued, and that recomputation is the feedback; the same argument is what puts direct Trajectory optimisation off the unifying diagram entirely. It is also the gap that Certainty equivalence quietly assumes away, legitimately for a known model with zero-mean noise, and not legitimately when the model itself is unknown (Week 4).
Key limitation
Optimising over policies is what makes the problem expensive: you compute the optimal response at states you never visit. Open-loop trajectory optimisation is cheap for exactly the reason it is worse.
Related concepts
Principle of optimality | Dynamic programming | MPC | Value function | iLQR
References

Primary: Bertsekas (2019), Ch. 1 §1.1–1.2

04_concepts/pomdp.title: POMDP
04_concepts/pomdp.content:
POMDP
A decision problem in which the state is not directly observed, so the controller must act on a belief over states rather than on the state itself.

Stub. This concept is planted in Week 1, named and defined in Week 3, belief states are built in Week 4, and partially observable problems are formalized in Week 12.
Expand this note after Week 12’s session.

Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting, and prior to the diagram. Every cell presumes a state that makes the process Markov, so partial observability is the failure of the assumption all six cells rest on
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T} on the belief, which is exact and out of reach at robot scale. Bayes-adaptive MDP is the identical construction with the belief taken over the model instead of over the state
Failure mode addressed: none of the six. Partial observability is named in the caveat that travels with Failure modes of approximate RL as one of the real modes sitting outside the taxonomy
Course first appearance: Week 1 as a warning about the Markov property; defined in Week 3, belief states built in Week 4, formalised in Week 12

Planted framing (Week 1)
Week 1 raises partial observability only as the failure of the Markov property: the assumption is a claim about the state variable you chose, not about the physical system, and joint encoder readings alone are not a Markov state for a manipulator under contact, backlash or thermal drift. When it fails, the Principle of optimality no longer applies to your model and a Value function of your state does not exist.
Named and defined (Week 3)
Week 3 attaches the name while listing the standing assumptions of the discounted finite MDP and the week each one dies. When the state is not directly available, the problem is a partially observable MDP, in which decisions are made on a belief over states instead of on the state itself, and the assumptions table sends the row forward to Weeks 4 and 12. The definition waits for this week because the MDP tuple has to exist before one of its components can be declared hidden.
Planted framing (Week 4)
Week 4 builds the belief-state construction with the belief taken over the model instead of over the state: augmenting x_t with the posterior b_t gives a Markov process, hence a Bayes-adaptive MDP with an exact Bellman equation and an optimal policy that is computationally out of reach. Week 12 climbs the same ladder with the belief over the state, so the machinery students meet there is already familiar in shape.

04_concepts/ppo.title: PPO
04_concepts/ppo.content:
PPO
Proximal policy optimisation: an on-policy actor-critic that approximates a Trust region by clipping the probability ratio, and fits its value network on bootstrapped GAE targets.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: both × no dynamics model, the bottom row. The placement follows the row rule and not the lineage.
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T}^\pi for the critic, on sampled transitions; none for the actor
Failure modes addressed: 2, by the critic and by advantage normalisation, and the reliability of each update, by the clip. It carries two legs of the Deadly triad.
Course first appearance: Week 10

Core idea
Two problems stand between the Policy gradient theorem and a method that survives a long training run. The multiplier on the score is too noisy, which a Critic fixes at the cost of bias, and a parameter step of fixed size moves the behaviour by an amount nobody controls, which a trust region fixes at the cost of a second-order solve. PPO takes the first repair unchanged and replaces the second by a clip, which is why it is the algorithm most implementations reach for first.
Formal definition
Writing \rho_t(\theta) = \pi_\theta(u_t\mid x_t)/\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(u_t\mid x_t) for the probability ratio, the actor maximises
\hat{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\min\big(\rho_t(\theta)\,\hat A_t,\ \mathrm{clip}(\rho_t(\theta),\,1-\epsilon,\,1+\epsilon)\,\hat A_t\big)\Big],
typically at \epsilon = 0.2, over several epochs on one batch of fresh transitions. The \min makes the objective pessimistic. When \hat A_t > 0 the term stops increasing once \rho_t passes 1+\epsilon, and when \hat A_t < 0 it stops decreasing once \rho_t falls below 1-\epsilon, so no gradient rewards moving the ratio further in the direction the advantage points. The value network is fitted by regression on the \lambda-return \hat A_t + V_w(x_t), and the advantages come from GAE, usually at \lambda = 0.95.
Why the placement is load-bearing. PPO descends from the policy branch, and the version everyone runs fits its value network on targets containing its own next prediction. By the definition of a Critic that is a bootstrapped estimate solving a fixed point of \mathcal{T}^\pi, so PPO represents both objects and belongs in the bottom row of the Unifying diagram. The test is the presence of a fixed-point equation, and “the method has a value function” does not decide it, which is exactly what keeps REINFORCE with a Baseline (variance reduction) in the middle row.
Connection to classical control
The clip is a saturation placed on the incentive rather than on the signal. A trust region states the desired property, that the closed-loop behaviour may not change by more than a set amount per redesign, and PPO enforces an approximation of it by removing the reward for exceeding it. This is the same engineering compromise as replacing a constrained optimisation by a penalty or a rate limiter, and it carries the same caveat, since nothing in the construction bounds the divergence and only the gradient’s incentive to grow it has been removed.
Key limitation
The clipped objective enforces no divergence bound, so a sequence of clipped updates can still move the policy far, and multiple epochs on one batch make that more likely. The measured differences between PPO and its neighbours on standard benchmarks are frequently smaller than the spread induced by the seed, the reward scale or the network initialisation, so a comparison without inter-seed bands establishes very little. Being on-policy, it discards every batch after use, which puts it well behind SAC in sample efficiency on continuous control and makes it a poor fit for a robot with a limited number of operating hours.
Related concepts

04_concepts/policy-gradient-(reinforce).title: Policy gradient (REINFORCE)
04_concepts/policy-gradient-(reinforce).content:
Policy gradient (REINFORCE)
Direct policy search: parameterise the policy, differentiate the expected return through the trajectory density with the likelihood-ratio identity, and ascend the resulting unbiased estimate, with no value function and no fixed-point equation anywhere in the method.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: a policy × no dynamics model — the second row of the model-free column, opened in the same session as the first
Bellman object approximated: none. The objective is differentiated directly, the target is an observed return, and nothing in the algorithm predicts its own next prediction. That answer describes a different attack on the same MDP and is stated positively.
Failure mode addressed: none; it introduces failure mode 2, high variance in policy optimisation, three weeks before the taxonomy names it
Course first appearance: Week 6, developed in Week 9

Core idea
Value methods store a prediction and read a decision out of it by maximisation. Policy search stores the decision and moves it up an estimated gradient of performance. The obstacle is that the parameter sits in the measure being averaged over, and that measure contains the transition kernel this half of the course does not have. The likelihood-ratio identity removes it, and the unknown dynamics cancel because they carry no \theta.
Formal definition
With \pi_\theta(u\mid x) differentiable in \theta, R(\tau) = \sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t r_{t+1}, and the trajectory density p_\theta(\tau) = p(x_0)\prod_t P(x_{t+1}\mid x_t,u_t)\,\pi_\theta(u_t\mid x_t), the objective is J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_\theta}[R(\tau)]. The Score function estimator gives \nabla_\theta p_\theta = p_\theta \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta, the log turns the product into a sum, p(x_0) and P differentiate to zero, and dropping the acausal terms leaves
\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t\,\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(u_t\mid x_t)\,G_t\right], \qquad G_t = \sum_{i\ge0}\gamma^i r_{t+i+1}.
REINFORCE runs one episode, walks backwards accumulating G, and applies \theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha\gamma^t G\,\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u_t\mid x_t) at each step. Its guarantee is that of stochastic gradient ascent with an unbiased estimate and Robbins-Monro step sizes, convergence to a stationary point of a J that is not concave in \theta. Week 9 puts the Policy gradient theorem behind the same estimator, which shows that the observed return occupies the place of Q^\pi and that any conditionally unbiased substitute is admissible there.
Connection to classical control
A control engineer has met this under other names. Iterative feedback tuning perturbs the parameters of a fixed-structure controller, measures the closed-loop cost, and steps down an estimated gradient; extremum-seeking control does the same continuously with a dither signal, estimating the gradient of a performance map nobody models. REINFORCE differs in where the randomness comes from. The dither is the policy’s own stochasticity, and the score identity converts it into an exact gradient estimate instead of a finite difference. The known limitations transfer with the structure: the achievable design is bounded by the parameterisation chosen in advance, and the estimate degrades as the number of tuned parameters grows.
Key limitation
Three prices are paid immediately and all three follow from building the estimator out of complete observed returns. The method is on-policy by construction, since the expectation is under p_\theta and one update invalidates the data. It is episodic, since G_t is a sum over the remainder of the episode, so a continuing task has to be cut into artificial episodes first. Its variance grows with the horizon, because one scalar return multiplies the whole gradient vector and that return accumulates the randomness of every transition after t. A further trap is the factor \gamma^t, which most implementations drop; the result is a different optimisation problem, one that weights a decision at step 200 as heavily as a decision at step 0.
Anchor numbers
On the 961-cell swing-up with five torques and the trip switched off, with a tabular softmax over the same 961\times5 numbers Q-learning stores: REINFORCE reaches -137.9 after 6.5\times10^6 transitions where Q-learning reaches -127.2 (97\% of J^\star = -123.1) after 7.5\times10^5. That is at least 8.6\times the data, a lower bound because REINFORCE never reaches Q-learning’s level inside its budget. At the matched budget of 7.5\times10^5 transitions the inter-seed spread is 18.4 against 2.4. The usable step sizes sit three decades apart, \alpha = 3\times10^{-5} against 0.2, so a range carried over from a value method is meaningless for a policy method. That experiment is run on ground chosen to favour tabular value learning, and it does not test continuous action spaces, structured policy classes, or problems where the optimal policy is easier to represent than the value function. Week 9 measures the variance directly at a frozen policy on the same chain, \mathrm{Var}(\hat g)/\|\mathbb{E}\hat g\|^2 = 2.0\times10^{3} for one episode of the reward-to-go estimator, and a state-dependent Baseline (variance reduction) cuts it by 11.3\times without moving the mean.

04_concepts/policy-gradient-theorem.title: Policy gradient theorem
04_concepts/policy-gradient-theorem.content:
Policy gradient theorem
The exact identity \nabla_\theta J = \sum_x d^\pi_\gamma(x)\sum_u \nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(u\mid x)\,Q^\pi(x,u), which factors the gradient of expected return into a state-visitation measure, a score the policy class supplies in closed form, and an action value, with no derivative of the transition kernel anywhere in it.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: a policy × no dynamics model. It is the theorem standing behind the cell that Week 6 opened with an estimator, and it holds equally when a model is available, since nothing in it uses one.
Bellman object approximated: none. The objective is differentiated directly. A Bellman recursion appears inside the proof, for \nabla_\theta V^\pi, and it is unrolled and discarded rather than solved.
Failure mode addressed: none. It localises failure mode 2 instead, by showing that Q^\pi is the only factor of three that has to be estimated.
Course first appearance: Week 9, three weeks after the estimator it justifies

Core idea
Week 6 obtained a usable gradient by applying the likelihood-ratio identity to the whole trajectory density, which is exact and keeps every structure of the problem hidden inside \tau. Nothing in that form distinguishes the decision at step 3 from the decision at step 200, and nothing names the quantity the algorithm is implicitly estimating. Grouping the same expectation by the states the closed loop visits separates three factors with three different origins. The visitation measure is a property of the closed loop that a rollout samples, the score is a property of a policy class we wrote ourselves, and the action value is the one factor that is neither given nor computable.
Formal definition
Let \mathcal{X} and \mathcal{U} be finite, let \pi_\theta(u\mid x) be differentiable in \theta, let the stage reward r and the kernel P be independent of \theta, and let \gamma\in(0,1). With J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x_0\sim\rho}[V^{\pi_\theta}(x_0)] and d^\pi_\gamma the Discounted state-visitation measure,
\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \sum_x d^\pi_\gamma(x)\sum_u \nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(u\mid x)\,Q^\pi(x,u).
The proof is a differentiation, a substitution and an unrolling. Differentiating V^\pi(x)=\sum_u\pi_\theta(u\mid x)Q^\pi(x,u) with the product rule gives a local term \varphi(x)=\sum_u\nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(u\mid x)Q^\pi(x,u) plus the effect of \theta on everything downstream. That second term is pushed one step into the future by \nabla_\theta Q^\pi(x,u)=\gamma\sum_{x'}P(x'\mid x,u)\nabla_\theta V^\pi(x'), which is where \nabla_\theta r=0 and \nabla_\theta P=0 remove the model. What is left is a Bellman evaluation equation in the vector of gradients, \nabla_\theta V^\pi = \varphi + \gamma P^\pi \nabla_\theta V^\pi, whose k-step unrolling leaves a remainder carrying \gamma^k that vanishes on a finite state space with bounded gradients. Two further exact rewritings make it samplable. The identity \nabla_\theta\pi_\theta=\pi_\theta\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta turns the action sum into an expectation the policy already draws from, and the definition of d^\pi_\gamma turns the state weighting into a \gamma^t weighting of the steps of a rollout, leaving
\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_\theta}\Big[\sum_t \gamma^t\,\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u_t\mid x_t)\,Q^\pi(x_t,u_t)\Big].
Any Y_t with \mathbb{E}[Y_t\mid x_t,u_t]=Q^\pi(x_t,u_t) may take the place of Q^\pi by the tower property, since the score is a function of (x_t,u_t) alone. REINFORCE takes Y_t=G_t; every method from Week 10 to Week 12 is a different choice at this one point.
Connection to classical control
The theorem is the sensitivity of a closed-loop performance index to the parameters of the controller, obtained without differentiating the plant. An engineer computing \partial J/\partial K for an LQR gain does the same thing analytically, by differentiating the Lyapunov equation that gives the closed-loop cost, and the resulting formula contains A and B explicitly. The exchange is visible in the statement. The analytical route needs a model and returns an exact gradient. This route needs no model and returns a gradient written in terms of Q^\pi and d^\pi_\gamma, neither of which is known, so both are paid for in samples. The cancellation \nabla_\theta P = 0 needs nothing of P beyond its independence from the controller parameters, so it survives contacts and friction alike.
Key limitation
The theorem is an equality and says nothing about the cost of evaluating either side. It also carries one hypothesis that decides the economics of the whole method. The states are weighted by d^\pi_\gamma, the visitation measure of the policy whose gradient is being computed, so the moment \theta moves every stored trajectory samples the wrong measure and the method is on-policy by construction. What the cancellation does not say is that the dynamics are irrelevant. They shape d^\pi_\gamma, which decides where the gradient is accumulated, and they shape Q^\pi, which decides its sign and size. They are sampled rather than differentiated.

04_concepts/policy-improvement-theorem.title: Policy improvement theorem
04_concepts/policy-improvement-theorem.content:
Policy improvement theorem
Acting greedily with respect to the exact value of the current policy gives a policy at least as good at every state, and equality certifies that the current policy is already optimal.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — it powers Policy iteration in the top-left cell and reappears as the justification for every actor update from Week 10
Failure mode addressed: none; its collapse under approximate evaluation is one root of failure mode 1
Course first appearance: Week 3

Core idea
Evaluation on its own improves nothing, and the maximisation on its own has no reference point. The theorem is what couples them: it says a single greedy pass against an exactly evaluated V^\pi can never lose ground at any state. Two structural consequences follow. Policy iteration terminates rather than merely converging, and the improvement is componentwise, so there is no state traded against another.
Formal definition
Let \pi be stationary with value V^\pi, and let \pi' be greedy with respect to V^\pi. Then V^{\pi'}(x) \ge V^\pi(x) for every x, and if V^{\pi'} = V^\pi then \pi is optimal.
The proof is two lines plus monotonicity of the Bellman operator. By construction \pi' attains the max, so \mathcal{T}^{\pi'}V^\pi = \mathcal{T}V^\pi, giving
V^\pi = \mathcal{T}^\pi V^\pi \;\le\; \mathcal{T}V^\pi \;=\; \mathcal{T}^{\pi'}V^\pi .
Applying \mathcal{T}^{\pi'} repeatedly preserves the inequality and produces the chain V^\pi \le \mathcal{T}^{\pi'}V^\pi \le (\mathcal{T}^{\pi'})^2 V^\pi \le \cdots, whose limit is V^{\pi'} by the contraction property. For the second claim, V^{\pi'} = V^\pi forces V^\pi = \mathcal{T}V^\pi, and uniqueness of the fixed point gives V^\pi = V^\star. On the Week 3 three-state MDP the theorem is visible in the table: V^{\pi_0} = (0,0,100) \le (0,71,100) = V^{\pi_1}, with strict improvement at one state only, which is all the theorem promises.
Connection to classical control
In the linear-quadratic case the improvement step is the Newton step on the discrete algebraic Riccati equation, and the componentwise inequality becomes the matrix ordering P_{k+1} \preceq P_k on the closed-loop cost matrices: each Newton iterate is a stabilising gain whose closed-loop cost dominates the next. Monotone-plus-bounded is the same argument shape that Lyapunov arguments use to conclude convergence, with the ordering supplied by the improvement step instead of by a decrescent function.
Key limitation
Every step of the proof uses V^\pi exactly, and the first equality V^\pi = \mathcal{T}^\pi V^\pi is precisely what an approximation breaks. With \hat V \approx V^\pi the chain stops telescoping and the improved policy can be strictly worse than the one it replaced. Week 6 meets that situation directly: a learner interacting with a robot has an estimate that is random, data-dependent and still changing, so the strict alternation becomes Generalised policy iteration and the finite staircase becomes an asymptotic statement whose hypotheses are GLIE and the Robbins-Monro step-size conditions. Weeks 9 and 10 buy back an approximate version by restricting how far the policy may move per update (trust regions, and the monotonic-improvement bound behind TRPO and PPO). Extracting the greedy policy also needs the model at decision time unless a Q-function is stored, which is why the model-free branch learns Q from Week 6 onward.

04_concepts/policy-iteration.title: Policy iteration
04_concepts/policy-iteration.content:
Policy iteration
Alternate an exact evaluation of the current policy with one greedy improvement step; on a finite MDP the loop terminates at an optimal policy after finitely many iterations.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value function × dynamics model available (the same cell as Value iteration and LQR)
Failure mode addressed: none; its monotonicity guarantee is the first casualty of approximate evaluation, which is failure mode 1 territory
Course first appearance: Week 3

Core idea
Holding the policy fixed deletes the maximisation from the Bellman recursion, and what is left is linear. Evaluation therefore becomes one matrix solve instead of a limit of sweeps, and the only nonlinearity left in the problem is concentrated in a single greedy pass over the states. The two algorithms of Week 3 differ in where they spend: Value iteration takes many cheap sweeps and converges asymptotically, policy iteration takes few expensive steps and stops exactly.
Formal definition
With (r_\pi)_x = r(x,\pi(x)) and (P_\pi)_{xx'} = P(x' \mid x, \pi(x)), evaluation is the linear system
(I - \gamma P_\pi)V^\pi = r_\pi,
invertible because P_\pi is row-stochastic, so \rho(\gamma P_\pi) \le \gamma < 1. The same discount that makes the Bellman operator a contraction makes this matrix nonsingular; the Neumann expansion (I-\gamma P_\pi)^{-1} = \sum_k \gamma^k P_\pi^k shows the entries are expected discounted visit counts. Improvement is one greedy sweep,
\pi_{k+1}(x) \in \arg\max_u \Big\{ r(x,u) + \gamma \sum_{x'} P(x'\mid x,u) V^{\pi_k}(x') \Big\},
and the loop stops when the policy stops changing. Termination is a counting argument: values improve monotonically (Policy improvement theorem), a monotone sequence cannot revisit a policy, and there are only |\mathcal{U}|^{|\mathcal{X}|} stationary deterministic policies.
Costs and iteration counts, measured on the two Week 3 examples. Evaluation costs \mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{X}|^3) against \mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{X}|^2|\mathcal{U}|) for one value-iteration sweep. On the three-state MDP, 3 evaluations against 110 sweeps for the same answer. On the 5\times5 gridworld (\gamma = 0.95, 4^{25} \approx 10^{15} policies), 6 evaluations reach 10^{-13} with errors 18.8, 17.8, 11.3, 3.01, 3.8\times10^{-2}, 10^{-13}, while value iteration needs 595 sweeps for 10^{-12}. Taking m sweeps of \mathcal{T}^\pi in place of the exact solve gives modified policy iteration, with m=1 recovering value iteration and m=\infty recovering policy iteration.
Connection to classical control
Specialised to the linear-quadratic case, evaluation is the discrete Lyapunov equation P = Q + K^\top R K + (A-BK)^\top P (A-BK), which is the Riccati equation with the minimisation deleted, and improvement returns K^+ = (R + B^\top P B)^{-1}B^\top P A. Alternating the two is a standard Newton method for the discrete algebraic Riccati equation (Kleinman 1968 in continuous time, Hewer 1971 in discrete time), which is exactly why the error sequence accelerates: the gaps widen from iteration to iteration, the signature of a Newton method, while iterating the Riccati recursion converges linearly. Policy iteration is therefore the same object control engineers already use to solve the DARE, stated for a general finite MDP.
Key limitation
The cubic evaluation cost is prohibitive well before the state space is interesting, which is why modified policy iteration exists. The whole guarantee rests on evaluating V^\pi exactly; with an approximation \hat V \approx V^\pi the improvement chain loses its telescoping structure and the improved policy can be strictly worse (Week 7). And like every method in this cell it reads P and r directly, so it does not survive the Week 4 assumption drop.
Related concepts
Value iteration | Policy improvement theorem | Bellman operator | Bellman residual | MDP | LQR | Dynamic programming | Curse of dimensionality | Actor-critic

Primary: Bertsekas, Dynamic Programming and Optimal Control, Vol. II, Ch. 1; Howard (1960)
Riccati connection: Kleinman (1968); Hewer (1971)
Secondary: Sutton & Barto (2nd ed.), Ch. 4
