04_concepts/policy-parameterisation.title: Policy parameterisation
04_concepts/policy-parameterisation.content:
Policy parameterisation
The choice of the family \pi_\theta(u\mid x) that a policy-based method searches over, which fixes the score used in every update and decides what behaviour the method can express at all.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: a policy × no dynamics model. In the value branch the approximator is a value function and the policy is read out of it by maximisation; here the approximator is the policy itself.
Bellman object approximated: none. The class is an object to be optimised, and no fixed-point equation is attached to it.
Failure mode addressed: none directly. It sets the exploration mechanism, which is failure mode 4, and its width sets the estimator variance, which is failure mode 2.
Course first appearance: Week 6 with a tabular softmax, developed in Week 9

Core idea
Choosing the class is a modelling decision of the kind this audience already makes when choosing PID over a state-feedback law, taken before any data arrives and binding on everything that follows. It admits the same kinds of prior knowledge that a controller structure does. Actuator bounds, symmetry between limbs and an existing controller can all be written into the class, where they hold by construction at every value of \theta and at every point during training. What the class cannot express, no amount of data will recover.
Formal definition
Two classes cover the course, and each is written out in its own note. The Softmax policy class over a finite action set, with features \phi(x,u)\in\mathbb{R}^p, is
\pi_\theta(u\mid x)=\frac{\exp(\theta^{\top}\phi(x,u))}{\sum_b \exp(\theta^{\top}\phi(x,b))},\qquad \nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u\mid x)=\phi(x,u)-\mathbb{E}_{b\sim\pi_\theta}[\phi(x,b)],
the feature vector of the action taken minus its average under the current policy, with the tabular case of Week 6 recovered by taking \phi to be the indicator of the pair. The Gaussian policy class for a continuous command, with a differentiable mean \mu_\theta(x)\in\mathbb{R}^m and fixed isotropic covariance, is
\pi_\theta(u\mid x)=\mathcal{N}\big(\mu_\theta(x),\sigma^2 I\big),\qquad \nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u\mid x)=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\big(\nabla_\theta\mu_\theta(x)\big)^{\top}\big(u-\mu_\theta(x)\big),
which points along the direction in parameter space that moves the mean towards the action sampled, scaled by how far that action fell. Structure enters the class directly and holds at every \theta. A squashed mean \mu_\theta(x)=u_{\max}\tanh(f_\theta(x)) cannot aim at a torque the actuator does not have, parameters shared across a quadruped’s four legs impose a gait symmetry, and \mu_\theta(x)=\mu_{\text{ctrl}}(x)+\Delta_\theta(x) learns a correction on top of a controller that already works.
Connection to classical control
This is controller structure selection, with the tuning done by measured gradients afterwards. A fixed-structure design fixes what can be achieved before any parameter is set, and the same discipline applies here. The saturation case is the sharpest instance. The actuator bound of Week 2 lives inside the class, where it holds identically, rather than inside a penalty the optimiser has to discover from data, which is the difference between a constraint and a preference. The bound covers the actuator and nothing else, since where the state goes is still unconstrained, and Week 13 takes up that distinction.
Key limitation
The class both explores and estimates, through the same parameter, in opposite directions, and no separate exploration mechanism exists to decouple them. It also fixes what is representable before any data arrive, so a behaviour outside the class stays out of reach whatever the optimiser does. Each class fails in its own way, the softmax by needing one preference per action and stalling once its probabilities saturate, the Gaussian by being unimodal where the optimal command is bang-bang. Both cases are worked in Softmax policy class and Gaussian policy class.
Related concepts
Softmax policy class | Gaussian policy class | Policy gradient theorem | Policy gradient (REINFORCE) | Score function estimator | Likelihood-ratio identity | Function approximation in RL | Torque-limited pendulum | Residual RL | Composition with classical control | Safe RL | Exploration-exploitation tradeoff | Baseline (variance reduction) | SAC
References

On the Gaussian class in robotics: Peters & Schaal (2008), Reinforcement learning of motor skills with policy gradients

04_concepts/principle-of-optimality.title: Principle of optimality
04_concepts/principle-of-optimality.content:
Principle of optimality
Once the current state is fixed, the remaining decisions of an optimal policy must themselves be optimal for the remaining problem: an optimal plan cannot contain a suboptimal tail.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — it is what makes every cell computable
Failure mode addressed: none (structural result, not a method)
Course first appearance: Week 1

Core idea
The principle is the structural observation that converts one optimisation over N coupled decisions into N decoupled one-stage optimisations. It is what makes Dynamic programming possible, and therefore what every method in this course is ultimately approximating. It holds because of two properties of the problem, additive cost and Markov dynamics, and it fails the moment either is removed.
Formal definition
Let \pi^* = \{\pi_0^*,\dots,\pi_{N-1}^*\} be optimal for the N-stage problem with cost J_\pi(x_0) = \mathbb{E}_w[g_N(x_N) + \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} g_k(x_k,\pi_k(x_k),w_k)]. Fix a stage i and a state x_i reached with positive probability under \pi^*. Then the truncated policy \{\pi_i^*,\dots,\pi_{N-1}^*\} is optimal for the tail subproblem
\min \; \mathbb{E}_w\Big[g_N(x_N) + \sum_{k=i}^{N-1} g_k(x_k,\pi_k(x_k),w_k) \,\Big|\, x_i\Big].
Proof by contradiction: splice a strictly better tail onto the optimal head. Additivity says total cost splits into head plus tail; the Markov property says the tail depends on the past only through x_i, so the head is unchanged. The composite policy then beats \pi^*, a contradiction.
Connection to classical control
This is the same argument that justifies the backward Riccati recursion: the stationary gain at stage k is computed as if stages k+1,\dots,N were already solved optimally, which is legitimate only because the tail is optimal by construction. In continuous time the identical argument, applied over an interval \delta t and taken to the limit, produces the HJB equation.
Key limitation
It requires additive cost and Markov dynamics. A risk-sensitive objective such as the variance of the total return is not additive over stages, so the principle fails, and with it the entire algorithmic chain of this course. This is one honest reason risk-sensitive control is harder than it looks.
Related concepts
Dynamic programming | Bellman equation | Markov property | HJB equation | Value function | Open-loop vs feedback
References

Primary: Bertsekas (2019), Reinforcement Learning and Optimal Control, Ch. 1
Original: Bellman (1957), Dynamic Programming

04_concepts/projected-bellman-equation.title: Projected Bellman equation
04_concepts/projected-bellman-equation.content:
Projected Bellman equation
The fixed-point equation \Phi w = \Pi_\mu \mathcal{T}^\pi \Phi w that TD learning solves under function approximation: one Bellman backup, then one weighted least-squares fit back into the representable family.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no model, as the object that replaces the Bellman equation once the table is gone
Failure mode addressed: it is where failure mode 1 is located, since the backup keeps its contraction and the fit is what can lose it
Course first appearance: Week 7

Core idea
A d-parameter family spans a d-dimensional subspace \mathcal{V} = \{\Phi w\} inside the |\mathcal{X}|-dimensional space of value functions, and the Bellman backup of a member of that family is a general vector outside it (Closure under the Bellman operator). The iteration a parametric method can afford is therefore a backup followed by a fit, and the fit is a projection weighted by whatever distribution the data have over states. Under on-policy data that weighting is the Stationary distribution d_\pi, both maps are nonexpansive in the same norm, and their composition is a \gamma-contraction with a unique fixed point.
Formal definition
For a distribution \mu with \mu(x) > 0 everywhere, put D = \mathrm{diag}(\mu), \|v\|_\mu^2 = v^\top D v, and
\Pi_\mu v = \arg\min_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\|u - v\|_\mu = \Phi(\Phi^\top D\Phi)^{-1}\Phi^\top D v .
Tsitsiklis and Van Roy (1997) established the following. With \Phi of full column rank, an irreducible aperiodic chain, bounded rewards, Robbins-Monro step sizes and on-policy data, semi-gradient TD(0) converges with probability 1 to the w_{\mathrm{TD}} solving
\Phi w_{\mathrm{TD}} = \Pi_{d_\pi}\mathcal{T}^\pi\bigl(\Phi w_{\mathrm{TD}}\bigr), \qquad \|\Phi w_{\mathrm{TD}} - V^\pi\|_{d_\pi} \le \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\gamma^2}}\,\min_w\|\Phi w - V^\pi\|_{d_\pi}.
The bound compares the limit against the best approximation the features allow, a quantity no learning rule can beat. The factor is 2.29 at \gamma = 0.9 and 5.0 at \gamma = 0.98. That factor is the price of learning by bootstrapping instead of regressing on true values, and better features improve the limit with no change to the update rule.
Connection to classical control
The argument is a cascade certified in one norm. The map \gamma P^\pi contracts by \gamma in \|\cdot\|_{d_\pi}, orthogonal projection is nonexpansive in the norm that defines it, and the composition inherits the modulus, which is the Banach argument of Week 3 run through one extra block. The subtlety is that both blocks must be certified in the same norm. That is the familiar situation in which two subsystems are each stable under their own quadratic form and the interconnection is proved only once a single common form works for both.
Key limitation
Everything rests on the weighting matching the operator and on the family being a subspace. Let a behaviour policy supply the data and the projection is weighted by d_b while the backup is still \mathcal{T}^\pi, so P^\pi can expand in that norm and the contraction argument disappears (Deadly triad, Baird’s counterexample). Replace \Phi w by a network and the representable set is curved, the best fit inside it is no longer an orthogonal projection, and the argument fails for a second reason that adds to the first. The bound is also silent about the size of \min_w\|\Phi w - V^\pi\|, which the feature map fixes before any data arrive.
Related concepts
Function approximation in RL | Stationary distribution | Semi-gradient update | Bellman operator | Closure under the Bellman operator | LSTD | Deadly triad | TD learning | Bellman residual | DQN
References

Primary: Tsitsiklis & Van Roy (1997), An analysis of temporal difference learning with function approximation
Sutton & Barto (2018), Sections 9.1 to 9.4
Operator-first treatment: Bertsekas (2019), Ch. 6

04_concepts/q-learning.title: Q-learning
04_concepts/q-learning.content:
Q-learning
Off-policy TD control: the same one-transition update with the successor value taken as the maximum over the row, which removes the behaviour policy from the target and leaves it in charge of nothing but which entries receive updates.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value function × no dynamics model
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T}, the optimality operator, on sampled transitions, with the maximisation inside the target
Failure mode addressed: none; it contributes two of the three Deadly triad ingredients, bootstrapping and off-policy data
Course first appearance: Week 6

Core idea
SARSA and Q-learning differ in one term. Where SARSA bootstraps from the action the behaviour policy took, Q-learning bootstraps from the best action available, so the target describes a policy that never explores while the data still contains exploration. The consequence is structural: the behaviour policy becomes a free choice, and a transition stays usable long after the policy that produced it has been discarded.
Formal definition
\delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma \max_b Q(x_{t+1}, b) - Q(x_t, u_t), \qquad Q(x_t,u_t) \leftarrow Q(x_t,u_t) + \alpha\,\delta_t .
The update consumes (x_t, u_t, r_{t+1}, x_{t+1}) alone, which is what makes replay possible.
Convergence (Watkins & Dayan 1992; Tsitsiklis 1994). With finite \mathcal{X} and \mathcal{U}, rewards of bounded variance, per-pair Robbins-Monro step sizes, and every state-action pair visited infinitely often with probability 1, then Q_t \to Q^* with probability 1. The behaviour policy may be arbitrary provided it supplies that visitation, which is a strictly weaker hypothesis than the GLIE condition SARSA needs.
Why the behaviour policy drops out. Conditioning on the executed pair,
\mathbb{E}\big[r_{t+1} + \gamma\max_b Q(x_{t+1},b) \,\big|\, x_t = x, u_t = u\big] = r(x,u) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}_{x' \sim P(\cdot\mid x,u)}\big[\max_b Q(x',b)\big] = (\mathcal{T}Q)(x,u),
whatever chose u. The mean flow \dot Q = \mathcal{T}Q - Q has Q^* as its unique equilibrium, and with D(t) = \|Q(t) - Q^*\|_\infty the contraction gives D^+D \le -(1-\gamma)D, so D(t) \le e^{-(1-\gamma)t}D(0). The rate degrades as \gamma \to 1, in step with the effective horizon 1/(1-\gamma). That argument locates the limit; the asynchronous proof also needs the iterates to stay bounded.
Connection to classical control
The contraction bound \|\mathcal{T}Q - \mathcal{T}W\|_\infty \le \gamma\|Q-W\|_\infty has now been read three ways in this course. Week 3 used it as a fixed-point argument supplying existence, uniqueness and the geometric rate of Value iteration. Week 5 used it as a spectral bound placing the eigenvalues of a linear mean flow in the open left half plane. Here it is a Lyapunov function, since \|Q - Q^*\|_\infty is a decreasing certificate for a nonlinear flow. Week 7 is where the certificate is lost, because a projection composed with a \sup-norm contraction need not contract in any norm the algorithm respects.
Key limitation
The maximum of unbiased estimates is a biased estimate of the maximum, biased upwards, so Q-learning overestimates action values while the table is noisy (Maximisation bias). On a table with decaying step sizes that bias vanishes with the noise, and with a function approximator it does not. Off-policy freedom buys no information: a pair the behaviour policy never visits carries no data, which is Coverage and is the constraint that survives every change of target policy. The greedy target also makes the learned policy sit against whatever boundary is cheapest, with no allowance for the exploration that is still being executed.
Anchor numbers
On the swing-up chain with the overspeed trip, at \varepsilon = 0.10 fixed: Q-learning settles at -160.0 while learning, trips 1.3 times per 100 episodes against SARSA’s 0.5, and ends 1.7 from J^\star = -124.0 when deployed greedily against SARSA’s 5.3. With the trip switched off it reaches -127.2, which is 97\% of J^\star = -123.1, after 7.5\times10^5 transitions, and its inter-seed spread at that budget is 2.4 against REINFORCE’s 18.4.
Related concepts
SARSA | TD learning | Off-policy learning | Coverage | Maximisation bias | Experience replay | Bootstrapping | Bellman operator | Value iteration | Deadly triad | DQN | Epsilon-greedy | GLIE | Stochastic approximation | Offline RL | Torque-limited pendulum
References

Original paper: Watkins (1989), thesis; Watkins & Dayan (1992), Q-learning, four pages, worth reading for the assumption list
Convergence: Tsitsiklis (1994), Asynchronous stochastic approximation and Q-learning

04_concepts/rl-as-approximate-dynamic-pr.title: RL as approximate dynamic programming
04_concepts/rl-as-approximate-dynamic-pr.content:
RL as approximate dynamic programming
Reinforcement learning is optimal control with an unknown transition model: a sample-based approximation of dynamic programming, not a separate intellectual tradition.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: the right-hand column of the Unifying diagram — the same problem as the left, with f replaced by interaction
Failure mode addressed: none (it is the framing of the course)
Course first appearance: Week 1

Core idea
Almost every algorithm in this course is a recognisable approximation of an object built in the first three weeks. RL trades model knowledge for data: what you do not know about f, you must pay for in interaction. Three regimes are worth separating: dynamics nonlinear but known (dynamic programming, iLQR, trajectory optimisation, MPC; Weeks 2–3); dynamics unknown but interaction allowed (reinforcement learning; Weeks 4–15); dynamics unknown and interaction expensive or dangerous (the specific difficulty that makes robotics hard; Weeks 11–13).
Formal definition
The problem statement is unchanged from optimal control:
V^*(x) = \max_{u}\ \mathbb{E}_w\big[r(x,u,w) + \gamma V^*(f(x,u,w))\big].
What changes is that f and the distribution of w are unavailable, so \mathbb{E}_w cannot be computed and must be replaced by sampled transitions. Everything that was a computation now carries statistical error, and every state you have not visited is a state about which you know nothing.
Connection to classical control
This note is the connection: the Bellman equation of RL is the Bellman equation of dynamic programming, the DARE is a fixed-point equation of the same kind, TD learning is Robbins–Monro stochastic approximation applied to it, and value iteration converges by the Banach fixed-point theorem. Read the field this way and the second half of the course is legible; read it as a branch of machine learning and it is not.
Not a generic machine-learning problem
In supervised learning the data distribution is fixed and given. Here the data is generated by the policy you are currently improving, so changing the policy changes the data, which changes the policy. That feedback loop is the source of most of the difficulties in the second half of the course (failure modes 2 and 3).
Key limitation
RL is not a replacement for classical control, and it is generally not sample-efficient. The claim that “end-to-end learning removes the need for engineering” is largely false for real robots in 2026: working systems are hybrid, combining system identification with learned residual dynamics, MPC with a learned model, or imitation learning followed by RL fine-tuning. See Composition with classical control.
Related concepts
Unifying diagram | Composition with classical control | Dynamic programming | Bellman equation | Sample complexity | Failure modes of approximate RL
References

Recht (2019), “A Tour of Reinforcement Learning: The View from Continuous Control” (arXiv:1806.09460)
Meyn (2022), Control Systems and Reinforcement Learning

04_concepts/regret.title: Regret
04_concepts/regret.content:
Regret
The shortfall of an algorithm’s expected reward against always playing the best arm, R_T = T\mu^\star - \mathbb{E}[\sum_t \mu_{a_t}], which prices exploration and exploitation errors on one scale.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational for the right-hand column, since it is the metric every exploration rule is designed against
Failure mode addressed: none; it is the measurement that makes insufficient exploration visible
Course first appearance: Week 4

Core idea
A learner that always pulls the arm with the highest current estimate can lock onto a bad arm for ever; a learner that pulls uniformly collects excellent estimates and acts on none of them. Regret is the scalar that charges both mistakes against the same benchmark, one that knows \mu^\star and that no algorithm has access to. It therefore measures the price of not knowing, which is the quantity the Exploration-exploitation tradeoff asks us to put a number on.
Formal definition
With n_i(T) = \#\{t \le T : a_t = i\} and \sum_i n_i(T) = T, the definition rewrites arm by arm:
R_T = T\mu^\star - \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu_{a_t}\Big] = \sum_{i=1}^{K}\Delta_i\,\mathbb{E}[n_i(T)].
The second form is the one every analysis manipulates. Gaps are properties of the instance and cannot be influenced, so the expected counts are the only quantities in the learner’s power: designing an exploration rule means deciding how many pulls each bad arm is allowed.
The achievable growth rate is settled by the Lai and Robbins (1985) asymptotic lower bound. For Bernoulli arms and any uniformly efficient algorithm,
\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{R_T}{\ln T} \;\ge\; \sum_{i:\Delta_i>0}\frac{\Delta_i}{\mathrm{kl}(\mu_i,\mu^\star)},\qquad \mathrm{kl}(p,q)=p\ln\tfrac{p}{q}+(1-p)\ln\tfrac{1-p}{1-q}.
Logarithmic regret is the best possible order, and it appears in the lower bound before any algorithm has been named. The coefficient says what makes an instance hard: the evidence a single pull provides about the difference between arm i and the optimum, measured by a relative entropy. For small gaps \mathrm{kl}(\mu_i,\mu^\star) \approx \Delta_i^2 / (2\mu^\star(1-\mu^\star)), so the coefficient reduces to the 1/\Delta_i price counted directly in Sample complexity. The lower bound and the sample-complexity argument are one statement in two notations.
Connection to classical control
Regret is a cumulative cost measured against an oracle benchmark, which places it beside the LQR cost functional with one difference in kind: the benchmark is unknowable to the controller, so regret is an analysis quantity rather than something the algorithm can evaluate online. Its role resembles that of a performance bound in adaptive control, certifying asymptotic behaviour while leaving finite-time performance to be measured.
Key limitation
Two limitations matter on hardware. The bound constrains a \liminf, so an algorithm may sit below the asymptote at any finite horizon: on the Week 4 instance the Lai-Robbins coefficient 36.47 evaluates to 420 at T=10^5 while Thompson sampling measures 215, with no contradiction. Quoting a limiting bound as a finite-sample guarantee is among the most common errors in reading this literature. Second, regret counts foregone reward only, and a reward-only accounting rates the dangerous algorithms highest: against the best admissible arm on the Week 4 safety instance, both unconstrained rules achieve negative regret by exploiting an arm the constraint forbids (Safe exploration).
Related concepts
Bandit problem | Exploration-exploitation tradeoff | Sample complexity | UCB | Thompson sampling | Epsilon-greedy | Safe exploration
References

Primary: Lattimore & Szepesvári, Bandit Algorithms (2020), Ch. 4 and Ch. 16
Original paper: Lai & Robbins (1985), Asymptotically efficient adaptive allocation rules

04_concepts/residual-rl.title: Residual RL
04_concepts/residual-rl.content:
Residual RL
Learning only a correction on top of a controller that already works, \mu_\theta(x)=\mu_{\text{ctrl}}(x)+\Delta_\theta(x), so that the classical law supplies the behaviour on day one and the learned term covers what the model missed.

Stub. This concept is planted in Weeks 2 and 9 and formalized in Week 12.
Expand this note after Week 12’s session.

Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: a policy × no dynamics model, since the learned object \Delta_\theta is a correction to a control law. The Week 2 planting sits one level down, on f, and belongs to the left-hand column
Bellman object approximated: none of its own. The residual inherits whatever object trains it, which in Week 12 is an offline value method
Failure mode addressed: 3 and 5 in practice, by keeping the deployed behaviour near a law whose properties are known. Neither is addressed by construction, and a residual large enough to matter is a residual large enough to leave that neighbourhood
Course first appearance: Week 9, on the policy class. The same shape is planted one level down in Week 2, on the dynamics, where the notes name Week 12’s residual RL by title; formalised in Week 12

Planted framing (Week 2)
Week 2 plants the shape one level down, on the dynamics. The forward reference at the end of the MPC section describes the effective recipe for a learned model as known rigid-body physics plus a learned residual for the effects nobody modelled, typically contact and friction, and it names Week 12’s residual RL as the second of the two places where this course argues that classical and learned components compose. The arithmetic is the same at both levels. A trusted term supplies the behaviour on day one and a learned term covers what the model missed, with Model bias as the price when the residual sits on f and the coverage of the training data as the price when it sits on the policy.
Planted framing (Week 9)
Week 9 reaches it from the policy class rather than from the safety argument. Choosing the parameterisation is a controller-design decision, and a class written as a trusted law plus a learned residual is one of the three kinds of structure the session shows a policy class carrying, alongside actuator saturation through a squashed mean and symmetry through shared parameters. A value function has no natural place to express any of the three, because they are statements about the map from state to command. The composition principle of the course appears here in its most literal form, and the notes point forward to Week 12 by name.

04_concepts/rollout.title: Rollout
04_concepts/rollout.content:
Rollout
One execution of a fixed policy on the system, from a drawn initial state until termination, producing the trajectory that is the unit of data and the unit of cost in every model-free method.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational, and specific to the right-hand column. It is what stands in for the transition kernel the model-free methods do not have.
Bellman object approximated: none. A rollout is a measurement, and what is done with it decides which operator, if any, is being sampled.
Failure mode addressed: none. It is the mechanism whose price is Sample complexity, and whose reach is Coverage.
Course first appearance: Week 6, where the trajectory density is written down and the name is attached. The object it names is already running in Week 5 as the episode averaged by Monte Carlo policy evaluation

Core idea
Every quantity a model-free method wants is an expectation over the closed loop, and the closed loop is the one object that can be run even when P is unknown. A rollout runs it once. Where dynamic programming evaluates an expectation by summing against a known kernel, a model-free method draws from the kernel by letting the plant advance and records what came back, so a single number such as \nabla_\theta J is measured by repeating the experiment instead of by computing an integral.
Formal definition
Running \pi_\theta on the environment produces \tau=(x_0,u_0,r_1,x_1,u_1,r_2,\dots) distributed as
p_\theta(\tau)=p(x_0)\prod_{t\ge0}P(x_{t+1}\mid x_t,u_t)\,\pi_\theta(u_t\mid x_t),
with discounted return R(\tau)=\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t r_{t+1}. One rollout is one draw from p_\theta, so for any f carrying no \theta the average over N independent rollouts,
\hat{J}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}f(\tau_i)\;\xrightarrow{\;N\to\infty\;}\;\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_\theta}[f(\tau)],
is unbiased at every N and has standard error falling as 1/\sqrt{N}. Two properties of the density carry most of the course’s weight. It factorises over time, which is what lets the score of a trajectory split into a sum of per-step policy scores, and it contains \theta only through \pi_\theta, which is why the unknown P cancels in the Likelihood-ratio identity. The factor p(x_0) matters as much as the kernel. A rollout samples the Discounted state-visitation measure of the current policy and nothing else, so states the policy does not reach are absent from every estimate formed this way.
Connection to classical control
A rollout is a closed-loop experiment, either on hardware or in simulation, and the whole apparatus of experiment design applies to it. The initial-state distribution is the operating condition, the policy’s randomisation is the excitation, and the episode length is the record length. The word also has an older and narrower meaning in dynamic programming, where the rollout algorithm evaluates a base policy by simulation and uses that estimate as the tail cost in a one-step lookahead. That is the same construction as MPC with the terminal cost obtained by running a controller forward instead of by solving a Riccati equation, and it is the direct ancestor of the Terminal cost approximation idea of Week 3.
Key limitation
A rollout needs a termination condition, so a continuing task such as a balancing controller meant to run for hours has to be cut into artificial episodes before any return exists. On hardware the count is the real budget, since each rollout costs wall-clock time and wear, with some risk of damage, and no amount of algorithmic care converts one rollout into two. On-policy methods add a second cost. The data are draws from p_{\theta_k}, so a single parameter update invalidates every rollout that produced it, and Importance sampling is the only exact repair.
Related concepts

04_concepts/sac.title: SAC
04_concepts/sac.content:
SAC
Soft actor-critic: an off-policy actor-critic with a stochastic actor that is paid for keeping its action distribution spread out, so exploration is written into the objective instead of bolted onto the data collection.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: both × no dynamics model, the bottom row, on the off-policy and stochastic corner of the Design-space diagram
Bellman object approximated: a softened \mathcal{T}^\pi. The entropy term makes the action aggregation in its Bellman equation a log-sum-exp, which interpolates between \mathcal{T}^\pi and the \mathcal{T} of Q-learning as the temperature goes to zero.
Failure modes addressed: 2, by the critic; 4, insufficient exploration, inside the objective; and sample efficiency through replay. It carries all three legs of the Deadly triad.
Course first appearance: Week 10, and it is the usual first choice for continuous-control robotics

Core idea
Epsilon-greedy and additive action noise treat exploration as something added to a policy after the fact, which is why they are unsafe by construction and why they need a schedule tuned per environment. Adding the policy’s entropy to the reward makes spread-out behaviour part of what is being optimised, so the policy gives up randomness only where the return pays for it. What results is a stochastic actor that keeps a replay buffer, which is the combination DDPG gives up and PPO cannot afford.
Formal definition
The objective becomes
J_{\mathrm{ent}}(\pi) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_t \gamma^{\,t}\big(r_{t+1} + \eta\,\mathcal{H}(\pi(\cdot\mid x_t))\big)\Big],
with \mathcal{H} the entropy of the action distribution and \eta a temperature, in practice tuned automatically against a target entropy. Twin critics are used with the smaller of the two entering the target, as in TD3, and the actor is a squashed Gaussian policy class reparameterised so that the gradient flows through the sampled action.
The footnote the row rule needs. Week 1 stated that a critic’s operator carries no \max, which is what separates it from Q-learning and what makes failure mode 1 arrive in a weaker form. SAC is the one place in the course where that reading needs qualifying, because the optimal value function of J_{\mathrm{ent}} satisfies a Bellman equation whose action aggregation is a soft maximum. The placement on the Unifying diagram is unaffected, since the row rule turns on Bootstrapping and not on the presence of a maximisation.
Connection to classical control
Maximum-entropy control is the stochastic-optimal-control problem with a relative-entropy penalty on the control distribution, the same regulariser that appears in risk-sensitive and minimum-relative-entropy formulations. The temperature \eta plays the part of the control-weighting matrix R in LQR, trading performance against how hard the controller is willing to commit, and the resulting soft optimal policy is a Boltzmann distribution over Q in the same way the linear-quadratic-Gaussian solution is a Gaussian around the certainty-equivalent gain.
Key limitation
The construction restores all three triad legs, so the stabilisation machinery is doing real work and the method is not exempt from failure mode 1. The entropy term changes the problem being solved, so the optimum of J_{\mathrm{ent}} is not the optimum of J, and the gap is set by a temperature that must be chosen or tuned. Entropy also buys exploration in the sense of keeping the action distribution wide, which is undirected: it is not the informed exploration of UCB or Thompson sampling, and it does not address a state the policy has no reason to move toward.
Related concepts

References

Primary: Haarnoja, Zhou, Abbeel & Levine (2018), Soft actor-critic
Twin critics and target smoothing: Fujimoto et al. (2018)
Maximum-entropy formulation: Ziebart et al. (2008) for the earlier statement of the objective

04_concepts/sarsa.title: SARSA
04_concepts/sarsa.content:
SARSA
On-policy TD control: Week 5’s TD(0) update with the table indexed by state-action pairs and the successor value read at the action the behaviour policy actually chose, so the exploration the learner performs enters the target it learns.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value function × no dynamics model — the same cell as TD learning, with the policy moved from the problem statement into the unknowns
Bellman object approximated: Exploration-aware Bellman operator \mathcal{T}_\varepsilon at fixed \varepsilon, and \mathcal{T} only in the GLIE limit
Failure mode addressed: none; it supplies the Bootstrapping ingredient that failure mode 1 needs in Week 7
Course first appearance: Week 6

Core idea
Week 5 could bootstrap from a single number because the policy had already fixed the action at the successor state. In control that action is an open question, and SARSA answers it with the action the behaviour policy is about to take anyway. The learned object is then the value of a policy that includes its own exploration, which is the correct object whenever the exploration is still running at deployment and a mistaken one when it is switched off.
Formal definition
Given the five quantities (x_t, u_t, r_{t+1}, x_{t+1}, u_{t+1}), where u_{t+1} is drawn from the same \varepsilon-greedy rule that produced u_t,
\delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma\, Q(x_{t+1}, u_{t+1}) - Q(x_t, u_t), \qquad Q(x_t,u_t) \leftarrow Q(x_t,u_t) + \alpha\,\delta_t .
The name records those five quantities, and the fifth is what makes the method on-policy.
Convergence (Singh, Jaakkola, Littman & Szepesvári 2000). With \mathcal{X} and \mathcal{U} finite, rewards of bounded variance, per-pair step sizes satisfying \sum_{t:(x_t,u_t)=(x,u)}\alpha_t = \infty and \sum_{t:(x_t,u_t)=(x,u)}\alpha_t^2 < \infty, and a GLIE behaviour policy, Q_t \to Q^* with probability 1. The two GLIE clauses do separate jobs. Infinite exploration supplies the samples; asymptotic greediness is what makes the limit Q^*, because the target evaluates whatever policy is generating the data, and that policy is becoming the greedy one.
At fixed \varepsilon clause 2 fails and the algorithm still converges, to the fixed point Q^*_\varepsilon of \mathcal{T}_\varepsilon. That limit answers a well-posed question: which policy is best among those that keep exploring at rate \varepsilon.
Connection to classical control
The block diagram is the self-tuning regulator’s. An estimator updates from closed-loop data, a design step recomputes a controller from the current estimate, and that controller decides what the estimator sees next, which is Generalised policy iteration with the plant model replaced by an action-value function. The fixed-\varepsilon reading is more specific still: \mathcal{T}_\varepsilon is the optimality operator of a plant with a known stochastic actuator fault, so SARSA at constant exploration is solving an optimal control problem exactly, for the perturbed plant instead of the nominal one.
Key limitation
SARSA reaches Q^* only under a schedule that vanishes, and any exploration rate held constant moves the target to Q^*_\varepsilon, whose margin away from expensive states becomes a cost the moment exploration stops. Everything above is tabular. The \sup-norm certificate that carries the proof has no analogue once Q becomes a parametric approximator (Deadly triad, Week 7), and the visitation condition on pairs is stronger than Week 5’s condition on states, so an action the policy stops trying is an action it stops learning about.
Anchor numbers
On the 961-cell torque-limited swing-up chain with an overspeed trip costing 3000 (about twenty-four nominal swing-ups), at \varepsilon = 0.10 held fixed, \alpha = 0.05, 1.5\times10^5 episodes and 10 seeds: SARSA settles at -148.6 against Q-learning’s -160.0, so it pays 7.2\% less while learning, and trips the drive 0.5 times per 100 episodes against 1.3. Executed greedily afterwards it ends 5.3 from J^\star = -124.0 where Q-learning ends 1.7, a factor 3.2 in the opposite direction. Computed exactly, the two fixed points separate by 5.3\% at \varepsilon = 0.05, 11.4\% at 0.10 and 22.1\% at 0.20.
Related concepts

04_concepts/safe-exploration.title: Safe exploration
04_concepts/safe-exploration.content:
Safe exploration
Exploration under a hard admissibility condition on a second outcome, so that the algorithm optimises reward subject to keeping the damage probability below a threshold instead of trading damage against reward.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting; it constrains any method in the right-hand column, since only interaction produces damage
Failure mode addressed: makes the cost of failure mode 4 (insufficient exploration) physical, and opens the reward-misspecification thread (failure mode 6) formalised in Week 13
Course first appearance: Week 4

Core idea
Every rule in Week 4 was designed under a quiet assumption: a bad pull costs its gap and nothing else, and foregone reward is recoverable by pulling well tomorrow. Hardware does not honour that assumption, because a pull that drives an actuator past its envelope costs the foregone reward and a gearbox, and the second cost appears nowhere in the regret decomposition. Adding a damage probability per arm changes the answer to the problem, since the reward-optimal action can be inadmissible, and then reward-optimal and safe are two different optimisation problems.
Formal definition
Each arm carries a damage probability h_i alongside its reward distribution, and an arm is admissible when h_i \le \tau. The h_i are unknown and estimated from the same pulls as the \mu_i. Safe-UCB adds three components to the index rule:

a constraint estimated separately from the reward, so \hat h_i carries its own confidence interval and never enters \hat\mu_i;
a conservative admissibility test using the lower confidence bound,
\hat h_i - \sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{2 n_i}} > \tau \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{ban arm } i,
so an arm is condemned only when even the most favourable reading of its data puts it over the threshold;
a known-safe fallback, one arm certified admissible before learning begins, which on a real system is the hand-tuned controller that was commissioned before anyone proposed learning anything.

On the Week 4 eight-armed instance (\tau = 0.05, horizon 2\times10^4) this cuts damage events from UCB1’s 6517 to 382 and pays 385 in regret against the best admissible arm.
Constraint against penalty
Folding safety into the reward with a large negative number leaves the optimiser free to trade safety against performance at whatever exchange rate the penalty implies, and it will find situations we did not anticipate when we picked the number. A constrained MDP keeps the two quantities separate: maximise expected return subject to an explicit bound on expected damage. The constraint does not trade. This is one of the falsifiers the course states directly, and CPO is built on it.
Connection to classical control
The admissibility condition is a state and input constraint of the kind MPC already enforces, with one difference that drives the whole design: MPC knows its constraint set in advance, whereas a learner has to discover h_i from the same pulls that cause the damage. The lower-confidence-bound test is the analogue of a conservative robustness margin, preferring to keep a good arm over banning a bad one quickly, and the known-safe fallback plays the role of the backup controller in a supervisory architecture. Barrier certificates encode the constraint in a form that needs no learning at all, which is the Week 13 route.
Key limitation
Learning a constraint from experience always pays for the first pulls of an unknown arm, since an arm has no safety record before it has been tried and several pulls are needed to separate a dangerous arm from an unlucky one. That investigation window is irreducible for any algorithm of this kind, and removing it requires structure the bandit formulation threw away: a damage model from the physics, a shared parameterisation that transfers evidence between arms, or a certificate. The bandit case is also the easy one. An arm can always be abandoned after one pull, while a robot in the wrong region of its state space may have no admissible action that recovers it.
Related concepts
UCB | Epsilon-greedy | Regret | Exploration-exploitation tradeoff | Safe RL | CMDP | Control barrier function (CBF) | CPO | Sample complexity | MPC
References

Primary: Achiam et al. (2017), Constrained Policy Optimization, for the constraint-against-penalty argument
Secondary: Lattimore & Szepesvári, Bandit Algorithms (2020), for the confidence-bound machinery the test reuses

04_concepts/sample-complexity.title: Sample complexity
04_concepts/sample-complexity.content:
Sample complexity
How much interaction it takes to know something: separating two means a distance \Delta apart needs \Omega(1/\Delta^2) samples, and on hardware every sample is measured in robot-seconds.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting, the currency in which every method in the right-hand column is priced
Failure mode addressed: none; it is the budget against which exploration, model learning and offline data are all judged
Course first appearance: Week 4

Core idea
Weeks 1 to 3 spent computation and Week 4 starts spending experiments, so the course needs a unit for the second resource. The unit comes from a hypothesis test: two arms whose means differ by \Delta are told apart only once their confidence intervals separate, and the width of an interval falls like 1/\sqrt{n}. Small differences are therefore expensive to resolve, and expensive in a way no estimator can negotiate away, because the bound is a statement about the information the samples carry.
Formal definition
For \sigma-sub-Gaussian rewards, the empirical mean of n samples lies within \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)/n} of the truth with probability 1-\delta, so separating two means at confidence 1-\delta needs
n \ \gtrsim\ \frac{8\sigma^2 \ln(1/\delta)}{\Delta^2}
samples from each. Priced in Regret, establishing that arm i is suboptimal costs about 1/\Delta_i^2 pulls at \Delta_i each, so the unavoidable bill for learning that the arm is bad is 1/\Delta_i. The same quantity appears inside UCB1’s count bound n_i \le 8\ln T/\Delta_i^2, with \ln(1/\delta) replaced by \ln T because the confidence must hold at every round, and inside the Lai-Robbins coefficient once the relative entropy is expanded for small gaps.
Connection to classical control
System identification asks the same question and answers it with the same 1/\sqrt{n} rate: parameter variance falls with the number of informative samples, and the informativeness is governed by the excitation. What Week 4 adds is the price tag. Persistent excitation asks for enough richness and never asks what the richness costs, whereas a sample-complexity statement converts the requirement into hardware hours and lets it be compared against the value of the resulting controller.
Key limitation
The bound counts samples and says nothing about which samples are available or what collecting them does to the robot. A gap that takes 400 trials to resolve is cheap in simulation and expensive on hardware, and some of those trials may be inadmissible in the sense of Safe exploration. The counting also assumes independent draws from a fixed distribution, an assumption that the state breaks from Week 5 onward, where coverage rather than sample count becomes the binding constraint.
Anchor number for the course
Ten candidate controllers separated by \Delta = 0.05 on a normalised success metric, evaluated by 30-second trials, need on the order of 10 \times 400 \times 30\,\text{s} \approx 33 hours of robot time to rank, and 33 hours is a floor: the confidence factor and the reward variance both multiply it, giving several times that for Bernoulli-like outcomes near 50\% at \delta = 0.05. Every later method is measured in the same currency.
Week 5 adds the second entry. Evaluating one fixed swing-up controller on a 961-state discretisation of the Torque-limited pendulum, to an RMS error of 1.62 against an exact V^\pi, costs 79\,350 transitions, which is 2.2 hours of hardware time at 10 Hz. No improvement step appears anywhere in that figure. The two numbers sit on the same axis and should be read together: 33 hours to rank ten controllers you already have, 2.2 hours to learn what one of them is worth from every state.
Week 6 adds the third entry, and it prices a branch of the diagram instead of a task. On the same 961-cell chain with the swing-up controller removed and five admissible torques, Q-learning reaches 97\% of J^\star after 7.5\times10^5 transitions, which is 21 hours at 10 Hz, and Policy gradient (REINFORCE) is still 8.7\% short after 6.5\times10^6. That factor of at least 8.6 is a lower bound, since the policy method never reaches the value method’s level inside its budget, and the inter-seed spread at the matched budget is 18.4 against 2.4. The experiment runs on ground chosen to favour tabular value learning and says nothing about continuous action spaces or structured policy classes.
Related concepts
Regret | Bandit problem | UCB | Exploration-exploitation tradeoff | Safe exploration | Model-based RL | Sim-to-real gap | Offline RL | Coverage | TD learning | Q-learning | Policy gradient (REINFORCE) | Bootstrapping | Bias-variance tradeoff in RL

04_concepts/score-function-estimator.title: Score function estimator
04_concepts/score-function-estimator.content:
Score function estimator
The estimator \nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_\theta}\big[R(\tau)\,\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)\big] obtained by applying the Likelihood-ratio identity to the policy-search objective and expanding the trajectory density until the unknown dynamics cancel.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — the mathematical device that makes the policy row of the model-free column reachable at all
Bellman object approximated: none. The objective is differentiated directly, so the method built on it solves no fixed-point equation.
Course first appearance: Week 6, inside Policy gradient (REINFORCE)

Core idea
The return R(\tau) is a property of a trajectory and carries no \theta, so differentiating it produces nothing. All the parameter dependence sits in the measure being averaged over, and that measure contains the transition kernel the model-free setting does not have. The identity moves the derivative onto the log of the density, where the kernel appears as an additive term that no longer depends on \theta and differentiates away.
Formal definition
The Likelihood-ratio identity applied to J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_\theta}[R(\tau)] gives
\nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_\theta}[R(\tau)] = \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_\theta}\big[R(\tau)\,\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau)\big],
which one Rollout measures without bias. Expanding the trajectory density and taking logs turns the product into a sum, in which \nabla_\theta\log p(x_0) = 0 and \nabla_\theta \log P(x_{t+1}\mid x_t,u_t) = 0, leaving a sum of policy scores \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(u_t\mid x_t). The score has zero mean under \pi_\theta,
\mathbb{E}_{u\sim\pi_\theta}\big[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u\mid x)\big] = \nabla_\theta\sum_u \pi_\theta(u\mid x) = \nabla_\theta 1 = 0,
which is what licenses dropping the acausal terms and, in Week 9, subtracting a Baseline (variance reduction). For a tabular softmax the score is \mathbf{1}\{b = u_t\} - \pi_\theta(b\mid x_t), positive for the action taken and negative for the others. See Softmax policy class and Gaussian policy class for the two forms the score takes in this course.
The zero-mean property holds for a continuous action set as well. The same two lines run with an integral, \int \pi_\theta(u\mid x)\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}u = \int\nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(u\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}u = \nabla_\theta 1 = 0, under the dominated-convergence conditions that hold for the classes used in this course, a softmax over a finite set and a Gaussian with differentiable mean and bounded \sigma. That generality is what the Week 9 practical depends on, since it runs a Gaussian policy on LQR. In conditional form, \mathbb{E}[s_t\mid\mathcal{F}_t]=0 with s_t the score at step t, the identity licenses two things at once. Rewards collected before the decision drop out by the tower property, and so does any Baseline (variance reduction) b(x_t). Dropping the acausal terms and centring are the same identity applied twice, the first forced by causality and the second chosen.
Connection to classical control
Extremum-seeking control estimates the gradient of a performance map nobody models, by injecting a dither and correlating it with the measured cost. The score function estimator is the same manoeuvre with the dither supplied by the policy’s own stochasticity, and the identity converts that randomness into an exact gradient estimate instead of a finite difference. The cancellation needs only that the plant does not depend on \theta: it does not need P to be linear, known, smooth in the state, or even continuous, so it holds unchanged for a system with contacts.
Key limitation
The identity is exact and says nothing about how many samples the resulting estimator needs. A single scalar return multiplies the whole gradient vector, and the variance of that product grows with the horizon, which is the cost that shows up as failure mode 2 in Week 9. Unbiasedness also requires the sampling distribution to be the current p_\theta, so every parameter update invalidates the data that produced it.
Related concepts
Likelihood-ratio identity | Policy gradient (REINFORCE) | Policy gradient theorem | Baseline (variance reduction) | Rollout | Policy parameterisation | Softmax policy class | Gaussian policy class | Discounted state-visitation measure | Importance sampling | Monte Carlo policy evaluation | Bias-variance tradeoff in RL | Sample complexity | Stochastic approximation | Actor-critic
References

Primary: Sutton & Barto (2018), §13.2
Original paper: Williams (1992), Simple statistical gradient-following algorithms for connectionist reinforcement learning
Estimator background: it is well established in simulation optimisation as the likelihood-ratio or REINFORCE estimator

04_concepts/semi-gradient-update.title: Semi-gradient update
04_concepts/semi-gradient-update.content:
Semi-gradient update
A parameter update that differentiates the current prediction and treats the bootstrapped target as a fixed number, ignoring the dependence of that target on the same parameters.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting, the form every TD update takes once the table is replaced by parameters
Failure mode addressed: none; it is the shape of the update whose stability failure mode 1 is about
Course first appearance: Week 7

Core idea
The TD error of Week 5 is built from predictions, and predictions survive the move to a parametric family, so the update rule needs no invention. What changes is the status of the rule. The target r_{t+1} + \gamma V_w(x_{t+1}) contains w, and the update differentiates only the left-hand prediction, so it descends no objective. The alternative, differentiating both occurrences, is a real gradient of the mean squared TD error and buys back descent at a price paid in data.
Formal definition
With V_w(x) = w^\top\phi(x), the semi-gradient TD(0) rule is
w_{t+1} = w_t + \alpha_t\,\delta_t\,\phi(x_t), \qquad \delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma V_{w_t}(x_{t+1}) - V_{w_t}(x_t),
while the full gradient of \tfrac12\delta_t^2 carries an extra term from the target,
\nabla_w \tfrac12 \delta_t^2 = \delta_t\bigl(\gamma\,\phi(x_{t+1}) - \phi(x_t)\bigr).
Setting \phi(x) = e_x recovers the tabular update of Week 5 exactly, so the tabular case is the special case in which one update writes to one entry.
Connection to classical control
Descent methods are certified by a cost that decreases; successive-approximation schemes are certified by the map they iterate. A semi-gradient update belongs to the second family. Its convergence argument has to come from the Bellman operator and from the geometry of the fit (Projected Bellman equation), the way the stability of a relaxation iteration comes from the spectral radius of its iteration matrix rather than from any Lyapunov function handed over in advance. The trace in the Week 7 notes also makes a familiar point about gains, since the prediction at the visited state moves by \alpha\lVert\phi(x_t)\rVert^2\delta_t, so a step size is safe or unsafe only together with the scale of the features.
Key limitation
No objective decreases along the update, so the standard stochastic-gradient argument is unavailable and convergence has to be re-established from scratch. It has been established only for linear features with on-policy data (Projected Bellman equation). The repair that restores an honest objective, residual gradient (Baird, 1995), needs two independent successor samples from the same state, which a simulator supplies by resetting and a physical plant does not.
Related concepts
TD learning | Bootstrapping | Function approximation in RL | Projected Bellman equation | Bellman residual | Stochastic approximation | Deadly triad | DQN | Bellman operator
References

Primary: Sutton & Barto (2018), Sections 9.3 and 11.5
Residual gradient: Baird (1995)

04_concepts/softmax-policy-class.title: Softmax policy class
04_concepts/softmax-policy-class.content:
Softmax policy class
The policy family over a finite action set that exponentiates a linear preference \theta^{\top}\phi(x,u) and normalises, whose score is the feature vector of the action taken minus its policy-weighted average.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: a policy × no dynamics model. It is the concrete class that occupies the policy row whenever the command set is finite.
Bellman object approximated: none. It is a family of controllers, and the method that searches it differentiates the objective directly.
Failure mode addressed: none directly. It supplies the exploration mechanism, which is failure mode 4, and its width sets the variance of the estimator, which is failure mode 2.
Course first appearance: Week 6 in tabular form, generalised to features in Week 9

Core idea
Many robotics commands come from a finite set with no useful geometry of its own. A contact mode, a gait, a gear, a discrete torque level. The softmax class assigns each such action a scalar preference and turns the preferences into probabilities by exponentiating and normalising, so the parameters can move continuously while the decision they produce stays discrete. Randomisation is a property of the class rather than an added dial, so the separate exploration schedule that Epsilon-greedy needs has no counterpart here.
Formal definition
With features \phi(x,u)\in\mathbb{R}^p and parameters \theta\in\mathbb{R}^p,
\pi_\theta(u\mid x)=\frac{\exp\big(\theta^{\top}\phi(x,u)\big)}{\sum_b \exp\big(\theta^{\top}\phi(x,b)\big)}.
Taking logarithms gives \log\pi_\theta(u\mid x)=\theta^{\top}\phi(x,u)-\log\sum_b\exp(\theta^{\top}\phi(x,b)), and differentiating the normaliser reproduces the softmax weights, so
\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(u\mid x)=\phi(x,u)-\mathbb{E}_{b\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}\big[\phi(x,b)\big].
That difference is the whole update rule in miniature. The action that was taken is pushed up and every action is pushed down in proportion to how likely the current policy already thought it was, which is why the score has zero mean under \pi_\theta. Choosing \phi(x,u) to be the indicator of the pair recovers the tabular parameterisation of Week 6, where the score reads \mathbf{1}\{b=u\}-\pi_\theta(b\mid x). Scaling \theta by a constant is the temperature knob. As \|\theta\| grows the distribution concentrates on the highest-preference action, so the greedy policy is the limit of the class rather than a member of it.
Connection to classical control
The class is a smooth relaxation of a mode-selection law. A switching controller commits to one of finitely many modes by an argmax over some criterion, and an argmax has a derivative of zero almost everywhere and no derivative at the switching surface, so no gradient method can tune the criterion that produced it. Exponentiating and normalising replaces the hard selection with a differentiable blend whose parameters can be moved by measured gradients, and the hard law returns in the limit of large gains. The same construction is what turns a min into a soft-min in entropy-regularised optimal control, which is where SAC picks it up in Week 10.
Key limitation
The class needs one preference per action, so a continuous command has to be discretised, and a Cartesian grid over m actuators grows exponentially in m. That cost is what the Gaussian policy class exists to avoid. The class also stalls when it becomes confident. Once the probabilities are near 0 and 1 the score is near zero for every draw, so a policy that saturated early on the wrong action explores almost never and receives almost no gradient, and nothing in the class separates those two effects.
Related concepts

04_concepts/stationary-distribution.title: Stationary distribution
04_concepts/stationary-distribution.content:
Stationary distribution
The long-run fraction of time the closed loop spends in each state, d_\pi^\top P^\pi = d_\pi^\top, and the weighting that on-policy data impose on any fit made from them.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational, a property of the chain a policy leaves behind rather than of any method
Failure mode addressed: none; its mismatch with the operator is the mechanism of failure mode 1, and in Week 12 of failure mode 3
Course first appearance: Week 7

Core idea
Fixing a policy removes the action from the description and leaves a Markov chain on states, P^\pi(x'\mid x) = \sum_u \pi(u\mid x)P(x'\mid x,u). On a finite state space an irreducible chain has a unique stationary distribution with d_\pi(x) > 0 everywhere, and if the chain is also aperiodic the law of x_t converges to it from any start. For learning, the probabilistic reading is the one that gets used. d_\pi is the distribution from which states arrive once the initial transient has washed out, so it weights every least-squares fit built from on-policy data whether or not anybody chose it.
Formal definition
P^\pi(x'\mid x) = \sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\pi(u\mid x)\,P(x'\mid x,u), \qquad d_\pi^\top P^\pi = d_\pi^\top, \qquad \sum_x d_\pi(x) = 1 .
The hypothesis does three separate jobs inside the convergence theorem of Week 7. It defines the weighting of the projection \Pi_{d_\pi}, so the Projected Bellman equation has a limit to name. Positivity everywhere makes \|\cdot\|_{d_\pi} a norm rather than a seminorm, so errors at every state stay visible to any bound written in it. And invariance is exactly the step that closes the Jensen argument proving \|P^\pi v\|_{d_\pi} \le \|v\|_{d_\pi}.
Connection to classical control
P^\pi is the stochastic analogue of the closed-loop matrix A - BK. Substituting the control law into the plant removes the input and leaves an autonomous system whose properties belong to the pair (plant, controller) rather than to either alone, and a stochastic policy fixes only the distribution of the action, so closing the loop averages over it. Irreducibility and aperiodicity then read as reachability-like conditions on that closed loop, and d_\pi is its steady-state distribution.
Key limitation
Nonexpansiveness of P^\pi is tied to its own stationary distribution. Under a different weighting \mu \neq d_\pi, one transition can increase the weighted distance between value functions, which is what off-policy data arrange and what Baird’s counterexample measures. The object also moves. Under Generalised policy iteration the policy changes and its stationary distribution changes with it, and a replay buffer holds a mixture of the distributions several past policies induced.
Related concepts
Projected Bellman equation | MDP | Markov property | Off-policy learning | Coverage | Deadly triad | Experience replay | Distribution shift | Generalised policy iteration
References

Primary: Tsitsiklis & Van Roy (1997)
Sutton & Barto (2018), Section 9.2, the on-policy distribution

04_concepts/stochastic-approximation.title: Stochastic approximation
04_concepts/stochastic-approximation.content:
Stochastic approximation
Root-finding for a function nobody can evaluate: given measurements whose conditional mean is h(\theta), the iteration \theta_{k+1} = \theta_k + \alpha_k H(\theta_k, w_k) reaches a root of h provided the step sizes travel far enough and fall quiet fast enough.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — the machinery that certifies every sampled update in the right-hand column
Failure mode addressed: none; it supplies the convergence argument that failure mode 1 later destroys
Course first appearance: Week 5

Core idea
Robbins and Monro asked in 1951 how to solve h(\theta^\star) = 0 when h is inaccessible and each query returns the value wanted plus a disturbance nobody controls. Their answer is to take a small step in the measured direction and let the noise cancel across many iterations, which turns a root-finding problem into a question about a step-size sequence. The framework predates Dynamic programming by five years and predates the algorithm it now certifies, TD learning, by thirty-seven.
Formal definition
Let h : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n have a root \theta^\star. At iteration k the algorithm observes H(\theta_k, w_k) with
\mathbb{E}\big[H(\theta_k, w_k) \mid \theta_k\big] = h(\theta_k),
and forms \theta_{k+1} = \theta_k + \alpha_k H(\theta_k, w_k). Convergence asks four things: an unbiased one-sample estimate of h, bounded noise variance, a stable mean flow \dot\theta = h(\theta) with equilibrium \theta^\star, and step sizes obeying
\underbrace{\sum_k \alpha_k = \infty}_{\text{reach any distance}}, \qquad \underbrace{\sum_k \alpha_k^2 < \infty}_{\text{settle on a point}}.
Both hold for \alpha_k = 1/k^p with p \in (0.5,\,1]. The first condition bounds nothing about noise and everything about travel: \alpha_k = 1/k^2 sums to \pi^2/6, so an iterate starting further away than that can never arrive. The second controls the disturbance each step injects, whose variance contribution scales as \alpha_k^2.
A constant \alpha fails the second condition on purpose. On the scalar problem h(\theta) = \theta^\star - \theta with measurement noise of variance \sigma^2, the error obeys e_{k+1} = (1-\alpha)e_k + \alpha w_k, a first-order filter whose stationary spread is
\text{sd}(e_\infty) = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{2-\alpha}}.
The iterate reaches a stationary distribution centred on the root, and shrinking \alpha shrinks the spread as \sqrt{\alpha} while slowing the approach in proportion to 1/\alpha.
The ODE method supplies the third requirement. In the small-step-size limit the iteration takes many steps per unit of algorithmic time, the zero-mean noise averages out over any such window, and what remains is the mean flow \dot\theta = h(\theta). Convergence of a noisy recursion then reduces to asymptotic stability of a differential equation.
Connection to classical control
This is the theory an adaptive-control course already teaches under other names. Recursive least squares and the LMS filter update parameters along a prediction error with a gain that decays as data accumulates, with P_k or 1/k playing the part of \alpha_k. Gradient adaptation in model-reference adaptive control, \dot\theta = -\Gamma e\phi, is the continuous-time version, and its Lyapunov proof is an analysis of exactly the mean flow the ODE method extracts. Stochastic gradient descent is the special case h = -\nabla f. Ljung’s 1977 analysis of recursive identification and Borkar’s monograph organise all of these under one theorem, and Week 5 adds TD to the list.
Key limitation
The conditions describe the limit as the number of updates tends to infinity, and a robot has a finite budget before a decision must be made. Measured on the Week 5 pendulum chain, the schedule the theorem prescribes, \alpha_t(x) = 1/n(x), ends at RMS error 6.25 while a constant \alpha = 0.03 reaches 0.25, a factor of 25 in favour of the schedule the theorem does not cover. Two mechanisms account for it: the TD target moves as the table changes, so a decaying gain loses alertness precisely when alertness is needed, and the effective horizon 1/(1-\gamma) = 50 steps means information needs many passes to travel. The framework also assumes the mean flow is stable, and Function approximation in RL is where that assumption stops holding. It assumes a single recursion as well. Week 10 runs two against each other, and the repair is a second condition on the step sizes, \alpha_k/\beta_k \to 0, which is Two-timescale stochastic approximation.
Related concepts
TD learning | Bootstrapping | Bellman operator | Discount factor | Eligibility traces | Coverage | Deadly triad | Sample complexity | Value iteration | Two-timescale stochastic approximation | Actor-critic
References

Original paper: Robbins & Monro (1951), A stochastic approximation method
Convergence for TD: Tsitsiklis (1994); Jaakkola, Jordan & Singh (1994)

04_concepts/td-learning.title: TD learning
04_concepts/td-learning.content:
TD learning
Policy evaluation run as Stochastic approximation: the fixed-point condition V^\pi = \mathcal{T}^\pi V^\pi is rewritten as the root-finding problem \mathcal{T}^\pi V - V = 0, and one executed transition supplies an unbiased sample of that residual at the state just visited.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value function × no dynamics model — the first cell in that column with a Bellman object in it
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T}^\pi on sampled transitions, with no \max, because the policy is fixed
Failure mode addressed: none; it contributes the Bootstrapping ingredient of failure mode 1 (Week 7)
Course first appearance: Week 5

Core idea
Week 3 could apply \mathcal{T}^\pi exactly because P and r were available. Without them the operator cannot be evaluated anywhere, which is precisely the situation Robbins and Monro described in 1951. Running the controller and recording one transition gives a noisy measurement of the residual, so the fixed point can be reached by an iteration that never sees the operator it is solving. The price is that the target contains the estimate being learned, which is what makes one transition enough and what makes Week 7 difficult.
Formal definition
For a fixed policy \pi, define the residual h(V) = \mathcal{T}^\pi V - V, so h(V^\pi) = 0. Take one transition (x_t, u_t, r_{t+1}, x_{t+1}) generated by \pi and form the temporal-difference error
\delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma V(x_{t+1}) - V(x_t), \qquad \mathbb{E}\big[\delta_t \mid x_t = x\big] = (\mathcal{T}^\pi V)(x) - V(x) = h(V)(x).
Substituting this measurement into the Robbins-Monro iteration and moving only the coordinate just visited gives
V(x_t) \;\leftarrow\; V(x_t) + \alpha\,\delta_t,
an asynchronous stochastic approximation. At \gamma = 0 it collapses to the Week 4 bandit update \hat\mu \leftarrow \hat\mu + \alpha(r - \hat\mu).
Tabular convergence (Jaakkola, Jordan & Singh 1994; Tsitsiklis 1994). With \mathcal{X} finite, rewards of bounded variance, every state visited infinitely often with probability 1, and per-state step sizes satisfying \sum_{t: x_t = x}\alpha_t(x) = \infty and \sum_{t: x_t = x}\alpha_t^2(x) < \infty, then V_t \to V^\pi with probability 1.
Why it is stable. The mean flow is
\dot V = \mathcal{T}^\pi V - V = (\gamma P^\pi - I)V + r^\pi,
linear with equilibrium V^\pi. Since P^\pi is row-stochastic its spectral radius is 1, so every eigenvalue of \gamma P^\pi - I has real part at most \gamma - 1 < 0. The contraction property proved in Week 3 is the stability certificate of the learning algorithm, read a second time.
Unbiased for the residual, biased for the value. \delta_t is unbiased for h(V) at the current table, which is a different quantity from the error V^\pi - V. The two are related by
h(V) = (I - \gamma P^\pi)(V^\pi - V),
so the TD target r_{t+1} + \gamma V(x_{t+1}) is a biased estimate of V^\pi(x_t) for as long as V \neq V^\pi. The fixed point is correct; every finite-time estimate on the way to it is not.
Connection to classical control
The correspondence is exact and it is the reason this audience meets TD before anyone mentions machine learning: TD is to the Bellman equation what recursive least squares is to the normal equations. Both drive a parameter along a measured prediction error with a decaying gain, both are analysed by looking at the deterministic flow they track, and both trade a permanent noise floor for the ability to follow a target that moves. The Bellman contraction plays the part a Lyapunov function plays in a gradient-adaptation proof.
Key limitation
Three assumptions carry the result and each is removed later. The table with one entry per state is what makes the mean flow linear with a boundable spectrum, and Function approximation in RL replaces the backup with a projected one whose flow can point outward (Week 7). The fixed policy is what removes the \max and keeps the operator affine (Week 6). On-policy data is what makes \delta_t unbiased at all, and correcting a mismatch needs reweighting with a variance problem of its own (Weeks 6, 7, 12). Beyond those, TD assumes the observed state is Markov and propagates any misspecification through every value that bootstraps through the affected states, which is why Monte Carlo policy evaluation remains the safer estimator when the sensor suite is leaving something out.
Anchor numbers
On the 961-cell torque-limited pendulum chain of Week 5, evaluating one fixed swing-up controller to RMS error 1.62, which is 12\% of \|V^\pi\|_{\text{rms}} = 14.05, costs 79\,350 transitions, or 2.2 hours of hardware time at 10 Hz. No improvement step appears anywhere in that calculation. Week 4 spent 33 hours choosing among ten fixed controllers.
Related concepts

Original paper: Sutton (1988), Learning to predict by the methods of temporal differences
Convergence: Tsitsiklis (1994); Jaakkola, Jordan & Singh (1994)

04_concepts/target-network.title: Target network
04_concepts/target-network.content:
Target network
A copy Q_{\theta^-} of the online network, frozen for C gradient steps and used only to build the bootstrap target, so the labels of the regression stay fixed between synchronisations.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no dynamics model, as one of the two objects DQN adds to Week 6’s loop
Failure mode addressed: 1, the moving-target part of it
Course first appearance: Week 7

Core idea
Every gradient step changes \theta and therefore changes the target that subsequent updates regress onto, so the algorithm is chasing labels it is itself moving. Freezing a copy stops that. Between two synchronisations the problem is an ordinary regression onto fixed labels, and the refresh performs one approximate Bellman backup on a clock of C steps rather than after every update.
Formal definition
y = r + \gamma\max_b Q_{\theta^-}(x',b), \qquad \theta^- \leftarrow \theta \ \text{ every } C \text{ gradient steps},
with C = 10^4 in the original Atari configuration and C = 500 in the Week 7 pendulum ablation.
Connection to classical control
This is a two-time-scale separation of a coupled problem into a fast inner loop and a slow outer one, the device adaptive control uses to let a fast estimator settle before the slow loop changes what it is estimating. The separation here is approximate. The regression is nonconvex, the inner loop is stopped after finitely many updates, and \theta^- tracks \theta rather than being independent of it.
Key limitation
The synchronisation period restores no theorem. The fixed point of the procedure is still the projected one determined by the function class and the update rule, and the Deadly triad is intact afterwards. Its measured worth is also easy to misread from final numbers alone. On the Week 7 pendulum chain the run without a target network ends at -128.5 against -125.8 for full DQN, and passes through a policy worth -140.6 on the way, so a bar chart of final values reports the mechanism as nearly free while the trajectory reports it as load-bearing.

04_concepts/terminal-cost-approximation.title: Terminal cost approximation
04_concepts/terminal-cost-approximation.content:
Terminal cost approximation
The function \hat J \approx J^\star that stands in for everything beyond a truncated horizon: the quantity that decides how well MPC performs, and the thing every learning method from Week 5 onward is trying to obtain from data.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — it is the bridge from the model-known column to everything else
Failure mode addressed: none directly; a bad \hat J is how model error and value-approximation error enter a planner
Course first appearance: Week 2; it is what Week 3 opens on — \hat J is a stand-in for -V^\star, so the MDP machinery is the theory of the object a planner guesses

Core idea
Any method that refuses to compute the whole tail of the Bellman recursion must guess it. Greedy control guesses zero and gets the pendulum failure. Dynamic programming computes all of it and pays |\mathcal{X}|. MPC sits in between and is explicit about it: N steps computed honestly with the true model and constraints, everything after step N compressed into \hat J. The horizon and the terminal cost are therefore substitutes, and the trade between them is the central design decision.
Formal definition
In the MPC problem \min_{u_{0:N-1}} \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} g(\hat x_i, u_i) + \hat J(\hat x_N), common choices are \hat J = 0, the LQR value \hat J(x) = (x - x^\star)^\top P_\infty (x - x^\star), or (from Week 5) a value function fitted from data.
The extreme case is exact: if \hat J = J^\star, then N = 1 is already optimal, and so is every N \ge 1. That is one line of the fixed-point equation J^\star = \mathcal{T}J^\star (Week 2, Exercise 2.2(c)). Read in reverse: horizon is only ever compensating for not knowing J^\star.
Why this is the bridge to the whole course
On the Torque-limited pendulum a good \hat J would have to report that a fast-moving state pointing away from the goal is nevertheless a good state. That is precisely the global object Week 2 spends a section establishing we cannot write down. Everything from Week 5 onward is a way of learning \hat J from data instead of guessing it, whether or not MPC is what consumes it.
Connection to classical control
In MPC stability theory the terminal cost is not a convenience but a certificate: with a control-invariant terminal set and a terminal cost that is a local Lyapunov function upper-bounding the true cost-to-go, stability and recursive feasibility are theorems. This gives the sign of the error a meaning that a regression loss does not see: an over-estimate of the cost-to-go preserves the Lyapunov argument, an under-estimate can destroy it, and a value function fitted by regression has no reason to err in the safe direction.
Key limitation
A terminal cost that is a good approximation near the goal and a bad one far from it can make a short-horizon controller worse than \hat J = 0: the planner is then confidently steered by a fiction. What matters is where in the state space the error sits, as much as the size of \|\hat J - J^\star\|. That is the question Week 2’s challenge problem asks quantitatively, and the reason approximate-DP bounds of the form \|J^{\pi} - J^\star\| \le \tfrac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma}\|\hat J - J^\star\| are usually loose in practice.
Related concepts
MPC | Bellman equation | Value function | LQR | Torque-limited pendulum | Model-based RL | Function approximation in RL | Discount factor
References

Secondary: Rawlings, Mayne & Diehl, Ch. 2 — terminal ingredients and their role in the stability proof
