04_concepts/thompson-sampling.title: Thompson sampling
04_concepts/thompson-sampling.content:
Thompson sampling
Keep a posterior over each arm’s mean, draw one plausible value from each posterior at every round, and pull the arm whose draw is largest, so an arm is selected exactly as often as it is probably the best.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no dynamics model, with exploration carried by the width of a posterior
Failure mode addressed: insufficient exploration (secondary failure mode 4), through randomisation proportional to the evidence
Course first appearance: Week 4

Core idea
Optimism converts the uncertainty into a bound and acts on the bound, discarding everything else the posterior knows. Sampling keeps the distribution and commits to one draw from it, so the shape of the posterior, and not only its upper end, decides how often an arm is tried. Since the arms are independent, the probability that a given arm is pulled equals the posterior probability that it is optimal, which is the property that makes the exploration rate self-regulating: no schedule is fixed in advance and no confidence level is chosen by hand.
Formal definition
For Bernoulli rewards with the uniform prior, the Beta family is conjugate, so the whole posterior for arm i is carried by two counters. With S_i successes in n_i pulls,
\theta_i \sim \mathrm{Beta}(1+S_i,\ 1+n_i-S_i),\qquad a_t = \arg\max_i \theta_i,
whose posterior mean is (1+S_i)/(2+n_i) and whose standard deviation shrinks like 1/\sqrt{n_i}. A young arm has a wide posterior, so its draw is occasionally large and the arm gets pulled; as its counter grows the posterior concentrates and large draws become rare. Exploration appears and disappears with the width, and nothing in the algorithm names it.
Connection to classical control
This is the Bayesian estimator of adaptive control with one change in how the estimate is used: the controller acts on a sample from the posterior instead of on its mean, so certainty equivalence is applied to a draw rather than to a point estimate. Read through the Bayes-adaptive MDP ladder, the three Week 4 rules are three collapses of the same belief, to a point, to a bound, and to a sample, and the one that keeps most of the distribution wins the Week 4 experiment (regret 215 against UCB1’s 1242 at T = 10^5).
Key limitation
The rule needs a likelihood model, and the quality of its exploration is the quality of that model. Beta-Bernoulli describes a trial that either succeeds or fails honestly, and it describes a shaped continuous reward with heavy tails badly; a misspecified likelihood gives a posterior of the wrong width and an exploration rate systematically too high or too low. The failure is silent, since the algorithm still runs and still produces plausible curves. UCB1 assumes less (bounded rewards) and carries a guarantee on every instance meeting that assumption.
Related concepts
UCB | Epsilon-greedy | Bayes-adaptive MDP | Bandit problem | Regret | Exploration-exploitation tradeoff | Certainty equivalence | Safe exploration
References

Primary: Lattimore & Szepesvári, Bandit Algorithms (2020), Ch. 36
Original paper: Thompson (1933), On the likelihood that one unknown probability exceeds another
Secondary: Russo et al. (2018), A Tutorial on Thompson Sampling

04_concepts/torque-limited-pendulum.title: Torque-limited pendulum
04_concepts/torque-limited-pendulum.content:
Torque-limited pendulum
A point mass on a rigid rod with one actuator whose torque limit is below the peak gravity torque: two states, one nonlinearity, one saturation, and enough to destroy every property that makes LQR work.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: not a method — it is the falsifier, the plant on which methods are tested for the rest of the course
Failure mode addressed: none; it exhibits the gap between local and global reasoning
Course first appearance: Week 2; recurs whenever a method claims to handle nonlinearity

Core idea
LQR is elegant enough to leave three false impressions: that value functions are quadratic, that optimal policies are linear, and that optimal control is the solution of a matrix equation. The pendulum is the smallest system that falsifies all three. Its role is deliberately paired with LQR’s: LQR is the analytical benchmark (the one problem whose exact solution is available, so an approximate algorithm can be validated rather than merely judged), and the pendulum is the benchmark that exposes LQR’s limits.
Formal definition
m\ell^2\ddot\theta = u - b\dot\theta - mg\ell\sin\theta, \qquad |u| \le u_{\max},
with \theta = 0 hanging (stable), \theta = \pi upright (unstable). The state space is a cylinder \mathbb{S}^1 \times \mathbb{R}, not a plane. Course parameters: m = 1 kg, \ell = 1 m, b = 0.1, u_{\max} = 5 N·m.
The entire difficulty is one inequality: u_{\max} = 5 < mg\ell = 9.81 N·m, short by a factor 1.96. Setting \dot\theta = \ddot\theta = 0 gives the required holding torque u = mg\ell\sin\theta, which exceeds u_{\max} for \theta \in (30.6°, 149.4°) and its mirror image. In that band the static problem is infeasible: no admissible input can hold the rod still. The only way through is dynamic: arrive with enough kinetic energy that you do not need to stop there.
What each feature breaks






























LQR assumptionPendulum realityConsequence for the DP objectslinear dynamics\sin\theta; two equilibria; state wraps on a circleJ^\star is not quadratic, so the quadratic family is no longer closed under \mathcal{T} — see Closure under the Bellman operatorunconstrained u\lvert u\rvert \le u_{\max} < mg\ellthe Bellman minimisation becomes constrained; the minimiser sits on the boundary over much of the state space, so \pi^\star saturates and is not linearquadratic cost, one equilibriumtwo ways round the circle to the goalJ^\star develops a ridge where the two routes tie: continuous but non-smooth, and \pi^\star changes abruptly across itwhole tail available analyticallyswing-up needs 2–3 s of planningtruncating the tail changes the solution, not just its accuracy
Connection to classical control
Everything here is classical, and that is the point of using it: the failure of an LQR controller on this plant is demonstrated with no learning anywhere in sight. Linearising about the upright and applying the saturated law u = \mathrm{clip}(-K(x - x^\star)) captures 74 % of a sampled box but only 19 % of the low-energy band |\dot\theta| \le 2 rad/s, and 0 % of the one initial condition the task actually starts from, hanging at rest. Raising the gain changes nothing: a command already clipped at u_{\max} is unchanged by multiplying it by two.
The failure is structural, not a matter of tuning. Reaching the upright requires moving away from the goal first to pump energy, and no law of the form u = -K(x - x^\star), which reads only the instantaneous error, can express that. J^\star for this plant is a genuinely global object: its value at the bottom depends on what happens near the top, seconds later.
Key limitation
The pendulum is small enough to be solved exactly: a 200 \times 200 grid and tabular value iteration (with \gamma slightly below 1) recovers the optimal swing-up policy, ridge and all, in seconds. It falsifies LQR’s structure but not its scale; the scale argument needs the Curse of dimensionality and a 7-DOF arm. It is also, precisely, not an example of Underactuation (one input for one DOF, full rank), and calling it underactuated is the single most common error on this material.
Related concepts
LQR | Underactuation | Closure under the Bellman operator | Energy shaping | MPC | Curse of dimensionality | Distribution shift | Value iteration
References

04_concepts/trajectory-optimisation.title: Trajectory optimisation
04_concepts/trajectory-optimisation.content:
Trajectory optimisation
Solve the finite-horizon optimal control problem once, offline, and execute the resulting input sequence open-loop: a plan for one initial condition, not a controller.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: none — and the absence is the point. It stores \{u_0,\dots,u_{N-1}\}: numbers, not a function of state, so by the row rule of the Unifying diagram it represents no policy at all. Placing it in the policy row would contradict Open-loop vs feedback
Failure mode addressed: none
Course first appearance: Week 2 (placement and contrast only)

Core idea
Direct trajectory optimisation, iLQR and MPC all solve the same finite-horizon problem. They differ in one respect only: what happens when reality departs from the plan. Trajectory optimisation never measures the state again, so a disturbance produces a permanent miss. iLQR’s backward pass leaves local gains behind, so the deviation is corrected while the state stays inside the tube where the local model is valid. MPC re-solves from the measured state every period and needs no tube. Re-solving is the only difference between the three, and it is the difference between a plan and a controller.
Formal definition
Given f, g, horizon N and a specific x_0, solve \min_{u_{0:N-1}} \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} g(x_i,u_i) + g_N(x_N) subject to x_{i+1} = f(x_i,u_i) and the admissible sets, then apply the sequence as computed. Transcriptions differ: single shooting eliminates the states by forward simulation, while multiple shooting and direct collocation keep them as decision variables with the dynamics as equality constraints, which conditions far better on unstable plants.
Where it sits on the “how much policy is stored” spectrum
Reading the model-known column of the diagram as one spectrum: LQR and Dynamic programming store a global policy through V; iLQR stores a local law along one trajectory; MPC stores none and recomputes online; trajectory optimisation stores none at all, only a plan for one x_0.
Connection to classical control
It is the natural output of the maximum principle and of any nonlinear program written over a discretised trajectory, and it remains the workhorse for offline motion planning where the environment is known and repeatable. The Week 1 branching argument says exactly when this is enough: an open-loop sequence is optimal among policies when the problem is deterministic, since then there is nothing to react to.
Key limitation
No feedback. A disturbance, a model error, or a different initial condition invalidates the plan and there is no mechanism to recover, which is why in practice it is wrapped in something that provides feedback (a tracking controller, iLQR’s gains, or a receding horizon).
Related concepts
iLQR | MPC | Open-loop vs feedback | Unifying diagram | LQR | Dynamic programming
References

Primary: Betts, Practical Methods for Optimal Control and Estimation Using Nonlinear Programming; Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics (trajectory optimisation chapters)

04_concepts/trust-region.title: Trust region
04_concepts/trust-region.content:
Trust region
A bound on how far a policy update may move the policy itself, measured in the space of action distributions rather than in the space of parameters.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: cross-cutting within the policy and actor-critic rows. It constrains the improvement step and leaves the row rule untouched.
Bellman object approximated: none. It is a restriction on the optimisation, not an estimator.
Failure mode addressed: 2, indirectly, by keeping the surrogate objective accurate over the region where the step is taken. It is also the machinery the safety thread of the course is built on.
Course first appearance: Week 10, formalized for safety in Week 13

Core idea
A gradient step moves \theta by a fixed amount, and how much that moves the behaviour depends on where \theta sits. A Gaussian policy class whose \sigma has shrunk during training changes its action distribution far more per unit of \theta than the same policy did at initialisation, so a step size that was safe early becomes destructive late. Constraining the change in the policy removes the dependence on the parameterisation, and the same constraint bounds how far the Critic’s target can travel between two evaluations.
Formal definition
Trust-region policy optimisation solves, at each update,
\max_\theta\ \hat{\mathbb{E}}\left[\frac{\pi_\theta(u\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(u\mid x)}\,\hat A_t\right] \quad\text{subject to}\quad \hat{\mathbb{E}}\big[\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}\,\|\,\pi_\theta)(x)\big] \le \epsilon,
where the objective is the surrogate obtained by Importance sampling the advantage estimates collected under \pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}, and the constraint bounds the average Kullback-Leibler divergence over the states visited. The ratio is the importance weight Week 9 priced in variance, and the constraint is what keeps it near one, so the surrogate remains an accurate model of J over the region where the step is taken. PPO replaces the constraint with a clipped objective that removes the incentive to move the ratio beyond 1\pm\epsilon, which costs one line of code and no second-order solve.
Why the same machinery carries safety. A method that bounds the change in one accumulated quantity bounds the change in a second by the same argument. Adding a cost constraint J_C(\pi)\le d, where J_C accumulates a cost signal exactly as J accumulates reward, gives CPO and an approximate guarantee that the constraint holds at every iterate rather than only in the limit.
Connection to classical control
This is a step-size bound stated in the space where the guarantee lives, which is what a Lyapunov-based controller redesign does. In gain scheduling and in adaptive control the analogous rule is that the controller may not be redesigned faster than the closed loop can settle, and the bound is placed on the closed-loop behaviour rather than on the gains. The KL constraint plays that role for a stochastic policy, and it is also a natural-gradient statement, since constraining the KL divergence to second order is constraining the step in the Fisher metric rather than in the Euclidean one.
Key limitation
The constraint bounds the movement of the policy and guarantees nothing about the plant. A policy that stays close to the previous one at every step can still drift anywhere over many steps, and closeness in KL over the visited states says nothing about a state the policy has never reached. The improvement guarantee behind the surrogate holds under a bound involving the maximum KL divergence, which practice replaces by an average, so what is run is a heuristic version of the theorem. The clipped form of PPO enforces no divergence bound at all and only removes the incentive to violate one.
Related concepts
PPO | Actor-critic | Importance sampling | Policy gradient theorem | Gaussian policy class | Policy parameterisation | Two-timescale stochastic approximation | CPO | CMDP | Safe exploration | Safe RL | Design-space diagram | Off-policy learning
References

Primary: Schulman, Levine, Abbeel, Jordan & Moritz (2015), Trust region policy optimization
Clipped surrogate: Schulman et al. (2017)
Constrained extension: Achiam, Held, Tamar & Abbeel (2017)

04_concepts/two-timescale-stochastic-app.title: Two-timescale stochastic approximation
04_concepts/two-timescale-stochastic-app.content:
Two-timescale stochastic approximation
Two coupled Stochastic approximation recursions run at step-size ratios that tend to zero, so that the fast process sees the slow one as frozen and the slow one sees the fast one as converged.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational. It is the convergence machinery for the bottom row, in the same position Stochastic approximation occupies for the right-hand column.
Failure mode addressed: none directly. It is the condition under which the actor-critic construction that addresses modes 1 and 2 can be analysed at all.
Course first appearance: Week 10

Core idea
An Actor-critic runs two learners against each other, and each one invalidates the other’s premise. The critic is fitted to the value of a policy the actor keeps moving, so its fixed point travels; the actor follows a direction supplied by a critic that has not caught up. Separating the rates repairs both analyses at once, because a fast critic looks converged from the actor’s vantage and a slow actor looks static from the critic’s.
Formal definition
Two recursions with step-size sequences \alpha_k for the slow process and \beta_k for the fast one satisfy the ordinary Robbins-Monro conditions individually,
\sum_k\alpha_k = \sum_k\beta_k = \infty, \qquad \sum_k\alpha_k^2,\ \sum_k\beta_k^2 < \infty,
plus the separation condition
\frac{\alpha_k}{\beta_k} \longrightarrow 0 .
The ODE method then applies twice. On the fast timescale the slow iterate is constant, so the fast one tracks the equilibrium of its own flow at that frozen value; on the slow timescale the fast one is already at that equilibrium, so the slow flow is the one obtained by substituting it. In actor-critic terms, \beta belongs to the critic and \alpha to the actor, the critic’s analysis is the policy-evaluation argument of Week 5 at a quasi-static \pi_\theta, and the actor’s is a gradient flow on J against V^\pi rather than against a moving estimate. What the pair delivers is convergence to a stationary point of a non-concave J, not to an optimum.
Anchor numbers
Implementations rarely tune a ratio of sequences and produce the separation by other means, all of which have the same effect on the ratio of evaluation to improvement. A large batch of fresh transitions per actor update, typically 10^3 to 10^5 steps in continuous control, holds the critic’s target stationary within the batch and makes the actor’s effective step small relative to the evaluation performed. Several critic epochs per actor update do the same more directly. Advantage normalisation across the batch controls the scale of the actor’s step without changing its direction. A bound on the policy change per update, the Trust region, limits how far the critic’s target can move between evaluations.
Connection to classical control
This is singular perturbation applied to an adaptive loop. A two-time-scale system \dot z = g(z,\theta), \dot\theta = \varepsilon h(z,\theta) is analysed by solving the boundary layer first and then studying the reduced slow model on the resulting manifold, and the separation condition here is the discrete-time, stochastic version of small \varepsilon. The failure mode is the classical one as well. When the rates are not separated the two loops interact and the reduced model stops predicting the behaviour of the full one, which is why every adaptive-control text insists that the identifier be fast relative to the controller redesign.
Key limitation
The condition is asymptotic and says nothing about a finite budget, which is the whole of a robot’s training run. Two symptoms show what happens when the separation fails, and they have opposite fixes. A critic that is too slow supplies advantages with a persistent sign error in regions the policy has recently entered, and the learning curve stalls while the critic’s loss stays high. A critic that is too fast for the amount of data overfits the current batch, its loss falls to near zero, and the advantages collapse because the value function has memorised the returns it was fitted on. Both are visible in the same plot, so the critic’s loss belongs on the same axis as the policy value.
Related concepts
Stochastic approximation | Actor-critic | Critic | Trust region | TD learning | Generalised policy iteration | Dual control | Certainty equivalence | Sample complexity | PPO | DDPG
References

Primary: Borkar (2008), Stochastic Approximation: A Dynamical Systems Viewpoint, Ch. 6
Original paper: Borkar (1997), Stochastic approximation with two time scales
Applied to actor-critic: Konda & Tsitsiklis (2003)

04_concepts/ucb.title: UCB
04_concepts/ucb.content:
UCB
Score every arm by the top of a confidence interval on its mean, \hat\mu_i + \sqrt{2\ln t/n_i}, and pull the maximiser, so an arm is abandoned only once its interval has shrunk below the leader’s.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value-based × no dynamics model, with the exploration driven by the width of the estimate rather than by a schedule
Failure mode addressed: insufficient exploration (secondary failure mode 4), with a guarantee attached
Course first appearance: Week 4

Core idea
A decaying \varepsilon schedule that works has to know the smallest gap, so the fix is to let the data set the exploration rate. Uncertainty is already measurable through a concentration inequality, and the arm worth a further look is the arm whose plausible range still reaches above the current leader. Optimism in the face of uncertainty is the resulting principle: act as though every arm is as good as its evidence permits, and the arms that are genuinely bad disqualify themselves as their intervals narrow.
Formal definition
For rewards in [0,1], Hoeffding gives \mathbb{P}(\mu_i \ge \hat\mu_i + c) \le e^{-2n_i c^2}. Fixing the per-round failure probability at t^{-4} and solving for c yields the width \sqrt{2\ln t/n_i}, and acting on the optimistic end of the interval gives UCB1:
a_t = \arg\max_i \Big\{\hat\mu_i + \sqrt{\tfrac{2\ln t}{n_i}}\Big\}.
The exponent 4 pays for a union bound over roughly t events per round, making the total failure probability \sum_t t\cdot t^{-4} summable. The regret bound (Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer, 2002) is
R_T \ \le\ \sum_{i:\Delta_i>0}\frac{8\ln T}{\Delta_i} + \Big(1+\frac{\pi^2}{3}\Big)\sum_{i=1}^{K}\Delta_i,
with no tuning parameter and no knowledge of the gaps. Its first term comes from the count bound n_i \le 8\ln T/\Delta_i^2, which is the Sample complexity statement with \ln(1/\delta) replaced by \ln T because the confidence has to hold at every round. The 8 is 2^2 \times 2: one factor of two from comparing two intervals, one from the constant inside the Hoeffding width. Neither is tight, and on the Week 4 instance the guarantee grows at 596\ln T against a Lai-Robbins floor of 36.5\ln T.
Connection to classical control
Optimism is the same device as designing against the most favourable member of an uncertainty set, with the sign reversed from robust control, which designs against the worst member. Robust design buys a guarantee on every plant in the set and pays in conservatism; optimistic design buys information, because whenever the optimistic guess is wrong the resulting data shrinks the set. The confidence interval plays the role of the uncertainty description that adaptive control carries around, and the width 1/\sqrt{n_i} is the usual estimator convergence rate. Week 11 applies the same three steps to a learned dynamics model.
Key limitation
The guarantee is asymptotic in character and its constants are loose, so on the Week 4 instance UCB1 trails a fixed \varepsilon = 0.10 until pull 64\,400, and at T = 10^4 it finishes behind both other rules. On hardware the mechanism is itself the hazard: the rule deliberately selects the least understood action, which is very often the action most likely to leave the safe envelope (Safe exploration).
Related concepts
Epsilon-greedy | Thompson sampling | Regret | Bandit problem | Sample complexity | Exploration-exploitation tradeoff | Safe exploration | Bayes-adaptive MDP | Model-based RL
References

Primary: Lattimore & Szepesvári, Bandit Algorithms (2020), Ch. 7–8
Original paper: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi & Fischer (2002), Finite-time analysis of the multiarmed bandit problem

04_concepts/underactuation.title: Underactuation
04_concepts/underactuation.content:
Underactuation
A system is underactuated when it has strictly fewer independent control inputs than configuration variables, \operatorname{rank} B(q) < \dim q: a rank condition on the actuation matrix, not a statement about how weak the actuators are.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: not a method — a property of the plant that decides which methods can work on it
Failure mode addressed: none
Course first appearance: Week 2, introduced by contrast with the saturated pendulum

Core idea
Two different plant properties produce the same visible symptoms, and conflating them is the most common error on this material. Torque limits are an inequality on an input that is otherwise sufficient: |u| \le u_{\max}. Underactuation is a rank deficiency: there is no input at all in some directions of the configuration space. Both give states no admissible input can hold and optimal solutions that must first move away from the goal, which is exactly why the saturated pendulum is a legitimate teaching object for both, yet the causes and the cures are different.
Formal definition
Write the manipulator equation M(q)\ddot q + C(q,\dot q)\dot q + G(q) = B(q)u. The system is fully actuated at (q,\dot q) if \operatorname{rank} B(q) = \dim q, and underactuated otherwise.
Applied to the Torque-limited pendulum: one input, one degree of freedom, \partial\ddot\theta/\partial u = 1/m\ell^2 \neq 0. It is fully actuated in the rank sense. Remove the bound |u| \le u_{\max} and the problem becomes trivial: feedback linearisation cancels \sin\theta outright and any trajectory is trackable. The whole difficulty comes from u_{\max} < mg\ell and vanishes with it.
Genuinely underactuated systems: the cart-pole, the acrobot, quadrotors, and legged robots. No bound needs to be imposed for these to be hard, and no amount of actuator power removes the difficulty. These are the systems the practical sessions and the cumulative project use.
Connection to classical control
The distinction is exactly the distinction between a constraint on an input and a structural property of the input matrix. Feedback linearisation, computed torque, and inverse dynamics all presuppose full rank; they fail on an underactuated plant for reasons no gain retuning touches. On a saturated but fully actuated plant they fail only where the required torque exceeds the bound, a set you can compute in closed form, as the pendulum’s forbidden band (30.6°, 149.4°) shows.
Key limitation
Knowing a system is underactuated tells you which design tools are unavailable; it does not tell you what to do instead. And the two causes being phenomenologically identical means the distinction cannot be diagnosed from a trajectory plot: you have to look at B(q).
Why the terminology matters here
Tedrake’s Underactuated Robotics is the right reference for this material, and its title invites precisely the confusion this note exists to prevent. Say which of the two you are looking at. A prediction that separates them: give the pendulum a bigger actuator and the problem disappears; give the acrobot a bigger actuator at the same joint and it does not.
Related concepts
Torque-limited pendulum | LQR | MPC | Energy shaping | Trajectory optimisation
References

Primary: Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics, Ch. 1–3
Course statement: 00_Meta/teaching_companion.md §3.1 (canonical), CLAUDE.md §7

04_concepts/unifying-diagram.title: Unifying diagram
04_concepts/unifying-diagram.content:
Unifying diagram
A 3×2 grid placing every method in the course by what it explicitly represents (value function / policy / both) against what is known about the dynamics (model available / interaction only).
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: it is the diagram
Failure mode addressed: none
Course first appearance: Week 1; repeated whenever a new method is introduced

Core idea
The usual taxonomy “value-based / policy-based / actor-critic” invites the reading that these are three different families of algorithm, which they are not. The honest distinction is about which objects a method actually stores and updates. The columns record what you know about the dynamics; the rows record what the method explicitly represents.

























Explicitly representsDynamics model availableNo dynamics model (interaction only)A value function (value-based)DP, Value iteration, Policy iteration, Riccati / LQR (Wk 1–3)bandit algorithms ¶ (Wk 4), TD learning ♭ (Wk 5), Q-learning, SARSA, DQN ‡, LSTD (Wk 6–7)A policy (policy-based)iLQR ‖ (Wk 2)Policy gradient (REINFORCE), REINFORCE with a Baseline (variance reduction) § (Wk 6, 9)Both (actor-critic)MPC † (Wk 2, 11)Actor-critic, PPO §, DDPG, TD3, SAC (Wk 10), Dyna (Wk 11)
‖ Direct trajectory optimisation is not on the diagram, and its absence is the point. It stores an open-loop plan \{u_0,\dots,u_{N-1}\} (numbers, not a function of state), so by the row rule it represents nothing reusable: off the planned trajectory it has no answer. Putting it in the policy row would contradict Open-loop vs feedback, where the optimisation variable is explicitly a sequence of functions \pi_k:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{U}. iLQR earns the cell: its backward pass leaves time-varying gains K_k, i.e. an explicit local feedback law u_k = -K_k(x_k-x_k^{\text{ref}})+u_k^{\text{ref}}.
Read the model column as one spectrum of how much policy is stored: DP / LQR (a global policy, through V) → iLQR (a local law along one trajectory) → MPC (none stored, recomputed online) → direct trajectory optimisation (none at all, one plan for one x_0, hence off the grid).
† MPC represents a model and a terminal value function, but its policy is implicit, recomputed online by optimisation at every timestep and never stored. This is the awkward cell and students should be told so.
♭ TD learning is the first occupant of that cell with a Bellman object in it, and the object is \mathcal{T}^\pi rather than \mathcal{T}: Week 5 holds the policy fixed, so no maximisation appears and the fixed point being solved is the evaluation equation. Week 6 puts the \max back and the object becomes \mathcal{T}.
‡ Q-learning, SARSA and DQN represent the state–action value Q(x,u), not V(x): the same object with one more argument, and what makes greedy action selection possible without a model. Introduced properly in Week 3.
Week 6 opens the second row. Both model-free cells of the top two rows are occupied from that session, by methods that ran on the same pendulum in the same week, which is the reason Policy gradient (REINFORCE) is taught before the deep value methods of Week 7 instead of after them. The two branches are siblings: value methods centre on a fixed-point equation and read a policy out of it by maximisation, policy methods parameterise the policy and move it up an estimated gradient of expected return. Actor-critic in Week 10 is their synthesis, and that framing needs both branches already on the table.
Week 9 tests the row rule with a method that holds a value estimate. REINFORCE with a baseline maintains b_w, and it stays in the middle row, because the rule asks a sharper question than whether a value estimate exists. The question is whether that estimate solves a fixed-point equation. b_w is fitted by regression on returns the episodes produced, so it predicts no prediction of its own and no Bellman object is involved. The bottom row is reserved for value estimates that bootstrap, which is the same line that puts PPO there, and it is the load-bearing distinction for Week 10. Week 9 also puts the Policy gradient theorem behind the cell, and the theorem supplies a property the columns cannot show. States are weighted by the Discounted state-visitation measure of the current policy, so everything in this cell is on-policy by construction.
Week 10 fills the bottom row, and the placement is what defines the row. A Critic is a value estimate whose target contains a value estimate, which is the same test that kept Week 9 in the middle row, applied to a method that now fails it. The substitution is one line long: fit the Week 9 baseline to r_{t+1}+\gamma V_w(x_{t+1}) instead of to the observed return, and the object stops being a regression and starts solving a fixed point of \mathcal{T}^\pi. Everything that arrives with it, PPO, DDPG, TD3 and SAC, sits in the same cell for the same reason, and the differences between them are recorded on a separate artifact, the Design-space diagram. The bottom-left cell keeps MPC, so the actor-critic row is now the one row occupied on both sides of the model column, which is the reading Week 11 needs when a learned model moves into the middle.
Week 7 changes nothing about the placement, and that is the lesson. LSTD, LSPI and DQN represent a value function and no policy, and all three learn from interaction without a model, so they join Q-learning in the shaded cell. What changed inside the cell is the representation, and the cell records what a method represents rather than how it stores it. Two methods can be neighbours here and carry entirely different guarantees, since LSTD keeps the on-policy linear guarantee that DQN gives up (Deadly triad).
¶ The Bandit problem earns the top-right cell because \hat\mu_i is \hat Q(x,a) evaluated at the only state there is, so the row rule is satisfied by a legitimate value function. It is the one occupied cell that approximates no Bellman object: with no successor state there is nothing to bootstrap from, so \hat\mu_i is an ordinary sample average and contraction, uniqueness and the greedy-optimality argument have no operator to act on. The gap closes in one step, since \hat\mu \leftarrow \hat\mu + \alpha(r-\hat\mu) is the \gamma = 0 case of the TD learning update \hat V(x) \leftarrow \hat V(x) + \alpha(r + \gamma\hat V(x') - \hat V(x)).
§ PPO is placed by the rule, not by reputation: it is policy-gradient by lineage, but the version everyone runs fits a value network to bootstrapped targets, so it represents both. The dividing line is bootstrapping, not “has a value function”: a Monte-Carlo baseline is variance reduction and involves no Bellman object, while a critic predicts its own next prediction and is solving a fixed-point problem.
The columns are the ends of a spectrum, not a binary. Real robotics sits in the middle: rigid-body structure known from CAD and identification, contact and friction not. A learned model lives between the columns and is made explicit in Week 11 (Model-based RL).
Reading the rows: which Bellman object is approximated?

































































RepresentsMethodWhat is done with \mathcal{T}value functionDP, [[Value iterationvalue iteration]]value function[[Policy iterationpolicy iteration]]value functionbandit algorithmsnone — no successor state, so nothing to bootstrap fromvalue functionTD learning, TD(\lambda)\mathcal{T}^\pi on sampled transitions: no \max, because the policy is fixedvalue functionQ-learning, DQN\mathcal{T} applied on sampled transitions, approximately; under approximation, composed with a fit onto what the parameters can representvalue functionLSTD, LSPI\mathcal{T}^\pi, solved exactly inside the representable subspace (Projected Bellman equation)value functionSARSA\mathcal{T}_\varepsilon on sampled transitions at fixed \varepsilon, and \mathcal{T} only in the GLIE limitpolicyREINFORCE (+ baseline)none — the objective is differentiated directly, and the baseline is fitted to observed returnsbothactor-critic, PPO, SAC\mathcal{T}^\pi for the critic, gradient for the actorbothDDPG, TD3\mathcal{T}^\pi nominally, with a \max hidden in a deterministic actor trained to ascend Q_wbothMPC\mathcal{T} over a truncated horizon, terminal value approximated
The critic row is \mathcal{T}^\pi, not \mathcal{T}: a critic evaluates the policy the actor currently has, so its fixed-point equation carries no \max. (SAC’s entropy term acts as a softened maximisation, which is the one footnote the row rule needs and which changes no placement, since the rule turns on Bootstrapping.)
The “none” in the policy row is a different attack on the same problem, not a weaker version of the value-based one. Policy-gradient methods never form a Bellman residual: they parametrise the policy and differentiate the expected return.
SARSA’s entry is the one students misread, since the algorithm is on-policy and its own exploration therefore enters the target it learns. At a fixed exploration rate it solves the Exploration-aware Bellman operator exactly, which is a legitimate question with a legitimate answer, and the distance between the two fixed points is measurable: 11.4\% at \varepsilon = 0.10 on the Week 6 swing-up when executed with exploration in place, and 0.8\% in the opposite direction when both are executed greedily.
What breaks when we leave the top-left cell





























We loseWhat replaces it, and whereExhaustive Bellman updatesSampling: only visited states get updated (Wk 5)Known f and computable \mathbb{E}_wSampled transitions; TD learning as [[Stochastic approximationFreedom to evaluate any stateExploration becomes a cost, and on hardware a safety question (Wk 4)Tabular representationFunction approximation — \mathcal{T} no longer applied exactly (Wk 7)A fixed data distributionThe data depends on the policy that generated it (Wk 9, 12)
Key limitation
The grid classifies what a method represents, which is not the same as how well it works, how many samples it needs, or whether it is safe on hardware. It is an orientation device, not a selection criterion.
Related concepts
Bellman operator | Bellman equation | Dynamic programming | Policy gradient theorem | Baseline (variance reduction) | Discounted state-visitation measure | Open-loop vs feedback | SARSA | Q-learning | Policy gradient (REINFORCE) | Exploration-aware Bellman operator | Bootstrapping | Composition with classical control | Failure modes of approximate RL | Model-based RL | Bandit problem | Actor-critic | Critic | PPO | SAC | DDPG | Design-space diagram

04_concepts/value-function.title: Value function
04_concepts/value-function.content:
Value function
The expected discounted return obtainable from a state: the reinforcement-learning name for the optimal cost-to-go, with the sign flipped.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: foundational — it is the object the entire top row of the diagram explicitly represents
Failure mode addressed: none (it is an object, not a method)
Course first appearance: Week 1

Core idea
A value function summarises the entire future in one number per state. That is only possible because of the Markov property: everything the future needs to know about the past is contained in the current state. Two objects must be kept apart from the outset, V^\pi, the value induced by a policy, and V^*, the best achievable value. Confusing them costs nothing while dynamic programming is exact and becomes the central issue from Week 7, where approximate value functions satisfy the Bellman equation only approximately.
Formal definition
For a stationary policy \pi, bounded reward r and discount \gamma \in (0,1):
V^\pi(x) = \mathbb{E}_w\Big[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma^k\, r\big(x_k,\pi(x_k),w_k\big)\,\Big|\,x_0 = x\Big], \qquad V^*(x) = \sup_\pi V^\pi(x).
The supremum is over all policies, including time-varying and history-dependent ones. That a stationary deterministic policy attains it is a theorem about discounted infinite-horizon problems (proved in Week 3), not a definition, hence \sup rather than \max until attainment is established.
Sign conventions. Control minimises accumulated cost g and calls the object the cost-to-go J; RL maximises accumulated reward r and calls it the value V. They are the same problem with r = -g, V = -J. These notes use the RL convention from Week 1 onward for the objective, and control notation (x,u,w,f) for the system until Week 3.
Connection to classical control
V^* is the cost-to-go of optimal control, up to sign. In the linear-quadratic case it is exactly x^\top P x with P the Riccati solution, a value function that happens to live in a finite-dimensional family. The state–action value Q(x,u) (Week 3) is the same object with one more argument, and it is what makes greedy action selection possible without a model.
Week 3 sharpens why the course carries both. Extracting a greedy policy from Q^\star compares |\mathcal{U}| stored numbers, while extracting it from V^\star evaluates r and P at decision time. A value function alone is a controller only if the dynamics are available, and Q is V^\star with one step of the model folded in and paid for in advance. That is why model-free methods from Week 6 learn Q, and the middle case, a value function plus an online optimisation supplying the missing step, is MPC.
Key limitation
Representing a value function requires a table or an approximator over the whole state space, i.e. the Curse of dimensionality. And a value function of your chosen state variable exists only if that variable is Markov; under contact, backlash or thermal drift, joint encoders alone are not.
Related concepts
Bellman equation | Bellman operator | Value iteration | Dynamic programming | Markov property | Discount factor | Curse of dimensionality
References

Primary: Bertsekas (2019), Ch. 1; Meyn (2022), Ch. 1
Secondary: Sutton & Barto (2nd ed.), Ch. 3

04_concepts/value-iteration.title: Value iteration
04_concepts/value-iteration.content:
Value iteration
Iterate the Bellman operator from an arbitrary starting function, V_{k+1} = \mathcal{T}V_k; the contraction property drives V_k \to V^* geometrically at rate \gamma.
Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: value function × dynamics model available
Failure mode addressed: none; it is the exact algorithm whose approximations produce failure mode 1
Course first appearance: Week 1

Core idea
Structurally, value iteration is the backward Dynamic programming recursion with the stage index dropped: the same one-stage maximisation, applied over and over to a single function instead of once per stage to a sequence of functions. That is what the infinite horizon buys: one stationary value function and one stationary policy, extracted greedily at the end. Like DP it is model-based: f and r must be known and \mathbb{E}_w computable.
Formal definition
Initialise V_0 arbitrarily (e.g. V_0 \equiv 0); repeat
V_{k+1}(x) \gets \max_u \mathbb{E}_w\big[r(x,u,w) + \gamma V_k(f(x,u,w))\big]\quad \text{for every } x,
until \|V_k - V_{k-1}\|_\infty < \varepsilon; return \pi(x) = \arg\max_u \mathbb{E}_w[r + \gamma V_k(f)].
The cost factors into two independent parts. Number of sweeps: set by \gamma alone, k \ge \ln(1/\eta)/\ln(1/\gamma), i.e. 44, 90, 459 sweeps for a 10^2 error reduction at \gamma = 0.9, 0.95, 0.99. Cost per sweep: |\mathcal{X}||\mathcal{U}||\mathcal{X}|, untouched by \gamma, and the term that explodes in robotics. Conflating the two is a common source of misplaced optimism.
Measured on a 5\times5 stochastic gridworld from a random V_0, \ln\|V_k - V^*\|_\infty has slopes -0.1054, -0.0513, -0.0101, exactly \ln\gamma to four digits. The contraction estimate is tight in the rate.
Week 3 adds the observation that matters in practice: the greedy policy is usually optimal long before the values are accurate. On the three-state MDP the greedy policy is optimal at sweep 3, while the value error is still 72.9 out of an initial 100; on the 5\times5 gridworld it happens at sweep 8 with the error still 13.3 out of 20. The reason is structural, since the \arg\max depends on the ordering of the Q-values at each state and an ordering can be right long before the numbers are. There is no way to detect this without already knowing \pi^\star, so it justifies a habit (watch the greedy policy alongside the Bellman residual) and never a stopping certificate. Policy iteration, by contrast, stops on the policy and its stopping test is a certificate.
Connection to classical control
In the linear-quadratic case, value iteration is the Riccati recursion iterated to its fixed point (see LQR). The scalar example x_{k+1} = x_k + u_k with cost x^2 + u^2 converges to P^\infty = (1+\sqrt5)/2, the golden ratio, and gain K \approx 0.618.
Week 2 sharpens the correspondence into three names for one object: the Riccati recursion is the backward Bellman recursion, Riccati iterated to the DARE is value iteration, and the DARE solution P_\infty is V^* up to the sign. It also shows that the contraction argument above is not the only route to convergence: the LQR sweep converges undiscounted, \gamma = 1, by monotonicity plus stabilisability. The geometric rate is still visible: on the pendulum linearised about the upright at 50 Hz, \|P_k - P_\infty\|_F decays at 0.882 per stage, which is |\lambda_{\max}(A-BK_\infty)|^2, but it comes from the closed-loop spectrum rather than from a discount.
Key limitation
Two traps. The stopping test compares successive iterates, not the distance to V^*; converting one to the other costs a factor \gamma/(1-\gamma), so an \varepsilon-gap between sweeps is consistent with being 99\varepsilon from V^* at \gamma = 0.99. And the contraction constrains only the distance to V^*, never the direction: iterates can look qualitatively wrong for many sweeps while decaying at exactly the guaranteed rate. Beyond that, it inherits the Curse of dimensionality and the model requirement.
Related concepts
Bellman operator | Bellman equation | Dynamic programming | Policy iteration | Bellman residual | MDP | Q-learning | Discount factor | LQR
References

Primary: Bertsekas (2019), Ch. 1–2; Meyn (2022), Ch. 1
Secondary: Sutton & Barto (2nd ed.), Ch. 4

04_concepts/ilqr.title: iLQR
04_concepts/ilqr.content:
iLQR
Trajectory optimisation by repeated LQR: linearise f and quadratise g about the current trajectory, run an LQR backward pass on that local model, take a step, and repeat.

Stub. This concept is placed in Week 2 and left there. The Week 11 deck carries it only as the model-known entry of the policy row on the Unifying diagram, so a planner inside a learned model is the natural place to develop it and no session currently does. Expand this note if a later week takes that up.

Where it sits

Unifying diagram cell: a policy × dynamics model available. The backward pass leaves the time-varying gains K_k, and that stored feedback law is what earns the cell Trajectory optimisation cannot occupy
Bellman object approximated: \mathcal{T}, applied exactly on a local quadratic model of a nonlinear problem
Failure mode addressed: none. Its exposure is failure mode 5 (Model bias) once the f it linearises is itself learned
Course first appearance: Week 2, placed and not developed; Week 11 restates the placement without adding to it

Planted framing (Week 2)
iLQR (and its close relative DDP) is introduced only to be placed. Its backward pass leaves behind something direct Trajectory optimisation does not: a sequence of local gains K_k, giving the law u_k = -K_k(x_k - x_k^{\text{ref}}) + u_k^{\text{ref}}, valid in a tube around the nominal trajectory. That local feedback law is why iLQR earns the policy × model-known cell of the Unifying diagram and trajectory optimisation has no cell at all.
In Bellman terms: iLQR applies \mathcal{T} exactly, on a local quadratic model of a nonlinear problem, as against LQR (exactly, on quadratics) and MPC (over a truncated horizon).
Related concepts
Trajectory optimisation | MPC | LQR | Unifying diagram | Model-based RL | Closure under the Bellman operator

course/syllabus.title: Syllabus and course guide
course/syllabus.content:
Reinforcement Learning in Robotics: Syllabus
240MAR45 · MSc in Automatic Control and Robotics · UPC Barcelona
Format: 15 weeks × (1.5 h theory + 1.5 h practical) = 45 h, partial exam in Week 8
Prerequisites: optimal control, linear systems, basic probability, Python
Course philosophy
This course presents reinforcement learning from a control engineering
perspective: as approximate dynamic programming under uncertainty about the
dynamics, with direct policy search as a parallel paradigm. You already know
LQR, Riccati, Bellman, and MPC, and the course builds on that scaffolding
rather than starting from scratch.
Two messages run through the semester:

RL is one tool among several. Competent robotics engineering means knowing
when to use RL and when to compose it with classical methods (SysID, MPC,
residual learning).
Fewer ideas, presented deeply, with more connections beats a survey.
Some fashionable topics (distributional RL, MuZero, decision transformers,
multi-agent RL, foundation models for control) are pointed to in Week 15 but
not developed.

Weekly schedule





















































































WeekTheoryPractical1Optimal control, Bellman equation, the unifying diagramSetup verification; value iteration on a gridworld2LQR, the torque-limited pendulum, MPC as receding-horizon DPLQR on cart-pole; LQR swing-up failure; basic MPC3MDPs, Bellman operators as contractions, curse of dimensionalityContraction proofs; policy iteration on a stochastic MDP4What RL is and isn’t; bandits, exploration, safetyε-greedy, UCB, Thompson; regret curves5TD learning as stochastic approximationTD(0) and TD(λ); convergence vs. λ6SARSA, Q-learning, and REINFORCE as siblingsQ-learning vs. REINFORCE on the same problem7Function approximation, the deadly triad, DQNBaird’s counterexample; DQN on CartPole with ablation8Partial exam (Weeks 1–7)No lab, optional office hours and project group formation9Policy gradient with function approximation; Monte-Carlo baselinesREINFORCE variance study; cumulative project starts10Actor-critic as synthesis; the critic, GAE, the algorithm design spaceMilestone 1 due: PPO + SAC analysis11Model-based RL, MPC + learned models, SysIDMilestone 2: learned dynamics + MPC12POMDPs and belief states, sim-to-real, residual RL, offline RLMilestone 3: offline RL, extrapolation error13Safe RL and reward engineeringMilestone 4: constrained policy optimization14Buffer: imitation learning or reviewMilestone 5 (optional): BC + DAgger15Synthesis; what the literature won’t tell youProject presentations
Assessment

























ComponentWeightExercises Weeks 1–715%Partial exam Week 8 (Weeks 1–7)20%Cumulative project (milestones 20% + report 15% + presentation 5%)40%Final exam25%

Final exam: conceptual, covering the full course with emphasis on Weeks
9–14, organized around the failure-modes framework: which failure mode a
method addresses, why, and at what cost. No algorithmic recitation.
Exercises from Week 9 onward are formative (not graded): the cumulative
project takes over the assessed practical workload.
Final project performance does not affect the grade. Depth of analysis and
quality of comparison are what’s evaluated. A group whose SAC run fails but
who analyze why thoughtfully scores higher than one that copies working code
without understanding it.

Cumulative project: Five Methods, One Task
From Week 9, groups of 2–3 apply successive method families to one task: a
planar 2-DOF manipulator reaching a target while avoiding an obstacle, under
torque bounds (fallback: pendulum swing-up with torque limit).









































MilestoneWeekTaskWeight19–10PPO + SAC model-free baselines5%211Model-based RL + MPC with learned dynamics5%312Offline RL: naive Q-learning failure + CQL/IQL5%413Safe RL: CPO or Lagrangian-PPO5%514Imitation learning: BC + DAgger (optional)replaces lowest milestone grade
Final deliverables (Week 15): an 8–12 page report centered on a cross-method
comparison (sample complexity, final performance, constraint satisfaction) and
a 15-minute presentation. A reference-results bundle (checkpoints, datasets,
learned models) is distributed before Week 10 so any group can rejoin the chain
at any milestone. Use it only if your own artifact doesn’t work.
All milestones are doable on a laptop CPU for at least one configuration; most
training runs as homework, lab time is for analysis and comparison.
Practical sessions
Every practical ships as a Jupyter notebook with the environment, logging,
plotting, and known-good hyperparameters pre-written. You complete the
conceptual cores: loss functions, update rules, gradient computations. A
30-second smoke test at the top verifies your setup before you start.
One pinned software stack, distributed Week 1 and unchanged all semester:
numpy, scipy, matplotlib, gymnasium, PyTorch, stable-baselines3,
mujoco/pybullet, python-control.
Reading list

Bertsekas, Reinforcement Learning and Optimal Control (2019): spine reference
Meyn, Control Systems and Reinforcement Learning (2022)
Recht, “A Tour of Reinforcement Learning: The View from Continuous Control”: read Week 1, reread Week 15; if it feels easy by then, the course worked
Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.): used selectively
Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics (free online): pendulum and MPC material
Original papers per method (DQN, PPO, SAC, CQL, CPO, DAgger): read the originals for methods you use in the project

Weekly reading assignments appear with the materials on the official university
course page.

index.title: RL in Robotics — Student Companion
index.content:
Reinforcement Learning in Robotics
240MAR45 · MSc in Automatic Control and Robotics · UPC Barcelona
This is the student companion site for the course: an interlinked knowledge base
of the core concepts. The materials themselves (slides, lecture notes, exercises,
code) are distributed on the official university course page, not here.


                  
                  How to use this site 
                  
                

Concepts are written to be self-contained and cross-linked. Start from
the unifying diagram below and follow the [[links]] by concept dependency,
not by lecture order. Use the search (top right) or the graph view to navigate.


The unifying diagram
Every method in this course lives in one cell of this table. The columns record
what you know about the dynamics; the rows record what the method explicitly
represents, i.e. which objects it actually stores and updates.


























Explicitly representsDynamics model availableNo dynamics model (interaction only)A value function (value-based)DP, value iteration, policy iteration, Riccati / LQRbandit algorithms ¶, TD learning, Q-learning, SARSA, DQN, LSTDA policy (policy-based)iLQR ‖REINFORCE, REINFORCE with a baselineBoth (actor-critic)MPC †Actor-critic, PPO §, DDPG, TD3, SAC, Dyna
‖ Direct trajectory optimisation is not on the grid. It stores an open-loop plan
\{u_0,\dots,u_{N-1}\} (numbers, not a function of state), so it represents no policy at
all. iLQR earns the cell: its backward pass leaves time-varying gains K_k, an explicit
local feedback law. Read the left column as one spectrum of how much policy is stored:
DP/LQR (a global policy, through V) → iLQR (a local law along one trajectory) → MPC (none
stored, recomputed online) → trajectory optimisation (none at all, one plan for one x_0).
¶ Bandit algorithms store one number per action, which is \hat Q(x,a) at the only state there
is, so they sit in the value row. They are the single occupied cell that approximates no Bellman
object. Without a successor state there is nothing to bootstrap from, and the update
\hat\mu \leftarrow \hat\mu + \alpha(r - \hat\mu) is an ordinary running average. Restoring the
successor state turns it into the temporal-difference update that drives the rest of the course.
† MPC represents a model and a terminal value function, but its policy is implicit,
recomputed online by solving an optimisation problem at every timestep, never stored.
§ PPO is a policy-gradient method by lineage, but the version everyone runs also fits a
value network on bootstrapped targets, so it represents both. The dividing line is
bootstrapping, not “has a value function”.
The columns are the ends of a spectrum, not a binary: robotics usually sits in
between, with a model partly known and partly learned.
Method names become links as their concept notes are published over the semester.
Course materials
Slides, lecture notes, exercises, and code are distributed on the official
university course page, released before each session.
Course information
Syllabus and course guide: schedule, assessment, the
cumulative project, software stack, and reading list.
Start here


Bellman equation — optimality as a fixed-point recursion; the foundation
underlying every method in the course.
Deadly triad: why function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy
learning together can diverge. Published with Week 7.
Failure modes of approximate RL: the six failure modes that organize the
second half of the course. Published with Week 7.

Studying with an AI assistant
This site is built to be AI-readable. To give your assistant (Claude Code,
Codex, ChatGPT, …) the full course context:

Best: clone the published site and run your assistant inside it, so that
the whole concept knowledge base works offline:
git clone github.com/AndreuCecilia/rl-robotics
Or point it at a single URL containing the full text of every published page:
andreucecilia.github.io/rl-robotics/llms-full.txt
(short index: /llms.txt · machine-readable: /static/contentIndex.json)



                  
                  Use it to understand, not to outsource 
                  
                

Ask your assistant to explain, quiz you, and check your derivations, rather than to
produce your exercise or milestone answers. Graded work is evaluated on your
depth of analysis, and the exams are written without an assistant:
understanding you didn’t build yourself won’t survive them.


Course framing
This course treats RL as approximate dynamic programming under uncertainty
about the dynamics. If you know LQR, Riccati, Bellman, and MPC, you already
have most of the scaffolding. RL fills in what to do when the model is unknown
or the state space is too large to solve exactly. RL is presented as one tool
among several, not a replacement for classical control.
